title: Comu’s Action Pro is a great meeting recorder that struggles to justify its AI premium
snippet: As my house becomes increasingly strewn with the detritus of parenting, I’ve made the inverse effort to eliminate excess, physical and digital, from my life. As much as it is about control, it’s also about mental health; I already use my phone too much, so adding yet another thing to the backpack, to the pocket, feels anything but additive. more…
fullText:
As my house becomes increasingly strewn with the detritus of parenting, I’ve made the inverse effort to eliminate excess, physical and digital, from my life. As much as it is about control, it’s also about mental health; I already use my phone too much, so adding yet another thing to the backpack, to the pocket, feels anything but additive.

But I’m also aware of the single-use gadget’s pull, increasingly powerful precisely because people are relying too much on their phones. Digicams to augment overly-processed smartphone photos. Writing tablets that feel like paper without the waste. Smart rings and health trackers to reduce notification overload.

And so it is with a product like the Comu Action Pro, a standalone note-taking gadget that attempts to turn a simple idea into something indispensable.

Pixel owners are likely well aware of the superlative built-in Recorder app that’s been around for years, adding features like real-time transcription and translation as it’s matured. The current app is about all you could want from a piece of software that leverages a phone’s built-in microphones.

	

It was with this framing that I undertook the review of a novel gadget category: the AI voice recorder. I’m not entirely unfamiliar with it: I’ve used early versions of Plaud’s NotePin and Note devices in the past, but never for long enough to feel acquainted with them. In response, I wanted to spend enough time with the Comu Action Pro to understand where and how it fits into my life, and why one may feel justified in spending the $180 it currently costs instead of just using the phone they already have in their pocket.

First, the basics: at a thickness of 7mm, it’s a svelte mixture of aluminum and plastic that’s designed to stick magnetically to the back of a compatible phone, like an iPhone or Pixel. (The box comes with a couple of circular magnetic stickers for devices without built-in MagSafe support.) That said, it’s nowhere close to the 3mm dimensions of the Plaud Note and Note Pro. But that additional girth comes with a few benefits: it fits a USB-C port, so you’re not forced to charge it with a proprietary magnetic cable that will almost certainly be missing when you need it most. And it carries a larger battery that pushes recording time to 70 hours, double that of the Plaud Note Pro.

The primary question I ask myself, and am asked by others, when I use the Comu Action Pro is, “Why?” Why do you need a separate piece of hardware when your phone will suffice, particularly in a world of inexpensive or free AI transcription services that can do most of the job? In short, it’s the passivity of it all; you can just leave the Action Pro running in the background whenever you’re going about your day to collect snippets of conversations, or covertly place it on a boardroom table to record a meeting.

The Action Pro has six far-field microphones that pick up voices from distances that phones are just not tuned for. That omnidirectional nature means the actual recordings sound thin and tinny, but the product is not the audio — it’s the data from the audio. Placing the Action Pro on the table in front of me next to my phone and recording the deliberately subdued tones of a conversation I was having showed the form factor’s inherent compromise; it picked up voices from the tables next to me, leading to audio that was basically unusable to listen to. Conversely, my Pixel 11 Pro did a great job isolating our two voices in the recording itself.

I was surprised, then, to discover the Action Pro transcribed our conversation with minimal errors. The company works with a number of AI vendors, including OpenAI and Google, and while it’s usually accurate, it made more errors than the competition.

It’s the “Action” in Comu’s Action Pro the company really wants to emphasize, and it’s what I believe has the largest potential — and the longest way to go to reach it. If you’ve ever used a cloud-based meeting recorder like Granola you’ll know that its primary job is to synthesize what it records into something compelling and useful, a summary that can lead to identifiable action items. From there you can ask it questions about the content or have it draft a follow-up email.

Comu’s Action Pro tries to go one step further by integrating with foundation models like Claude Opus 5 or GPT-5.6 Terra to turn those summaries into more than just emails; you can ask it to create a summary document or even a presentation, choosing from a number of predefined templates. All of this is done through the app, which is poorly designed, making for an awkward experience.

I’ll give you a small example: I had the Comu Action Pro record all 20 minutes of a YouTube video that was playing at a pretty comfortable volume from my Mac Mini’s thin but capable internal speaker. It was a video I watched doing research for this review, attempting to grasp the scope of the AI note taking market, since I’d really only ever heard of and used Plaud’s products.

As a baseline, I also used my Pixel 11 Pro’s Recorder app alongside a Plaud Note. All three were sitting four or so inches from the speaker and there was little ambient noise in the room. After the recording was finished, I compared the transcripts of each recorder for accuracy, and then delved into the post-production aspects of each product. For full transparency, here are links to both Comu’s and Plaud’s outputs from that recording:

Summaries are good on both, but Plaud’s are neater and better organized.

Plaud’s transcript is slightly more accurate.

Ironically, the Action Pro kept referring to Plaud as “Plot” throughout, though that can be traced to the word’s pronunciation by the host.

Plaud’s output included a mind map and a summary image, whereas Comu’s was text-only.

Comu’s custom documents and presentations are basic, hard to read, and rarely useful as standalone assets.

The Comu app is buggy and, in places, poorly translated into English.

The Comu web app is basically unusable in its current state.

The issue I keep returning to is that the Action Pro really only solves a real-world problem. While you can attach it to the back of the phone to record both sides of a conversation (with consent, of course), there’s no mechanism to record or sync web-based meetings. Plaud, being the more mature product, boasts a much better app, a usable web interface, and a desktop app that records and transcribes video calls, usage of which is included even in the free Starter plan.

Comu’s best features are also gated behind a subscription. Unlike Plaud, which provides access to most features for free but limits transcription minutes to 300 on the free Starter tier, Comulytic goes the other way, offering unlimited transcriptions indefinitely and putting its AI workflows, including translation and document generation, behind a $10/month paywall. Access to Anthropic’s Claude model is also limited to paid subscriptions.

Those are the actions meant to be solved by the dedicated AI button that sits above the record button which, when pressed, acts like a voice-powered agent for your work needs. Anything recorded when the button is pressed goes into a general ChatGPT-like stream, where the data source is the transcribed meeting notes. Unfortunately, that’s where the “Action” part of the Action Pro breaks down: the Comu agent is brittle, and doesn’t interface with other parts of the phone. 

For instance, there’s a “Schedule Tasks” prompt that Comu invites you to use, and tapping it pre-fills a number of templates, including “Schedule a deep work block for this week.” I completed the prompt and wrote “Schedule a deep work block for this Friday from 1 to 5 PM,” but at the moment the model isn’t able to connect to my external calendar. 

In fact, as of writing, every calendar- and task-based connection is listed as “Coming soon.” Once these connections are added, Comu’s offering may be more competitive, but given the proliferation of similar services like Gemini Spark, Meta Muse, Town, Poke, and many others, I’m doubtful that most users will be willing to shell out the monthly fee that Comu is asking for.

At its core, the Action Pro is a competent meeting transcriber with some impressive hardware and lackluster software that, at least right now, doesn’t justify its asking price. If you’re looking for something from the company that’s thinner, lighter, and cheaper, and still has some AI capabilities, Comu’s own Note Pro is a decent alternative at under $120. If you need something a bit more full-featured, including better web and desktop support, I’d go with something from Plaud.

					

A competent meeting recorder and digital note taker whose ambitions to be an AI project manager don’t quite work.

Great audio transcription quality

											

Good build quality

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

App is a mess

											

AI features are half-baked or missing entirely

fullText:
Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

The White House claims the Donald Trump-owned Truth Social is the “most powerful and popular social media platform in the world.” The statement, provided to The New York Times by White House spokesperson Davis Ingle, is at odds with the user counts from some of the biggest social media platforms on the web.

Data gathered by Search Engine Land shows YouTube is the most popular platform in the world, with 2.65 billion monthly active users. Facebook comes in second with 2.39 billion active users around the globe, followed by TikTok with 2.21 billion and Instagram with 1.99 billion. Truth Social doesn’t make Search Engine Land’s top 10 list, which shows Elon Musk’s X and Meta’s Threads at the bottom with 450 million and 223 million users, respectively. Even those platforms trail Pinterest, which is listed with 579 million global users.

Truth Social’s traffic appears to be declining. As reported by the NYT, data from Similarweb suggests that the number of monthly visitors to Truth Social dipped 36 percent in July compared to the same time last year. From January to July 2025, an average of 28 million people visited Truth Social each month, while this number fell to 25 million during the first seven months of 2026, according to the NYT. Last month, Truth Social launched its $100,000 / month subscription to gain early access to posts from Trump and other prominent users, raising concerns about corruption.

The NYT report details Trump’s posting patterns on Truth Social, which often include AI-generated images, such as one showing his head on Hulk Hogan’s body and another hitting a cut-out of Iran with a hammer brandishing the American flag. Ingle cites President Trump’s “authentic voice” as the reason for the platform’s so-called popularity, adding it’s where “he communicates directly with the American people and the world without the biased media taking him out of context.”

A justice asked, ‘Counsel, do you watch the news?’ when a lawyer admitted to relying on ChatGPT without understanding the risks.

by  Emma Roth

Sep 11, 2026, 8:44 PM UTC

Illustration by Cath Virginia / The Verge | Photos from Getty Images

Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

New Mexico’s Supreme Court is punishing a lawyer for including AI-fabricated witnesses and fake police testimony in an appeal for his client’s murder conviction, according to a report from Reuters. In a filing on Wednesday, the court fined Stephen Aarons $5,000 and held him in contempt for failing to “verify the factual claims and legal authority in his AI-generated brief.”

The filing says the brief “contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses,” along with “false testimony” about the shooter’s clothing and appearance. Justice C. Shannon Bacon questioned how Aarons wasn’t aware of the risks posed by AI during an August hearing, where he admitted to using ChatGPT and thinking it would generate a “bulletproof summary” of the trial. “Counsel, do you watch the news? Do you ​listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what’s going on in the world?” Justice Bacon said, according to Reuters. “Because the problem with ​lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an above-the-fold story every single day.”

With the number of lawyers using AI tools in their work increasing, so are the instances in which a court discovers citations that are fabricated — or hallucinated — by AI. Last year, a judge slammed two law firms for submitting a brief with “numerous false, inaccurate, and misleading legal citations and quotations,” while lawyers for MyPillow’s Mike Lindell were also fined for putting AI-generated misquotes and fake AI citations in a brief.

”I am remorseful but hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake,” Aarons says in a statement to Reuters.

title: Over 153 Million Driver’s Licenses Were Stolen by Hackers. Here’s What to Know
snippet: The hackers allegedly spent a year hoarding documents before IDScan closed the door.
fullText:
If you’ve used your driver’s license to verify your information either in the real world or online, there’s a chance that some of your driver’s license information was stolen by hackers in a security breach against the ID verification giant IDScan that was reportedly active for a year.

“On or around Sept. 1, 2026, IDScan.net received information indicating that certain data may have been accessed without authorization,” IDScan said in a statement on Sept. 4. “Upon this discovery, we took immediate steps to secure our systems and engaged a team of third-party specialists to help determine the full nature and scope of the incident.”

The hack is discussed in more detail by Brian Krebs, a security researcher who runs the website Krebs on Security. He says he was first made aware of the breach after a source alerted him to a post on a Russian cybercrime forum from a hacker offering digital scans of identity documents for more than 170 million people from a service called Nexus.

Krebs was able to access Nexus and verify that it did indeed have the documents it said it had, including a scan of his own driver’s license.

The data includes 153 million driver’s licenses, 10 million ID cards, 3 million travel documents like passports and, according to Krebs, “at least 579,000” medical cards. Most of these records are for US residents, but about 1.1 million Canadian driver’s licenses were also found.

Per IDScan, hackers weren’t able to get every piece of information from those documents, but most likely obtained full names, driver’s license numbers and government-issued ID numbers. 

The hackers who ran Nexus boasted that they had obtained the information by “continuously exfiltrating new data for over a year” into a private database from “a major identity verification company.”

The data collected likely came from a range of sources. Krebs says the leak of his information could have resulted from renting a car from Hertz, which uses IDScan to verify driver’s licenses. Other companies named on IDScan’s website as customers included FedEx, GameStop and over 1,000 cannabis dispensaries, car rental agencies and gun shops across 19 states. A screenshot of IDScan’s website also included Target as a customer, and a representative for Target told CNET that while the retailer uses some of IDScan’s hardware, it did not transmit customer data to IDScan and Target customer data was not included in a data breach. IDScan reported that it scanned 150 million IDs in 2024 alone.

The New Orleans field office of the FBI is investigating the matter. The FBI has not responded to a request for comment. 

Here’s what you can do

IDScan says it will notify everyone who was affected by the breach and “provide access to free credit monitoring and identity protection services” for those people. If you end up being one of them, IDScan says to contact it at 1-833-516-2980 (Monday-Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET) to enroll in those services. 

Those concerned they may have been affected have a few options. The easiest and quickest is a credit freeze, which makes it much more difficult for cybercriminals to open new accounts in your name. CNET has a guide for that if you need help. Freezing your credit is free, but it requires you to set up individual accounts with the three major credit bureaus. 

Since cybercrime can strike anywhere and at any time, it’s also good to follow some tips to keep yourself safe, including using strong passwords, familiarizing yourself with the latest AI-powered phishing scams and considering using a VPN to help obfuscate your online presence so you can’t be tracked. 

The unfortunate reality is that cybersecurity breaches are getting bigger, and companies are telling consumers less about what’s happening, so it’s worth staying vigilant, even if your driver’s license wasn’t stolen.

title: Jensen Huang explains why Nvidia will grow an astounding 70% next year
snippet: Nvidia has its finger in every pie, and sees another year of plenty in its future, Jensen Huang says. But, he insists, its deals are not circular.
fullText:
Founder, CEO, and tireless Nvidia hype man Jensen Huang told attendees at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology conference on Thursday why his company’s AI domination — and revenues — will continue its record-breaking growth streak through the end of next year.

He can see the future. 

There’s been endless hand-wringing over whether Nvidia’s party will end as it faces increasing competition for GPUs and AI chips from all directions: the hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, each building their own) and the AI labs (Anthropic and OpenAI, which are building their own), as well as from newly public competitor Cerebras and startups such as Etched.

“Most people think Nvidia builds a chip. I mean, you need airplanes to ship what we build,” Huang said, adding that the company continues to battle a perception from its early days. Nvidia invented the GPU, which back then were largely sold to consumers to improve PC gaming. “One GPU now is not $399. It’s $8.5 million dollars. That’s one GPU, all connected with NVLink, 2 million parts, right? 250,000 kilowatts. That’s a GPU, and we ship thousands of them.”

He added that orders for just one product, a computer system that combines 36 Grace CPUs with 72 Blackwell GPUs, is currently experiencing 27% month-to-month sales growth.

Huang didn’t limit his bullish view to current sales though. He took the opportunity to reiterate Nvidia’s revenue outlook for next year — guidance the company provided last month when it reported yet another record-breaking revenue quarter. That’s when he first said revenue could grow by 70% next year.

“I think we could grow 70% year over year. We’re confident about that,” Huang said again on Thursday. Analysts expect the company to end its current fiscal year at about $400 billion in revenue. So 70% growth would mean around $680 billion next year.  

Huang explained why he’s confident: His company is so embedded in every area of AI that he believes he can see the future.

“Nvidia runs every model. Every single lab can use us,” the CEO said, mentioning that this includes models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, as well as open-weight offerings. “We are a foundational platform of the AI ecosystem, foundational platform of the AI industry.”

Nvidia’s fingers extend all the way from its suppliers, such as memory chip makers, to data center projects and startups. 

“We’re tracking every single gigawatt of land, power, shell around the world. Literally everything on the planet,” he said. (“Shell” refers to the shell of a data center building before it is outfitted with computers).

“I mean, just think about all my partners. How many neoclouds are reporting back to us? How many OEMs are reporting back to us? How many clouds are reporting back to us? How many AI-native companies are reporting back to us? We’re working with everybody, and so we kind of know where everything is,” he said.

That comment led to inevitable questions about Nvidia’s so-called circular deals, in which it invests in companies that turn around and buy its wares. Such schemes famously contributed to the downfall of a previous generation of internet build-out suppliers like Lucent Technologies.

Huang had a simple, albeit cheeky, response. “Well, it’s not circular because we put a little bit of money in, and a lot of money comes back.” He went on to joke, “I look at the spreadsheet, we put in $1 and $100 comes back in. Is that circular? If that is, let’s do more of that.”

Quips aside, he insisted that before any of these companies gets an investment, Nvidia makes sure it has real contracts generating revenue from customers. All told, he said he’s seen $100 billion worth of such contracts, “I’m not taking any risks. … I need a sure thing.”

Time will tell whether Nvidia’s stronghold on AI can really persist long term. If there’s one golden rule of the tech industry, it’s that all big things get disrupted. Right now, even Huang admits that much of AI’s growth is coming from AI-native startups that are raising vast sums and spending most of that cash on their own AI use. As the AI industry matures, expect companies to become more efficient in how they use infrastructure and tokens.

But for now, Nvidia has its finger in every pie and sees another year of plenty in its future.

title: Siri AI is coming: Here are three times it’s really impressed me so far
snippet: Siri AI launches next week in iOS 27, and it’s a huge upgrade to Apple’s assistant. There are tons of ways Siri is new and improved, but here are three examples of times Siri has impressed me so far. more…
fullText:
Siri AI launches next week in iOS 27, and it’s a huge upgrade to Apple’s assistant. There are tons of ways Siri is new and improved, but here are three examples of times Siri has impressed me so far.

#1: Adding NFL games to my calendar

It’s football season again, and every year when the NFL schedule comes out, I go through the tedious but important work of adding games to my calendar.

Sometimes the NFL provides a .ics file to make this a little easier. But it can still be convoluted to do this from my iPhone, and doesn’t typically include the info I want.

So this year, I tried using Siri AI—and it was a big time saver.

I asked Siri to find all the Dallas Cowboys games and add them to my calendar. Yes, I’m a fan of America’s Team, and I’ll accept your pity.

In my request, I specified that Siri should include info on where each game will be available to stream. NFL games these days can air on FOX One, Paramount+, Peacock, Prime Video, ESPN, or even Netflix. It’s a lot to keep up with.

Impressively, Siri did exactly what I wanted. All the games were put on my calendar like I wanted, with info on how to watch.

#2: Finding my vehicle license plate info

Just last week, I was filling out a form online that asked for my vehicle license plate number.

I don’t have my license plate memorized, and my wife had the car with her at the time. But I was pretty sure I had a photo or some other record of the plate number somewhere on my iPhone.

I asked Siri: “Can you find my current license plate number?”

Within a few seconds, it came back with the answer. My plate number was included, along with a link to an email where Siri found the number. It was in a registration renewal email—which I didn’t even remember having.

#3: Apple Watch band size

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 went on sale right after the September event earlier this week (you can pre-order here: Series 12, Ultra 4).

I’ve opted for an Apple Watch Series 12 this year, and initially was looking to get a Braided Solo Loop band. I had one a few years ago and really loved it.

Though I ultimately opted for a different band, I did hit a roadblock when browsing the Solo Loop options: I didn’t remember my size.

Unlike most Apple Watch bands, you need to select a very specific size for the Solo Loop to ensure a good fit. And in the rush of trying to get my pre-order in, I didn’t want to be delayed by a size test. 

So instead, I told Siri that I’d purchased an Apple Watch before with a Solo Loop and was trying to find my size. It located the info in an old note I’d saved years ago. Like the license plate discovery, I didn’t even remember that such a note existed.

Siri AI wrap-up

	

Siri can do much more than the few things I’ve mentioned above. For example, I use it all the time for world knowledge questions that I previously would have asked ChatGPT or Google Gemini. 

But these three use cases highlight a core advantage Siri now has: tapping into your personal data in an intelligent and privacy-friendly way.

title: Google Gemini’s New Windows Desktop App Is Here
snippet: Certain Gemini features require a paid subscription.
fullText:
Google has released a Windows desktop version of its Gemini AI technology, bringing tools like image generation and AI search into an app that runs on Windows 10 or Windows 11.

The company released a similar desktop-native app for Mac back in April and has been adding new features to it, including more voice capabilities and screen awareness.

In a blog post about the new app, Google touted its ease of access. Once installed, the Gemini app can be launched by pressing Alt and the spacebar on Windows. The AI models you have access to in the app depend on your paid Google subscription tier. For instance, Gemini Spark, the company’s AI agent software, is only available if you’re 18 or older and have a Gemini AI subscription.

What’s available in the app

In our testing, using a paid, non-AI Google Workspace account, we had the option to use Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.6 Flash, 3.1 Pro and a toggle for “Extended thinking,” which Google says is for complex problem-solving.

For images, the app uses Nano Banana. Video generation is available with a Google AI subscription using Gemini Omni. That also requires you to be 18 or older. 

If you’ve used Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT apps, the design will look very familiar, with a left sidebar for chats and a search bar as the main interface. You can create notebooks for group chats with Gemini Notebook and access documents or media created in the Library section. Google Docs and Gmail can be connected to the app to access documents or emails.

Google said in an email to CNET that it will continue to roll out new features for the desktop app over time.

Apple today unveiled AirPods 5, available to order now starting at just $129, the new version of its entry-level AirPods. 

The biggest takeaway is that — among a sea of Apple price increases — the new AirPods are actually cheaper than ever, despite coming with Active Noise Cancellation as standard, and a few other niceties. Here’s what’s new compared to the outgoing AirPods 4 …

There are two models of AirPods 5, AirPods 5 and AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case. This replaces the old lineup of AirPods 4 and AirPods with ANC models.

We’ll cover the differences in the AirPods 5 line a bit further down, but first here’s what’s new across both models compared to AirPods 5.

Upgraded active noise cancellation

Active noise cancellation is now available on all AirPods 5 models. Customers previously had to spend $179 for AirPods 4 with noise cancellation included, but that is now standard with AirPods 5. So if noise cancellation in an open-ear design is what you cared about most, you just saved $50 compared to the same AirPods options a week ago. 

Apple also says that the quality of noise cancellation on AirPods 5 is greatly improved, up to 50 percent better compared to AirPods 4. AirPods 5 noise cancellation uses new algorithms and a new acoustic architecture to achieve this. 

Apple claims AirPods 5 offer the best noise cancellation of any earbuds that rest on the ear. (AirPods Pro will still offer the world’s best noise cancellation overall, thanks to their in-ear design with plastic tips that physically plug the ear).

More natural Transparency mode

As well as noise cancellation, Apple has also improved the quality of Transparency mode compared to AirPods 4. Transparency mode helps the user hear the sounds of the world around them, as if their headphones were not in their ears. On AirPods 5, Transparency mode more naturally represents the sounds of voices and nearby environmental sounds.

Improved sound quality 

Based on the learnings from AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 5 feature a richer, more detailed sound profile compared to AirPods 4. This is enabled through hardware changes, like the new multiport acoustic system as well as next-generation Adaptive EQ. The acoustic architecture enables Apple to deliver sound more precisely to a range of human ear shapes and sizes, dynamically adjusting how the audio is delivered on the fly for best results.

Better water and dust resistance 

Apple has also updated the durability of the AirPods when it comes to water, dust and sweat resistance. The old AirPods 4 had an IP54 rating. The new AirPods 5 boast an IP57 rating, which should make them survive better when exposed to water and the elements, although still not waterproof. 

Lower price with ANC included 

All of the above new features are included with AirPods 5, priced at just $129. This is the same price as AirPods 4, except now you get all the active noise cancellation features in the base model. The upgraded AirPods 5 is priced at $149, which is $30 less than the old higher-end AirPods 4 option.

What do you get if you upgrade to AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case

For the jump from $129 to $149, you get a few niceties although nothing dramatic. Firstly, the AirPods come with a wireless charging case, supporting both Qi chargers and the Apple Watch charging puck. It also integrates a speaker for use with Find My.

Secondly, you actually get better battery life if you opt for the $149 model. The base $129 configuration offers the same 4 hours of listening time with ANC enabled as the AirPods 4, but the $149 model offers an extra hour of listening on a single charge. Including the case, that means 22 hours of total listening time. 

Thirdly, new with AirPods with Wireless Charging Case is a fan-favorite feature from AirPods Pro: the addition of the volume swipe gesture on the stem. This lets you raise or lower the volume just with a quick swipe on the earbud, without needing to reach for your phone or use Siri.

It’s up to you whether these differences are worth the extra $20 at checkout, but nevertheless, it still represents much better value overall than the equivalent AirPods 4 lineup. After today’s introduction, Active Noise Cancellation is now available at a $50 lower price point … and even the more expensive model is still $30 less than AirPods 4.

AirPods 5 are available to pre-order right now from the Apple Store, with first deliveries shipping on September 18.

title: Samsung has just one piece of advice for Apple’s first iPhone foldable
snippet: Samsung has been pushing the foldable market ahead for several years now and, arguably, makes some of the best foldable devices out there. But Apple is about to make its long-awaited debut with the first iPhone foldable, and Samsung has some advice. more…
fullText:
Samsung has been pushing the foldable market ahead for several years now and, arguably, makes some of the best foldable devices out there. But Apple is about to make its long-awaited debut with the first iPhone foldable, and Samsung has some advice.

Speaking to Wired, Samsung’s Hee-Cheul Moon, head of the company’s Advanced Mechanical R&D group, and Seungki Choi, head of Smartphone R&D group, discussed Apple’s incoming debut on the market. Samsung’s sentiment towards an Apple foldable hasn’t changed since last year – it’s “absolutely welcome” as Apple will bring some much-needed attention and legitimacy to the foldable space.

Moon says:

Seeing these other brands entering the market, we feel very proud of ourselves that the value that we pioneered with this new category of foldables is being acknowledged and recognized. 

Weight is a key aspect that Samsung is focused on, though, with Moon saying that the key “to providing the highest customer value in this market is all about the weight of the device.” Samsung has cut a huge amount of weight out of its foldables since the first generation, with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 weighing in at just 201g, less than even most slab smartphone flagships. Galaxy S26 Ultra weighs 214g, for example. Meanwhile, as Wired points out, Apple’s foldable is expected to weigh around 230-241g while the iPhone 17 Pro Max weighs 233g.

	

Samsung has certainly figured out a lot over the years from its foldables, but thickness and weight are perhaps the biggest improvements you’ll find if you pick up an older generation and compare it to the latest models. 

With Apple’s first foldable iPhone – apparently called “iPhone Duo” – set to have the same core form factor as the Galaxy Z Fold 8, these two devices are set to battle. Apple is expected to be a major player in the foldable space within a year or so, despite Android’s major head start in this market. 

All will be revealed later today – stay tuned to our sister site 9to5Mac for more!

title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 unveiled with upgraded health tracking system
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are official. Apple has announced its two new Apple Watch models as part of its product event today. An upgraded health tracking system is key to both models. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are official. Apple has announced its two new Apple Watch models as part of its product event today. An upgraded health tracking system is key to both models.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 details

While both new models feature a familiar design, an upgraded heart rate monitor is key to the new health sensing system. 

For example, the new system now measures heart rate data every five seconds, a 60x frequency increase over previous models. 

Apple is also measuring HRV every five minutes. The new system is called the most accurate heart rate sensor in a wearable, according to Apple. 

Apple is also introducing a new readiness feature. This is based on activity, vitals, and sleep data.

Readiness is a new feature based on activity, vitals, and sleep data

Audio Intelligence

Additionally, Apple is adding a new Audio Intelligence feature to Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.

This includes sound recognition, like doorbells. There’s also a “live rewind” feature that lets you go back 15 seconds to transcribe what someone just said. It’s invoked by double-clicking the Digital Crown, which used to be multitasking.

Apple has published a new support document that details what audio intelligence does and how it works.

Siri recaps is another new feature. When enabled, it can summarize things like meetings, based on audio notes. Apple Watch also gains a new Siri Modular face as part of the new system.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 run on Apple’s new S11 chip. It includes A20 Pro-derived CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine components.

Colors, prices, availability

Colors include space gray, black, light gold, and bronze aluminum. Ceramic Shield 2 protects the front glass.

Radiant gold and natural make up the polished titanium finishes. Ceramic returns in pearl white and a new dark blue option. Hermes adds gold to the lineup.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 includes a larger battery with over two days of battery life. Black and natural titanium remain the two finish options. There’s also a new titanium band. 

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are available for pre-order from today. Both launch on September 18. Pricing remains the same as the Series 11 and Ultra 3, from $399 and $799, respectively.

Here’s the official Apple Watch Series 12 press release. Apple Watch Ultra 4 has its own press release as well.

title: iPhone 18 Pro can authenticate that your photo wasn’t edited with AI
snippet: Apple is introducing a new Reference Image feature as part of the new iPhone 18 Pro, which digitally authenticates that the image you took with the camera has not been altered later by AI. If edits have been made, users can see the ‘digital negative’ original and compare the differences. This is Apple’s answer to the rise of synthetic AI-generated imagery. Reference Image ensures that people looking at your photos know if it reflects the true reality or not. more…
fullText:
Apple is introducing a new Reference Image feature as part of the new iPhone 18 Pro, which digitally authenticates that the image you took with the camera has not been altered later by AI. If edits have been made, users can see the ‘digital negative’ original and compare the differences.

This is Apple’s answer to the rise of synthetic AI-generated imagery. Reference Image ensures that people looking at your photos know if it reflects the true reality or not.

Reference Image incorporates Apple Private Cloud Compute to sends some details about the photo you take with the iPhone 18 Pro lenses, essentially creating a cryptographic signature. 

The Reference Image indicators are not just limited to showing on the phone you took them with. You can also share the signed images with other people, including the reference signatures for later authentication.

Apple Reference Image will not be available in the European Union or China. 

For Apple’s image generation features, including Image Playgrounds or the new Apple Intelligence editing tools like Extend and Spatial Reframe, the generated images will include SynthID markers.

title: Apple shares more details about Apple Intelligence usage limits and terms
snippet: Apple today published a new support article that provides more detail on Apple Intelligence usage terms, limits, and restrictions. Here’s what the company says. more…
fullText:
Apple today published a new support article that provides more detail on Apple Intelligence usage terms, limits, and restrictions. Here’s what the company says.

A bit of context

When Apple first announced the new Apple Intelligence during WWDC26, the company said “some images, including image generation,” would have usage limits, because “they rely on powerful server models.”

The company added that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans and would also include Apple Intelligence support for compatible home cameras.

Earlier today, Apple reaffirmed these limitations during the “Surprise and Shine” event. However, it didn’t offer further details on what those limits will be or how much additional access iCloud+ subscribers will get.

Now, the company has published a new support article titled “Learn about Apple Intelligence usage limits,” where it goes into more detail on these limitations.

‘Increased access will be available for a fee’

According to Apple, the following features will rely on server-side models and may be subject to usage limits:

Siri AI

Intelligent Photo Editing Tools including Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing

Image Playground

AFM 3 Cloud and AFM 3 Cloud Pro Models in Shortcuts

Developer apps using Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute

Apple says that it will implement usage limits on these and other Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features “in the future,” but does not offer specifics on what those limits will look like or when they will take effect.

The company does confirm, however, that once users reach those limits, the affected features will become unavailable for a period of time before access is restored.

Apple also notes that the limits themselves won’t necessarily be the same across features, but that users will be able to pay for increased access:

Limits may vary by feature, request complexity, system demand, system policies, and other factors. Increased access to such features will be available for a fee.

As for the Apple Intelligence features that will work with home cameras, the company says:

Some Apple Intelligence features in the Home app, such as video summaries, are available for a limited number of cameras depending on your iCloud+ plan — up to 1 camera in the 2 TB plan, up to 2 cameras in the 6 TB plan, and up to 5 cameras in the 12 TB plan. Supported camera counts and other iCloud+ plan features may change over time.

Apple adds that both Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage will be subject to the Apple Intelligence Usage Terms, which also outline restrictions on excessive or abusive use, availability and device requirements, age restrictions, and how Apple may enforce violations.

Here are two of the most relevant tidbits:

Unreasonable Use

Excessive, abusive, automated, fraudulent, illegal or otherwise unreasonable use, including use that materially impacts service availability or other users, may be restricted, throttled, suspended, or subject to additional limits. We may determine what constitutes unreasonable use based on factors including usage volume, frequency, request complexity, system demand, and patterns of use.

Enforcement

Apple reserves the right to investigate and take action against any use that violates these Usage Terms, including restricting, suspending, or terminating access to Apple Intelligence Features. Apple may update these Usage Terms from time to time, and continued use of Apple Intelligence after changes constitutes acceptance of the updated Usage Terms.

snippet: The No. 2 exec at OpenAI also led Instacart through its IPO in 2023.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

9:46 AM PDT · September 11, 2026

Image Credits:David Paul Morris/Bloomberg / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Nscale, the buzzy U.K.-based AI data center startup, has appointed former OpenAI, Meta, and Instacart executive Fidji Simo to its board.

Simo joins high-profile tech executives Sheryl Sandberg, Susan Decker, and Nick Clegg on Nscale’s board ahead of the startup’s anticipated IPO this fall.

Formerly CEO of AGI deployment at OpenAI, essentially the No. 2 executive at the AI lab, Simo left the company in July citing health reasons. She still advises the company on a part-time basis. Before OpenAI, Simo was chair and CEO of Instacart, where she led the company through its 2023 IPO. She also spent more than a decade at Meta, including as head of the Facebook app. Simo also sits on Shopify’s board.

Nscale’s founder and CEO, Josh Payne, said Simo is one of the few leaders who understand what it means to scale products used by billions of people and the demands those products place on the underlying systems.

“That’s what we’re building for at Nscale,” he said in a statement. “Fidji joins a board we’ve built deliberately, with the experience of scaling platforms to the largest in the world, and the independence, financial rigor and operating depth to which companies at this scale are held.”

Nscale’s valuation has skyrocketed since it was founded just two years ago on the back of booming demand for AI infrastructure. The startup, which designs, builds, and operates AI data centers, is reportedly trying to raise up to $3.5 billion ahead of a planned IPO, Bloomberg reported last week, citing unnamed sources.

title: Google Chrome starts two-week release cycle with version 153
snippet: As previewed earlier this year, Google Chrome is now operating on a two-week release cycle. more…
fullText:
As previewed earlier this year, Google Chrome is now operating on a two-week release cycle.

Previously, Chrome received a major “milestone” update — like going from version 100 to 101 — every four weeks. Before 2021, Google had a six-week cycle.

The aim of releasing big updates every two weeks is to deliver “new features, performance improvements, and bug fixes faster.” Less is included with each update, but that will be paired with the increased frequency.

Meanwhile, Google says this “increased cadence is a win for the entire web.” Developers will be able to “ship modern web features with confidence, knowing that deployment windows are tighter, interoperability updates arrive quickly, and safety improvements reach users faster across platforms.” The fact that the “scope per release is smaller” will make “regression isolation faster.”

	

On the security front, Google says this change will “protect against fast-moving threats” given the rise of AI.

For enterprise customers, Chrome offers the “Extended Stable” channel that updates in eight-week increments: Chrome 156 followed by version 160. Google says most enterprise users should be on the two-week Stable option.

Chrome 153 is rolling out starting today for desktop, Android, and iOS. Meanwhile, version 154 will be available on September 22.

title: iPhone Air’s $200 premium disappears when you trade it in
snippet: Following the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo announcement this week, Apple has started accepting iPhone Air and iPhone 17 trade-ins for credit. However, the iPhone Air offer is a bit of a sore spot, especially after this week’s price increases. more…
fullText:
Following the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo announcement this week, Apple has started accepting iPhone Air and iPhone 17 trade-ins for credit. However, the iPhone Air offer is a bit of a sore spot, especially after this week’s price increases.

Apple usually waits for a new version of an iPhone to come out before accepting trade-ins. That’s not the case for the iPhone Air and iPhone 17. There’s no iPhone Air 2 or iPhone 18 yet. We expect to see these new models early next year at the soonest.

But Apple does want to give iPhone Air and iPhone 17 users a chance to upgrade to an iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo. For that reason, both models still being sold by Apple without newer versions are eligible for trade-in. 

For the iPhone 17, which now starts at $899 after a $100 price increase this week, Apple offers up to $585.

iPhone Air also saw a $100 price increase this week, bringing the starting price to $1099. And what does the $200 premium over the iPhone 17 net you in trade-in? The same $585 offer. Ouch. 

Apple’s trade-in value table almost makes it look like a $100 error. In reality, Apple is probably basing it on demand and the value of parts. That’s too bad, considering the iPhone Air uses almost the same chip as the iPhone 17 Pro. 

To recap, iPhone Air’s value went up $100 for new customers. However, iPhone Air’s trade-in value, at least according to Apple, is the same as a $200 cheaper model. Not great, Bob.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 4: Clash of the Newest Apple Watches
snippet: The newest Apple smartwatches have premium features — and prices to match.
fullText:
At its Surprise & Shine event on Sept. 9, Apple revealed its newest devices, including its latest smartwatches. Here’s how the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 compare.

The new Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are premium wearables running the company’s WatchOS 27 software, which have plenty of features that interact with paired iPhones and a growing number that work even when apart (handy when out on a run). The Series 12 is the standard model, while the Ultra 4 is the higher-end version with more durability and features.

This year, the Apple Watches got more software upgrades than hardware upgrades, but one important thing that didn’t change with either was the price. Whereas the iPhones all got price bumps (even the older models Apple still sells), the Apple Watch Series 12 still starts at $400 and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 at $800. Both models can be preordered now and ship on Sept. 18.

Note that while the Ultra 4 only has its titanium finish (and can be pricier with fancier bands), the Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $400 for 42mm in aluminum finish, jumps to $699 for titanium and tops out at $899 for its new ceramics case material.  

Here’s how Apple’s latest smartwatches compare.

	

		

	

									

									

						

	

				

			Apple/CNET		

	

		

							

											

							$399 (Save with trade-in)						

											

							Apple Watch Series 12 at Best Buy						

									

			

	

			

			

				Get it now			

		

					
			

				

The latest 42mm Apple Watch Series 12 is available for preorder at Best Buy for $399. If you have an older device, you can trade it in for a new one at a lower price. Every purchase also comes with up to four free months of Apple Fitness and three free months of Apple Music.

			

		

	

		

	

									

									

						

	

				

			Apple/CNET		

	

		

							

											

							From $799 (Save with freebies)						

											

							Apple Watch Ultra 4 at Best Buy						

									

			

	

			

			

				Get it now			

		

					
			

				

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is available for preorder at Best Buy for $799. The preorder comes with a few freebies, including four free months of Apple Fitness Plus and three free months of Apple Music. You can choose to pick it up in store on the release date or have it shipped to arrive by the release date, so you can start using your new watch as soon as it’s released.

			

		

	

			

Design and display

The Apple Watch Series 12 looks practically identical to its predecessor, the Apple Watch Series 11 released in 2025, with a rectangular OLED display (up to 2,000 nits brightness) and rounded edges. The 42mm and 46mm sizes return along with aluminum and titanium body versions — as well as a new ceramic material (returning from the Apple Watch 5 in 2019) that adds a hair more size and about 10g of weight. For a comparison, the 42mm aluminum model is 32.2g, the titanium is 36.5g and the pearl white color of ceramic is 41.7g (the night blue hue of ceramic is 42.8g). 

The Apple Watch Series 12 comes in a variety of colors depending on the case material. For aluminum, you can pick between dark bronze, light gold, black and space gray. Titanium comes in radiant gold and natural hues, while the ceramic comes in pearl white and night blue. 

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 in both colors with different watch bands.Vanessa Hand Orellana/CNET

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 likewise looks identical to its predecessor, with a larger, rectangular OLED Retina display that stretches flat to the watch’s edges. It still only comes in the 49mm size and titanium body. The bigger size makes room for a customizable Action button. The Ultra 4 comes in natural and black case colors.

The sensor array on the underside of both watches has been redesigned to increase the surface area for readings, but most folks won’t notice — until they realize the watch can take heart rate readings every 5 seconds, compared to roughly every 5 minutes on older models.

Both watches are rated IP6X for dust resistance, but while the Apple Watch Series 12 is water resistant to 50 meters — “swimproof,” according to Apple — the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is water resistant to 100 meters and rated for recreational scuba diving to 40 meters. It’s also tested to MIL-STD 81H to continue functioning at altitude, in high and low temperatures, frozen and thawed, in ice and freezing rain and through shock and vibration.  

Given how similar the models are to their predecessors, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the superior model in display size and durability, surviving more extreme conditions. At literally twice the base price of the Apple Watch Series 12, though, you’ll be paying for this privilege.

The Apple Watch Series 12, in gold titanium (left) and bronze aluminum (right).Vanessa Hand Orellana/CNET

Specs and battery life

Both watches run the S11 chip, the newest Apple wearable silicon that enables features such as the every-5-second heart rate readings. They also have 64GB of onboard storage apiece, which can be used to save music and other media or app data such as hiking trails, though a good portion is reserved for the operating system.

Battery life is another area in which the watches strongly diverge. Apple shares battery life estimates rather than battery capacities. The Apple Watch Series 12 lasts about 24 hours, or 38 hours in Low Power Mode. The Ultra 4 extends its lead over its predecessor, offering up to 50 hours of battery life, compared with 42 hours for the Ultra 3. That can be expanded up to 84 hours on Low Power mode. 

While both watches have Low Power modes to last longer in the day, the Ultra 4 has two additional versions specifically tuned for workouts. The Extended Workout mode can track a workout for up to 25 hours by shutting off the always-on display and the running-form metrics while still tracking GPS and heart rate. If somehow 25 hours isn’t enough, there’s a Max Extended Workout mode that lasts up to 48 hours, though the tradeoff is dropping from multiband to single-band GPS and slowing heart rate readings to a 5-minute average instead of sampling live (you also can’t use custom workouts, get alerts or split the exercise). 

Similarly, Apple doesn’t share wattage specs for its smartwatch chargers, but when using the company’s proprietary fast charger, the Series 12 can go from 0% to 80% in 30 minutes, while it takes the Ultra 4 around 45 minutes to hit the same percentage.

While both of Apple’s latest watches are almost equally powerful, the Ultra 4 beats the Series 12 by a landslide when it comes to battery life. According to Apple, the premium model can last about two days between charges — roughly twice as long as the Series 12. This is likely due to the Ultra 4’s larger battery.

The Apple Watch Series 12 on either side, with the Apple Watch Ultra 4 in the middle.Screenshot by CNET/Apple

AI and software

Both watches come with WatchOS 27, the latest version of Apple’s operating system at the time of their launch. New features include Siri AI, which CNET principal writer Vanessa Hand-Orellana found to be “miles ahead of traditional Siri.” 

New to both watches is Audio Intelligence, a suite of AI-powered features that uses their microphones to continuously analyze surrounding sounds. For instance, Live Rewind allows you to press the digital crown to see a transcription of the last 15 seconds of conversation around you, and in early testing, it was able to pick out voices pretty well. Another feature, Siri Recap, detects conversations throughout the day or at set times to generate summaries or notes — say, for work meetings — which can be triggered manually or scheduled ahead of time. Apple says it’s designed the features so audio isn’t stored on the device and only keeps transcripts the wearer chooses, but it’s already spurred some privacy concerns.

Upgraded sensors on both watches allow them to take readings more often, sampling how your body is doing across various metrics. This is mined and represented in a new Readiness score, which represents how well your body recovers from exercise over the course of the day. The Vitals app also has a new Daytime toggle that allows you to compare your health metrics throughtout the day to compare with the usual overnight measurements.  

Both watches also get a redesigned Health app with AI insights and biometrics provied in daily summaries, which replicate findings from other wearables such as the Fitbit Air and Oura. It’s also gotten a more comprehensive health test to measure VO2 max and mobility, which is done in combination with the cameras on a paired iPhone. 

While both watches can be connected to cellular service (the Series 12 must be purchased in the 4G LTE version), the Ultra 4 inherits its predecessor’s capability for 5G connectivity as well as linking up to satellites to contact emergency services when outside mobile network range. The premium watch also has fall detection and crash detection.

Those last emergency connectivity features should give the Ultra 4 the edge over the Series 12, but virtually every other software and AI feature is shared between the smartwatches.

Live Rewind on the Apple Watch generates a transcription of what was said during the last 15 seconds around you.Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Which watch should you pick? 

Which smartwatch you pick between the Series 12 and the Ultra 4 is an easier decision than it might seem, as the more premium option is twice the price of the most affordable configuration of the Series 12. The two watches share nearly all the same features, so only the most serious athletes need consider the more expensive model.

If you have $800 to spend, the decision becomes tougher. Of the Ultra 4’s handful of advantages over the Series 12, the one you’ll likely appreciate most is its longer battery life. Charging a standard Apple Watch every day can be tedious, and if you forget to top it up at the end of the day, it may not last through the night. That makes it tough for the Series 12 to measure health and sleep metrics while you’re snoozing.

The Ultra 4 is the obvious choice for outdoorsy folks with deep enough pockets, as it’s more rugged, can survive in deeper waters and has satellite connectivity to help when running into trouble off the grid or away from your phone. 

That said, both smartwatches improve on their predecessors and are excellent options for anyone seeking a watch that works seamlessly with an iPhone.

title: WhatsApp rolling out redesigned iPad interface with Mac-like sidebar
snippet: Following a few months of Liquid Glass beta testing, WhatsApp is expanding access to a redesigned interface for its iPad app, including a new Mac-like sidebar. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following a few months of Liquid Glass beta testing, WhatsApp is expanding access to a redesigned interface for its iPad app, including a new Mac-like sidebar. Here are the details.

WhatsApp working on new iPad app layout

Although WhatsApp initially started working on adapting its iOS app for the Liquid Glass visual overhaul last October, the company only brought the redesign to iPad much later, with a limited beta test last June.

At the time, WABetaInfo reported that the redesign included Liquid Glass-style tabs, buttons, and context menus, while retaining the same bottom tab bar used on iPhone.

Image: WABetaInfo

Now, the site reports that WhatsApp is rolling out another major interface change to some iPad users, with a new Mac-like sidebar replacing the bottom tab bar by default.

The sidebar, which mirrors the layout already available on WhatsApp for Mac, provides quick access to Chats, Updates, Communities, Calls, Meta AI, and other sections of the app. Users can also hide it to give more space to the chat list and conversation view.

Image: WABetaInfo

From the report:

The sidebar takes up a portion of the screen. On iPad, this is rarely a problem since the display is large enough to show the sidebar, the chat list, and the conversation interface. However, some users may prefer a larger conversation interface. When users hide the sidebar, WhatsApp expands the chat list and the conversation toward the center of the screen, making both feel less compressed. Users who prefer to keep focus on the conversation will notice the difference immediately.

WABetaInfo notes that the new sidebar is available to some beta testers running the latest TestFlight build, although some users on the regular App Store version are also beginning to see it.

As is often the case with WhatsApp rollouts, it may take some time before the new interface reaches everyone, whether they’re using the beta or stable version of the app. Still, iPad users should benefit from the more tablet-friendly layout once it becomes available to them.

title: Khosla Ventures is opening a New York office this fall — its first outpost outside Sand Hill Road
snippet: "It's actually allegedly being built out now," said Rabois, who has clearly dealt with a missed construction timeline or two.
fullText:
Keith Rabois has spent most of his 13-year career in venture capital associated with Khosla Ventures’ longtime home in Menlo Park, California. But that’s changing. Speaking Thursday night at TechCrunch’s StrictlyVC event in New York’s West Village, Rabois confirmed that Khosla Ventures is opening its first-ever office outside Sand Hill Road. The new outpost will be in New York, on 14th Street, and is expected to open this fall.

“It’s actually allegedly being built out now,” said Rabois, who has clearly dealt with a missed construction timeline or two. “We’ll see. This fall opening date is very vague in my mind.”

The move is notable partly because of how unusual it is for Khosla Ventures specifically. “We don’t even have an SF office, so this is a very big step for us,” said Rabois.

The office will house a handful of Khosla investors, Rabois among them, but its more unusual feature is what he called an “executive briefing center.” That will be a space where the firm will bring 10 or 12 portfolio companies at a time to meet with a Fortune 500 company, four days a week. “The portfolio companies love this,” he told attendees. “They get pilots and customers, and so it’s going to be a very vibrant office because of that.”

The announcement comes months after Rabois himself relocated to the East Coast, moving to be closer to his husband, Jacob Helberg, the Under Secretary of State for Economic Growth, Energy, and the Environment, and their children, who are currently based in Washington, D.C.

That move prompted an obvious question from this editor, which is whether he thinks New York has the density of talent that he has spent his career recruiting from in the Bay Area. He paused, then said it depends on seniority.

At the junior end, Rabois was unequivocal. “Individual contributor level, right out of school, absolutely,” he said, pointing to Ramp, the fintech company he has backed repeatedly, as proof. “We’ve been tapping into right-out-of-school graduates and been able to create a critical density of talent from the intern class [onward] that is extraordinary.”

Senior technical talent is a different story. “Senior engineers, architect-level — no, I think that’s a challenge,” he said, adding: “Fortunately, maybe in the modern age, you need less of these people per company than you have historically.”

But the biggest pain point for companies is talented senior executives, Rabois said, explaining that it has less to do with supply than with geography and lifestyle. “If you have an in-office culture, most of the more senior people that live and reside in the New York area live outside the city, and the commute in and out of the city for an office environment can be very painful,” said Rabois, who grew up in a New York commuter suburb himself. “We were like a 32-minute express train into the city, but many people live two concentric circles further away. When you need to recruit proven executive talent, and you really believe in an in-office culture, [that has] been very challenging.”

Ramp’s solution, he said, has been to mostly opt out of that problem entirely. “We don’t hire senior people. We just build from the bottom up, ground up. It’s been a very conscious strategy, very intentionally, for the last three years,” he said. “That can work,” he continued. “But if you need a CFO, an SVP of sales, someone who’s got a lot of gravitas and experience, it’s really hard to have them in the office five days a week, because unless they’re very independently wealthy, they really can’t afford to raise a family right in the middle of the city.”

Khosla’s move puts it in a small but, potentially, growing club. Other major Bay Area venture firms have maintained a New York presence for years, though typically a modest one. For example, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz both employ New York-based partners, if in comparatively small numbers relative to the Bay Area.

It also comes on the heels of a report released last month by commercial real estate services firm CBRE that found New York has narrowly overtaken the San Francisco Bay Area in total tech talent headcount for the first time in the 13 years CBRE has tracked the data. This has been driven largely by finance firms hiring aggressively for AI talent while Bay Area tech employers cut staff.

Could it be coincidence? Judging by the room Thursday night, plenty of New Yorkers aren’t ready to believe the headline yet. 

“I heard about that study,” said one attendee. “I don’t buy it.”

title: Google’s AI also cheats, but a little more honestly
snippet: Hey, happy Tuesday. How was your long weekend? I hope it involved a little Windows 98-style downtime, maybe some pickleball with Andre Agassi, a dive into the origins of the newly UN-endorsed Equal Earth map, and a few examples of GPT-6 Astra blowing some minds. fullText:
Hey, happy Tuesday. How was your long weekend? I hope it involved a little Windows 98-style downtime, maybe some pickleball with Andre Agassi, a dive into the origins of the newly UN-endorsed Equal Earth map, and a few examples of GPT-6 Astra blowing some minds.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

In early September, Google DeepMind published a paper (via Import AI) that had a few parallels to the OpenAI-Hugging Face attack, though without the sandbox-escaping consequences. Instead, the company challenged 100 autonomous agents to solve 71 math problems. Though they could talk to one another and were allowed to share resources, they were explicitly warned not to cheat.

	

However, several minutes into the run, one of the agents found an exploit: “Over the following 27 minutes, the exploit spread virally through the swarm’s shared knowledge library, and the research collective unexpectedly ‘solved’ the remaining 34 problems.”

What’s really interesting about these findings is the percentage of agents complicit in the mischief: only 9% actively took advantage of the exploit; 5% were “converted” by the exploiters; 24% were considered “whistleblowers” and refused to cheat, attempting to contact the authorities instead; and 62% stayed unaware of the contagion and continued to operate as normal.

The paper ultimately argues that while some of the agents are prone to taking advantage of exploits, it’s largely a product of design and oversight more than inherent behavior. “Our findings show that the same infrastructure that allows the agents to coordinate and collaborate, if left unmanaged or poorly designed, also makes the system highly vulnerable to rapid pollution with specification gaming and reward hacks. Equipping agent collectives with the institutional infrastructure to translate emergent peer oversight into actionable self-governance offers a promising blueprint for scaling autonomous scientific discovery reliably.” 

In other words, they want to be good; they just need the right environment in which to do so. Sound familiar?

✉️ Inbox

A pile of MacBook Neo clones gives Googlebook all the more of an uphill battle. Ben’s Weekender essay dives into the miasma of what Google is jumping into with its Googlebook line.

Gemini Spark rolling out Google Photos control for automated editing, sharing, & more. I’m really curious about whether people will use this to batch-edit or better organize their libraries. I’m going to be testing it out.

Ugreen’s ‘HomeAgent’ is a local AI smart home ecosystem for its new line of cameras, more. This, along with Anker’s MindBase, is the beginning of what I think is a long road toward bringing local AI into the mainstream. Having a dedicated box with enough compute to control a smart home or NAS, and be a centralized hub for distributed private AI, is pretty compelling.

This Android phone has a detachable action camera, coming to the US for $999. I hate how much I love this idea.

Sony WH-1000XM4C launch for $299 alongside two more affordable headphones. In a world where everything is getting more expensive, it’s a pretty good idea to relaunch a 6-year-old product at half its original price. Still nowhere near a bargain, though.

🤝 Cc: Will Sattelberg

Welcome to a new project I’m calling Cc, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, 9to5Google’s superb podcast host and long-suffering Bills fan, Will Sattelberg.

Who are you?

Isn’t that the question we all ask ourselves in front of the mirror every morning? (I’m Will Sattelberg.)

What do you do for work?

I’m some combination of a writer and a podcaster. I guess I mostly make things online for people to enjoy, hopefully.

What do you do for fun?

Some combination of indoor kid hobbies (gaming, movies, cooking, D&D) and outdoor hobbies (running, long walks, traveling). We also have two cats in our house that we enjoy hanging out with, although only one of them is really playful in any sense of the word.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

In all honesty, not great — click on any random episode of The Sideload to hear my mental anguish on a near-weekly basis (Ed. Also listen to Pixelated, the other show he co-hosts.). I really fell in love with technology as an adolescent (I started listening to CNET’s Buzz Out Loud when I was 13) and getting to cover it professionally was sort of the end result of a dream I didn’t even realize I was chasing. But like lots of things that are in your life long enough, eventually your relationship with an interest begins to reshape itself.

Frankly, a lot of the elements of technology that first got me hooked on gadgets have been left in the rearview mirror by the most notable names in the industry — Google included — while the slow death of both traditional websites with front pages worth visiting and the feed-based social networks that originally killed them off has made it more difficult to really feel like you’re in the conversation to begin with. 

These days, the technology that makes me happiest tends to be single-purpose devices designed to accomplish a few things really well, rather than following through on the jack-of-all-trades, AI-will-fix-it routine. Mostly, I just hope brighter days are around the corner.

What are a few apps you can’t live without and why?

I’ll need to start by echoing David Imel on Pocket Casts. I haven’t used the app quite as long as him (mine says I’ve been listening since November 22nd, 2015), but my listening time is, no joke, just two days’ worth of playback away from hitting a full 365 days. Crazy stuff.

Letterboxd remains indispensable for movie fans, even if — like me — you mostly use it these days just to log whatever you’re watching to your diary. I have over a decade’s worth of movie-watching experiences logged on there with only a couple of gaps, and being able to look back at what I was watching 10 years ago is a genuinely cool feat. I just hope the app doesn’t sell.

Finally, this one’s actually fairly new to my app drawer, but I’ve been using Rise to get my sleep schedule back under control, and even after just a few weeks of use, I have been going to bed at a more regular (and reasonable) time, and I’m already noticing an overall difference in my energy levels.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Technically it started shipping to early adopters late last year, but the AYN Thor is by far my contender for favorite gadget of 2026. It’s an Android-powered emulation handheld designed to mirror Nintendo’s 3DS family, but with all sorts of modern touches. I’d love to tell you I’ve finally filled in my DS and 3DS gaps, but truth be told, I mostly use it to play all sorts of weird and wild Pokémon ROM hacks, like — most recently — the Creepypasta-inspired entry Pokémon: Ghost Grey.

What’s a recent TV show you loved?

My fiancée and I, frustrated as ever with the current slate of streaming shows, have mostly been diving into the archives to fill in some backlog gaps (most recently Sex and the City, which I enjoyed far more than I thought I would. Carrie Bradshaw deserves as much credit for the antihero trend as Tony Soprano and I’ll die on this hill), but I will shout out two fairly different shows as recommendations. 

First, Widow’s Bay really is as good as everyone is saying. Blew me away in pretty much every way it could, from the acting to the writing to the cinematography. A really fresh spin on “horror-comedy,” a genre I think can get old fast.

I’ll also shout out Taskmaster, which, full disclosure, my friend and former boss James Peckham recommended to me in 2023 at a cafe in Barcelona and I still dragged my feet for two additional years until Jason Mantzoukas showed up. Anyway, the entire 21-season (series, Jason) run is officially available on YouTube, and series 22 just started airing, so it’s a great time to check it out. If you have any love or fondness for classic Whose Line is it Anyway?, I think you’ll get a huge kick out of it.

What’s a recent movie you loved?

I’ll be honest, I’ve been slacking on my new release movies this year, but I’ll echo David’s shoutout of The Drama as a film I both liked more than I thought I would and one that has stayed with me longer than I anticipated. My favorite Zendaya performance so far, and it’s not even close.

What’s a recent game you loved?

As for games, “recent” gets complicated (I’ve been trying to clear out some of my backlog), but I’ll shout out the 2019 Resident Evil 2 remake as something that I really fell in love with over the summer. I’m also really excited about Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, set to launch in about two weeks. That game looks to be, um, about one million hours long.

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

I don’t run every day, but I do love to run as a way to clear my mind, and we’re entering my favorite season to run in. And you know what? Maybe I should run every day.

Thank you, Will, for being the best co-host a boy could ask for. And for not writing about Lost.

“We sent it out to actors, and no Black actors wanted to play in a movie where there are no good Black people. And it sort of died. But then AI came along, and I didn’t need Black actors.”

-Paul Schrader, director of the upcoming film “Three Guns At Dawn” (via The Playlist)

title: DOJ wins pause on order requiring documents from 14 agencies in Apple antitrust case
snippet: The DOJ has won a temporary pause on an order requiring it to respond to Apple’s requests for documents from 14 federal agencies, while the government appeals the ruling in its ongoing antitrust case against the company. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
The DOJ has won a temporary pause on an order requiring it to respond to Apple’s requests for documents from 14 federal agencies, while the government appeals the ruling in its ongoing antitrust case against the company. Here are the details.

A bit of background

A few weeks ago, Special Master Judge Jose Linares sided with Apple in its effort to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies as part of the ongoing antitrust case brought against the company by the DOJ.

In a nutshell, Apple is seeking the documents to examine how these agencies evaluate privacy and security when setting smartphone policies and making purchasing decisions.

The company argues that the records could support its case that some of the practices challenged by the DOJ are legitimate product differentiators and security safeguards, rather than anticompetitive restrictions.

Specifically, Apple is seeking documents from these agencies:

Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)

Department of Commerce

Department of Homeland Security

Department of Defense

Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)

Federal Trade Commission (FTC)

General Services Administration

Department of Labor

National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)

National Security Agency (NSA)

Office of the Director of National Intelligence

Office of Management and Budget

Office of Personnel Management

Department of State

When Judge Linares sided with Apple, the DOJ asked him to reconsider the decision. After Linares rejected that request, the DOJ appealed his ruling to District Judge Julien Neals, and asked Linares to pause the discovery order while that appeal is considered.

Which brings us to today.

DOJ gets temporary relief

In a decision issued earlier today, Judge Linares granted the DOJ’s bid to pause the discovery order while District Judge Julien Neals considers the government’s appeal over whether it can be required to respond to Apple’s discovery requests for documents.

Judge Linares said that although he agrees with Apple that the DOJ faces “an uphill battle” in succeeding on its appeal, that alone wasn’t enough to deny the government’s request for a stay.

He also agreed with the DOJ’s argument that requiring the 14 agencies to undertake the “purportedly extensive amount of work” involved in responding to Apple’s discovery requests would be “simply unfair” if Judge Neals ultimately reverses his ruling.

Additionally, Judge Linares rejected Apple’s argument that pausing the decision while Judge Neals weighs whether to reverse it would prejudice the company by further delaying its efforts to obtain the documents. He said the case remains “very much in the earlier phases of discovery,” and that other discovery can continue in the meantime.

With that decision now stayed, Apple will have an opportunity to respond to the government’s appeal, after which the DOJ will have seven calendar days to file a reply. Judge Neals will then decide whether to uphold or reverse Judge Linares’ original discovery order.
