title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Hands-On: A Closer Look at Its Biggest Upgrades
snippet: Finally a battery worthy of an ultramarathon, better health sensors and a powerful processor that keeps it running.
fullText:
The Apple Watch Ultra 4, which starts at $799, has a new processor and reengineered health sensors that unlock more frequent health measurements, new recovery insights and AI-powered audio tools.

I got to test the Apple Watch Ultra 4 to see some of these new features in action in a demo room at the Steve Jobs Theater after the company’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday.

At first glance, the Ultra 4 looked and felt very familiar. But when I flipped it over, the difference was obvious. Compared with the sensor array on my Ultra 3, the back of the Ultra 4 looks almost flower-like, with 32 electrodes resembling the thin petals of a gerbera daisy replacing the previous ring of two. That gives the electrodes more surface area to capture ECG readings. Apple also rearranged the green and infrared LEDs into a new, smaller circular cluster in the middle of the petals with smaller dots.

	

			

Those redesigned sensors, combined with the new S11 processor, allow the Ultra 4 to take heart-rate readings every 5 seconds, compared with roughly every 5 minutes on previous models. The same goes for heart-rate variability, or HRV, which the watch can now measure every 5 minutes instead of just a few times throughout the day. Apple says the increased sampling frequency makes it the most accurate wearable on the market. It also powers a new Readiness score, a measure of how well your body is recovering from exercise during the day.  

The sensors on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are different from those on earlier models.Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Unlike many wearables that give you a recovery or readiness score based largely on what happened overnight, Apple’s score changes throughout the day. Because the Ultra 4 samples heart rate and HRV more frequently, Readiness can react in real time as you drain or recharge your body.

I also found a new Daytime toggle in the Vitals app on the watch that lets you view daytime heart rate and HRV alongside the overnight measurements already available in Vitals, like temperature and SpO2. Both features require seven days of data to unlock, so I’ll need at least a week to test them and see whether they align with how I’m feeling, which has often been at odds with what I’ve seen on other devices.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12 are available for preorder and will arrive on Sept. 18. 

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Your Apple Watch is listening, but not recording

The Ultra 4 and Series 12 also gained new Audio Intelligence features, including one called Live Rewind that lets you jump back and hear the previous 15 seconds of a conversation with just a press of the digital crown. During my live demo, the transcription was spot-on, despite the noisy environment. 

The other AI audio feature is Siri Recap, which lets the watch actively listen and detect conversations throughout the day (or at set times) to generate high-level notes and summaries from meetings or other conversations you may want to revisit. You can trigger a recap manually or schedule one ahead of time. 

Apple says it designed the features so audio isn’t stored and instead only keeps the transcripts you save, which only you can access.  

Read more: I Ran 30 Miles With 5 Smartwatches. Here’s the One You Can Actually Trust

S11 chip absorbs background tasks

The S11 chip is a big part of how the watch pulls this all off without destroying its battery life. It has a dedicated always-on processor that handles background tasks such as heart-rate monitoring and audio processing without constantly waking the main processor.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Battery life remains one of the biggest reasons to choose an Ultra over the flagship Series 12. Apple also slightly increased the battery capacity this year, bringing the estimated battery life to roughly 50 hours, up from 42 hours on the Ultra 3.

That’s still nowhere near the weeks of battery life you can get from some Garmin watches. But Apple seems to be making a different trade-off that favors accuracy (via more frequent reads) over saving on battery life.  

Battery trade-offs for endurance athletes 

For endurance athletes, though, the more interesting upgrade is its battery life during workouts.

The Ultra 4 now has two sports-specific low-battery modes meant to keep it tracking for much longer without sacrificing core fitness metrics.

Extended Workout mode: Can track a workout for up to 25 hours by turning off the always-on display and running-form metrics, while keeping GPS and heart-rate tracking at full fidelity.

Max Extended Workout mode: Pushes tracking to as long as 48 hours. GPS still records at 1-second intervals, although it drops from multiband to single-band GPS and heart rate shows a rolling 5-minute average instead of the live metric. The mode also disables custom workouts, alerts and splits, along with certain other metrics.

Apple is essentially letting athletes choose which compromises they’re willing to make depending on how long they need the watch to last.

My take 

The 49mm screen and rugged build are too bulky for me to use the Ultra as my everyday Apple Watch. But the new readiness features, better battery life and more accurate data collection make it tempting for endurance athletes and anyone upgrading from an older Ultra.

Rather than compete head-on with sports watches like Garmin or Coros, Apple is betting that athletes will trade some of that battery life for subscription-free data, high-accuracy tracking and a watch that can now make better use of all that data throughout the day.

title: Google upgrades all Gemini side panels in Workspace to have the same features
snippet: Gemini in Google Workspace can now “complete complex, cross-app tasks” from whatever app you’re working in. more…
fullText:
Gemini in Google Workspace can now “complete complex, cross-app tasks” from whatever app you’re working in.

Previously, the Gemini side panels found in each Workspace app had capabilities specific to that service: “generating a personalized document with Gemini required being in Docs while building AI-powered spreadsheets required being in Sheets.”

Google is now upgrading each instance of Gemini in Workspace to have the same feature set. This applies to the side panels in Gmail, Drive, Docs, Slides, and Chat. The upgrade is made possible by Workspace Intelligence and deeper app integrations.

For example, you can have Gemini “send an email to my sales team for their review and feedback” from Google Docs instead of needing to be in Gmail. 

	

In Google Chat, you can “find open times, schedule meetings, or resolve calendar conflicts.” Google Tasks also lets you “instantly log a reminder or create a to-do list” from any service.

On the content creation front, example prompts include:

When in Gmail (via the side panel) to create a doc: “Create a strategy brief for this project with goals, milestones and next steps.“

When in Gmail (via the side panel) to create a spreadsheet: “Create a tracker for this project in a new spreadsheet”

title: Apple’s iPhone Duo foldable has the same IP68 protection as Pixel Fold – temporary
snippet: Apple did the thing. The first foldable iPhone has arrived with the new iPhone Duo delivering a pretty compelling package for interested foldable customers who don’t want to give up on iOS. It also addresses a durability gap that few others have managed with IP68 protection but, like Pixel 11 Pro Fold, that’s only a temporary rating for the iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
Apple did the thing. The first foldable iPhone has arrived with the new iPhone Duo delivering a pretty compelling package for interested foldable customers who don’t want to give up on iOS. It also addresses a durability gap that few others have managed with IP68 protection but, like Pixel 11 Pro Fold, that’s only a temporary rating for the iPhone Duo.

In a footnote on Apple’s iPhone Duo listing, the company admits that the IP68 dust/water protection won’t last forever:

iPhone Duo is splash, water, and dust resistant and was tested under controlled laboratory conditions with a rating of IP68 under IEC standard 60529 (maximum depth of 6 meters up to 30 minutes). Splash, water, and dust resistance are not permanent conditions. Resistance might decrease as a result of normal wear…

It’s a bit less of a thought for a typical slab-style smartphone, as the dust/water resistance there shouldn’t change drastically unless there is external damage. But, with a foldable, there are moving parts to account for and, as such, the rating may wane over time.

Apple’s not alone.

	

Google was the first to manage an IP68 rating on a foldable with last year’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold, a spec that’s since carried on to the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. In Google’s own footnote, the company explains:

Designed to comply with dust and water protection rating IP68 under IEC standard 60529 when each device leaves the factory but the device is not water or dust proof. The accessories are not water or dust resistant. Water resistance and dust resistance are not permanent conditions and will diminish or be lost over time due to normal wear and tear, device repair, disassembly or damage. Phone is not drop/tumble proof and dropping your device may result in loss of water/dust resistance.

As pointed out in our comments, Google also carries the same disclaimer on standard Pixel phones, but the same isn’t true of every brand. Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro listings, for example, don’t mention anything about the water resistance waning. Honor does say the same about its Magic V6 foldable, with the IP68/69 rating “not permanently effective, and the protective performance may decrease due to daily wear and tear,” with the same disclaimer on Magic 8 Pro. Foldables are still more prone to this problem than typical slab smartphones, though.

Still, it’s good to see that Apple is getting right out of the gate with IP68 on the iPhone Duo. Samsung, for comparison, still lacks the heightened dust resistance of the three devices mentioned here, with IP48 dust/water resistance on the latest Galaxy foldables.

title: Possible Google device at FCC could be Wear OS-powered fitness tracker
snippet: A new piece of hardware passed through FCC certification today, and the evidence points to it being a Wear OS-powered device made by Google. more…
fullText:
A new piece of hardware passed through FCC certification today, and the evidence points to it being a Wear OS-powered device made by Google.

This “Wireless Device” — as it’s officially labeled — comes from Goertek, which is already known for manufacturing various generations of Pixel Buds.

The “G8BL6” model name matches Google’s usual pattern for first-party hardware. Meanwhile, the e-label points to the existence of a screen, with the access method being Settings > System > Regulatory Information. That is identical to how you access the e-label on the Pixel Watch today. 

This would suggest the presence of Wear OS, with that possibility further bolstered by how the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) was leveraged during the testing process.

	

On the connectivity front, this device has Bluetooth LE and Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), or GPS. The former uses a “Metal frame Antenna.”

Taken together, G8BL6 is most likely a Google fitness tracker powered by Wear OS, though the lack of Wi-Fi is curious. This would be a new form factor for the platform, raising questions about whether the OS is battery-efficient enough.

This filing comes as an unknown Google tracker was spotted in Pixel 11 advertising this August. We saw a vertical, pill-shaped display with a Pixel Watch-esque band. The watch face is very familiar, down to the existing Wear OS complications for fitness.

Following the Fitbit Air, this would make sense as a successor to the popular Fitbit Charge line, which is currently priced at $160 and last updated in 2023.

fullText:
With the “Surprise and Shine” event now in the books, Apple is now rolling out the first developer and public Release Candidate of macOS 27 Golden Gate ahead of the operating system’s public launch. Here are the details.

First macOS 27 RC rolling out

With the official release of macOS 27 Golden Gate fast approaching, Apple has now moved the operating system into the Release Candidate stage, signaling that development of the initial release is essentially complete. The macOS 27 RC is now rolling out to developers. Here are the details.

While macOS 27 Golden Gate beta 8 didn’t include any notable user-facing changes, beta 6 introduced redesigned traffic light window controls with a more Liquid Glass-like appearance.

At this stage of the beta cycle, Apple appears to be increasingly focused on bug fixes, performance improvements, and other under-the-hood changes ahead of macOS 27’s public release.

macOS 27 Golden Gate introduces the new Siri app alongside Apple’s revamped Siri AI, as well as an AI-powered Shortcuts app that can create shortcuts from natural-language prompts. Safari also gains a prompt-based extension builder.

The update additionally includes new Golden Gate-themed wallpapers and screensavers, while restoring fixed-radius corners for windows and apps after macOS 26 introduced dynamically changing corner radii.

The release build for macOS 27 RC 1 is 26A5428. We’re digging through the release and will report back if we find anything new.

Installing macOS 27 Golden Gate RC

Here’s how to install the first macOS 27 Golden Release Candidate:

Back up your Mac

Open System Settings

Go to General ⇾ Software Update

Click the ‘i’ icon next to Beta Updates

From the dropdown menu in the top-right, select the macOS Developer Golden Gate Beta

Hit ‘Done’

title: Google Wallet passes get fullscreen redesign on Android
snippet: Following the homepage revamp with search in May, Google Wallet is now rolling out a redesign of passes on Android. more…
fullText:
Following the homepage revamp with search in May, Google Wallet is now rolling out a redesign of passes on Android.

Instead of a small rectangular card against the Dynamic Color background, passes in Google Wallet now take up the entire screen. This includes theming the entire background of the page with the brand’s primary color. 

Scrolling down lets you access key actions like calling associated phone numbers and visiting the official website. Under “Settings,” you can edit the nickname and control how it’s used. These preferences were previously accessed from the three-dot overflow menu.

Old vs. new

	

Curiously, this redesign allows you to access the old look in its entirety by tapping the rewind icon in the top-right corner. 

This redesign applies to all loyalty cards and boarding passes, including manually created ones. Transit cards still use the old design. 

Visually, it’s absolutely a nicer experience, though some backgrounds can be quite bright, especially if you’re using passes at night.

As of today, we’re seeing this redesign widely rolled out.

title: Motorola briefly teases ‘Signature 27’ phone, hints it might come to the US
snippet: Motorola hasn’t had a proper flagship in the US in quite some time, but a brief appearance of “Signature 27” hints that might change in the coming months. more…
fullText:
Motorola hasn’t had a proper flagship in the US in quite some time, but a brief appearance of “Signature 27” hints that might change in the coming months.

The Motorola Signature launched in early 2026 as the first big launch in quite a while that (mostly) fits the “flagship” bill. High-end materials, solid specs, and no slouch in software updates either. It was fairly compelling, but never saw a US debut. 

For a brief little while earlier this week, Motorola’s website was showing a banner teasing the “Signature 27,” an apparent successor to the initial Signature release. The banner was spotted by Reddit users as well as GSMArena, with the single image (above) showing a large camera lens and the name of the device, and nothing else. 

The notable thing here is that the same banner also appeared on the US site, as the folks over at Android Authority noticed, with the tagline “a new perspective is coming” underneath. There’s little here to confirm it’s coming to the US market, but it’s hard to imagine any other reason for this to show up on the US site at all. 

	

The banner has since vanished across all of Motorola’s sites, suggesting it was probably posted too early. The first Motorola Signature launched in January, and the “Signature 27” name alone suggests this one is at least a couple more months away from launch.

title: How to fast charge iPhone 18 Pro
snippet: The new iPhone 18 Pro has much better battery life than its predecessors, but it also has even faster wired charging. To fast charge the new iPhone, Apple says you need to use its dynamic 40-watt power adapter with 60-watt max output and USB-C cable. With this combination, you will charge at the maximum possible speed, which is about 33% faster than previous pro iPhones could. more…
fullText:
The new iPhone 18 Pro has much better battery life than its predecessors, but it also has even faster wired charging.

To fast charge the new iPhone, Apple says you need to use its dynamic 40-watt power adapter with 60-watt max output and USB-C cable. With this combination, you will charge at the maximum possible speed, which is about 33% faster than previous pro iPhones could. 

Maximum charging speed on iPhone 18 Pro with a 60-watt charger means you can charge from zero to 50% in about 15 minutes. That’s about 5 minutes faster than iPhone 17 Pro, for comparison.

Also, at that faster charging rate, Apple says users can get about 6 hours of video playback time with just a quick five minute top-up charge.

Specifically, Apple’s specs for the new iPhone 18 fast charging times require a 60-watt USB PD 3.1-compatible power adapter with Adjustable Voltage Supply feature. Right now, the only charger readily available that meets those requirements is the Apple 40W dynamic power adapter.

When we get the phones in our hands, we’ll be able to do some hands-on battery charge time tests with other third-party adapters to see how they fare. For instance, the MacBook charger you already own will likely be rated for 96W or 140W, but it lacks the Adjustable Voltage Supply feature. 

There are also a bunch of third-party chargers rated above 40-watts, like this Anker 45W brick. Presumably, iPhone 18 Pro will achieve the same as iPhone 17 Pro did here, fast charging from empty to 50% in about twenty minutes. This is still very fast charging when you are in a pinch.

For wireless charging, iPhone 18 Pro can go from 0 to 50% in about 30 minutes when paired with the Apple MagSafe Charger and any 35-watt power brick.

iPhone 18 Pro goes up for preorder this Saturday, with first units shipping on September 18. When Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo ships next month, it will also support the same faster charging speeds as iPhone 18 Pro, if you have the right accessories as described above. 

Remember, Apple doesn’t include power bricks with their phones anymore — just a USB-C cable.

title: Apple now accepting App Store submissions built for iOS 27, macOS 27, more
snippet: Developers can now submit apps built for iOS 27 and Apple’s other new operating system releases, ahead of their official rollout next Monday. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Developers can now submit apps built for iOS 27 and Apple’s other new operating system releases, ahead of their official rollout next Monday. Here are the details.

Developers can now submit iOS 27-ready apps

During yesterday’s “Surprise and Shine” event, Apple confirmed that iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, tvOS 27, visionOS 27, and watchOS 27 will launch next Monday, September 14.

Today, Apple announced that developers can now download the Xcode 27 Release Candidate and submit apps and games built with the latest SDKs for approval.

Apple also took the opportunity to remind developers that macOS 27 will only support software built for Apple silicon:

Optimize your app for macOS 27. macOS 26 is the final release supporting Intel Mac computers and Rosetta — macOS 27 will be Apple silicon only. To limit your app to Macs with Apple silicon, set your Xcode build architecture to arm64 only, then rebuild and resubmit. Removing support for Intel-based apps lets you further simplify your development and optimize your app for Apple silicon.

Additionally, Apple reminded developers to answer the new age rating questions required for features such as Time Allowances, and encouraged them to prepare their App Store listings for the new product page headers and search result assets, with updated design guidance and templates available for product pages, screenshots, app previews, and In-App Events.

Finally, Apple reaffirmed that “starting April 2027, apps and games uploaded to App Store Connect need to meet the following minimum requirements”:

iOS and iPadOS apps must be built with the iOS 27 & iPadOS 27 SDK or later

tvOS apps must be built with the tvOS 27 SDK or later

visionOS apps must be built with the visionOS 27 SDK or later

watchOS apps must be built with the watchOS 27 SDK or later

title: Apple announces A20 Pro chip with 2nm design and major performance gains
snippet: Apple today unveiled the A20 Pro, its first chip built on 2nm technology at its “Surprise and Shine” event, bringing major CPU, GPU, and AI upgrades to the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple today unveiled the A20 Pro, its first chip built on 2nm technology at its “Surprise and Shine” event, bringing major CPU, GPU, and AI upgrades to the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Here are the details.

Apple announces A20 Pro chip

Apple today unveiled the A20 Pro chip, which will power the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

The A20 Pro features a new architecture built on 2nm technology, with smaller and more densely packed transistors that Apple says enable upgrades across the entire chip.

The new A20 Pro chip packs six CPU cores, featuring two supercores that Apple says are 20% faster, alongside four efficiency cores. All are integrated with neural accelerators for low-latency AI workloads.

The A20 Pro’s GPU has a seven-core design, which Apple says enables up to a 40% performance increase. Apple also introduced a new version of its neural accelerators, with 2x faster 8-bit floating-point math, aimed at advanced AI workloads such as running third-party LLMs on-device.

The Neural Engine has also been upgraded with a second engine, bringing the total to 32 cores and delivering twice the compute performance.

Apple says these CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine improvements are supported by a 50% increase in memory bandwidth, enabled by what it calls the widest memory interface ever shipped in an iPhone.

The A20 Pro also introduces a new packaging design inspired by Apple’s M-series chips, placing the silicon die side by side with the memory. According to Apple, this removes the memory from the SoC’s thermal path and allows the silicon to connect directly to its next-generation vapor chamber, significantly improving thermal performance.

To support the iPhone Duo’s dual-display design, the A20 Pro also features a new display engine that drives both displays simultaneously and enables smooth transitions between them.

Apple says it also blends the unique pixel layout around the under-display camera area of the iPhone Duo to deliver a consistent visual experience.

title: OpenAI’s feud with mathematicians is only escalating
snippet: Twenty-five leading mathematicians signed an open letter arguing that AI labs are threatening their intellectual work.
fullText:
Twenty-five leading mathematicians signed an open letter arguing that AI labs are threatening their intellectual work as they seek to one-up each other with solutions to famous math problems. Each signatory has been awarded the Fields Medal, considered the most prestigious prize in mathematics.

This week, NYU professor Tristan Buckmaster accused OpenAI of pressuring him not to credit a collaborator who works for Anthropic for solving an important math problem, and wondered if the company had used their work with Codex to produce its own groundbreaking proof over a marathon weekend of inference.

On Thursday, OpenAI withdrew its sponsorship of a math event at CalTech after the company was criticized by researchers at the university.

While the ability of AI models to solve the world’s outstanding mathematical challenges could be a boon to humanity, the signatories of the new letter argue that will only be the case if those solutions can be understood and communicated by the math community and, ultimately, the rest of the world.

“Often these solutions are announced in a rush, leaving no time for a proper writeup, the isolation of new methods and ideas, and citing relevant previous work of others,” they wrote — and OpenAI’s proof remains unverified. “As in all creative professions, this raises severe attribution and plagiarism questions. Moreover, without the willing mathematicians who must take care of their development and integration into the mathematical canon, AI-conceived ideas would never become fully alive and the crucial human transmission chain between mathematicians would be lost.”

With other mathematicians growing paranoid and wondering if their Codex use was in turn fed into OpenAI’s new models, there is real fear that the culture of open research will be threatened. Today, if frontier labs see a useful path to a discovery, they can spend tens of millions of dollars using LLMs to beat the original researchers to a proof — a dynamic that will incentivize secrecy.

This letter follows the Leiden Declaration, released by a working group of mathematicians in June. That document also grapples with the ways that LLM proofs will change their work and offers a set of recommendations for mathematicians, institutions, and policymakers.

As with software engineering and other areas where AI tools are changing workflows, mathematicians find a justification in the work around the work: The value in math isn’t just the proofs and who gets credit, but the intellectual super-structure that nourishes students, finds new questions and ideas, and integrates them into broader human civilization.

And if you don’t particularly care about the cutthroat world of high-stakes mathematical proofs, don’t forget: Your field of interest is next.

“The issues the mathematical community faces now are similar to issues that other scientific and creative professions are facing, and indicate issues that all of humanity might face: how to make sure that, as AI changes the way work is done, we do not lose sight of what that work was meant to achieve in the first place,” they wrote.

title: iPhone Duo is thicker and heavier than basically every Android foldable
snippet: The days of foldables being an Android-only experience are over. The iPhone Duo is set to arrive next month for a relatively-competitive $2,000 price point, and it seems like Apple’s decision to sit back and observe since the launch of the original Galaxy Fold more or less paid off — that is, until you consider the iPhone Duo’s size and shape. more…
fullText:
The days of foldables being an Android-only experience are over. The iPhone Duo is set to arrive next month for a relatively-competitive $2,000 price point, and it seems like Apple’s decision to sit back and observe since the launch of the original Galaxy Fold more or less paid off — that is, until you consider the iPhone Duo’s size and shape.

I won’t lie — there’s plenty of things I find intriguing about the iPhone Duo. Sure, it apes almost everything we know about modern folding phones from Samsung and Google, but with a couple of interesting twists. Keeping the under-display camera and stylus support from earlier Galaxy Z-series entries? A very smooth transition between inner and outer displays? A Made You Look clone but with Snoopy? I might prefer Android to iOS, but at the end of the day, I’m only human.

But no matter how “modern” the iPhone Duo appears at first glance compared to Google and Samsung’s respective first-gen entries, it loses out on one big metric: bulk. The iPhone Duo measures in at 11.3mm thick when closed and weighs a whopping 254 grams. Compared to Apple’s most recent foldable rivals, that’s 15 grams (or three nickels worth) heavier than the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, 39 grams heavier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and a whopping 53 grams heavier than the similarly-shaped Fold 8. Each of those phones is significantly thinner too, ranging anywhere between 8.9mm to 10.1mm when closed.

iPhone Duo: 254g, 11.3mm closed

Pixel 11 Pro Fold: 239g, 10.1mm closed

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: 215g, 8.9mm closed

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: 201g, 9.7mm closed

It is, undoubtedly, a miss from Apple’s design, especially considering the push for lightweight devices with last year’s iPhone Air. However — and here’s where I have betray the most dedicated Android fans just a tiny bit — while I absolutely think Apple’s foldable is bulkier and heavier than it should be in 2026, I can’t pretend like Google is that far ahead here. Yes, this year’s foldable finally managed to shed a few grams, but the iPhone Duo still manages to be lighter than 2025’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold, a device Google was pushing to users but a month ago. Samsung, though? It’s eating Apple’s lunch all day.

	

I also have no idea how much of that extra bulk can be chalked up to Apple Pencil support. Samsung upset a pretty sizable portion of its audience when it dropped the S Pen from the Galaxy Z Fold 7, but that sacrifice came with a significantly slimmer and lighter chassis. Comparing the iPhone Duo to 2024’s Fold 6 — the last foldable Samsung shipped with stylus support — it measures in at 12.1mm thick. That said, the Fold 6 still had Apple beat on weight, even with a device that’s now over two years old.

At the end of the day, the size and weight of the iPhone Duo really only matters if you’re completely platform-agnostic, a foldable-first fan who simply wants the most refined hardware experience around. I expect most Android fans won’t be tempted with a big-screen experience not all too dissimilar from what they’ve had access to for the better part of a decade now, and I expect iOS fans who have held out for an Apple-made foldable won’t be put off by a device that’s a bit bulkier than its rivals. But hey, if you’re an early adopter looking to lord something over your Apple-loving co-workers in a couple of months, you’ve already found your first opportunity.

title: Pixel 11 gets early September update, not Android 17 QPR1 [U: OTA images]
snippet: We’re expecting the stable release of Android 17 QPR1 in September. Before that, Google is rolling out an out-of-cycle update to the Pixel 11 series with a September 2026 security patch. more…
fullText:
We’re expecting the stable release of Android 17 QPR1 in September. Before that, Google is rolling out an out-of-cycle update to the Pixel 11 series with a September 2026 security patch.

Update 9/9: Following the on-device update that some users received last week, Google has posted updated factory and OTA images for manual install. The September 1 patch ended in A1, while today’s release is B1.

It comes as not all users received last week’s OTA, with Google appearing to pull the update at some point. Those that received the previous update are getting another one that comes in at 97~ MB.  

The four updates for the Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold are labeled “Sep 2026.” Curiously, Google has yet to announce the Android 17 QPR1 update and expected Pixel Drop.

	

Original 9/1: On Tuesday afternoon, Pixel 11 series users received an OTA update to CD1A.260905.001.A1 (from CD1A.260714.001.A9).

The Android security update level is “September 1, 2026.” (Note: Not September 5.) The install screen has the usual generic security message: “This update fixes critical bugs and improves the performance and stability of your device.”

So far, we have reports of an under 100 MB OTA hitting the Pixel 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold. Google has yet to post factory or OTA images as of Tuesday afternoon.

This is not Android 17 QPR1. Several of the visual changes coming in that release are not yet present, so this is still the initial release of Android 17.

Rather, Google is likely rolling out this update as a hot patch for Pixel 11 issues discovered since last month’s launch. The fact Google did not wait for Android 17 QPR1 should be telling.

title: Apple ranks third on TIME’s World’s Best Companies list after last year’s absence
snippet: TIME’s “The World’s Best Companies 2026” list is out, with Apple returning at No. 3 after dropping off the ranking last year. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
TIME’s “The World’s Best Companies 2026” list is out, with Apple returning at No. 3 after dropping off the ranking last year. Here are the details.

Apple returns to TIME’s World’s Best Companies list

Apple’s performance on TIME’s The World’s Best Companies list has been rather interesting.

After topping the list in 2024, the company was notably absent from last year’s list “due to a decline in revenue from 2022 to 2024, which many Wall Street analysts have postulated could be due to the company falling behind on AI,” said TIME.

At the time (no pun intended), the publication also noted:

“But tides may be turning as the behemoth figures out its footing in the new tech landscape; CEO Tim Cook said on a third quarter earnings call that the company is significantly growing investments in AI, embedding it across devices and platforms. In July, after the study period for this list, Apple reported a 10% year-over-year revenue growth—the biggest bump since 2021.”

This week, TIME published its 2026 list, which saw Apple return to third place with a 93.16 overall score, behind Cigna at 94.37 and Nvidia, which topped the list at 97.51.

TIME calculates the score based on three equally weighted factors: employee satisfaction, revenue growth over the previous three years, and sustainability transparency. The three scores are combined into an overall rating out of 100.

Apple also ranked third for employee satisfaction, behind Microsoft and IBM, which ranked first and second, respectively. In sustainability transparency, however, Apple fell to 24th after topping that category in 2024.

TIME also gave Apple a “Very High” rating for revenue growth, the highest of its four designations, ahead of “Outstanding,” “High,” and “Moderate.”

title: Counterpoint: Apple foldable panel shipments could rise 167% by 2030
snippet: Counterpoint Research has released a new report examining the impact of the iPhone Duo on the foldable smartphone market, display suppliers, and the segment’s growth through 2030. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Counterpoint Research has released a new report examining the impact of the iPhone Duo on the foldable smartphone market, display suppliers, and the segment’s growth through 2030. Here are the details.

Apple to account for 27% of 2026 foldable panel shipments

In a new report published yesterday, Counterpoint Research outlines broadly similar expectations to those set by TrendForce for the iPhone Duo’s performance through the end of 2026.

According to Counterpoint, Apple is expected to account for 27% of foldable smartphone panel shipments in 2026, despite the iPhone Duo launching only next month.

Samsung, meanwhile, is expected to retain the top spot with a 33% share, following an 8% year-over-year increase in shipments. Huawei is forecast to rank third with a 25% share, two percentage points behind Apple, as its shipments decline 6%.

Looking further ahead, Counterpoint expects foldable panel shipments to grow 74% between 2026 and 2030, “equivalent to a compound annual growth rate of about 15%.”

The report notes that “Apple shipments are forecast to increase 167% from their H2-only 2026 base to 2030, lifting the brand’s share by about 15 percentage points to 42%,” while Samsung’s shipments are expected to grow 27%, even as its share falls to 24%. Huawei, in turn, is forecast to see shipments rise just 3%, with its share declining to 15%.

Finally, Counterpoint also forecasts how foldable panel shipments will break down across in-fold, multi-fold, and clamshell designs by 2030:

In-fold panel shipments are forecast to grow 79% from 2026 to 2030, raising their share from 81% to 84%. Multi-fold shipments are expected to increase 179%, lifting their share from 2.8% to 4.5%. Clamshell shipments are forecast to grow 27%, but their share would decline by about 4 percentage points to 12%.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 makes a big change to a small complication that I’m excited about
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 is a major upgrade to the core health and fitness tracking wearable. That’s because of the new Health Sensing System that includes an even more capable heart rate monitor. The new hardware doesn’t just extend to more accurate health data. There’s a big change to a small complication that I’m seeing in Apple’s marketing material. It’s just one thing I’m excited about with the new Series 12 and Ultra 4 models. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 is a major upgrade to the core health and fitness tracking wearable. That’s because of the new Health Sensing System that includes an even more capable heart rate monitor. 

The new hardware doesn’t just extend to more accurate health data. There’s a big change to a small complication that I’m seeing in Apple’s marketing material. It’s just one thing I’m excited about with the new Series 12 and Ultra 4 models.

Apple’s Heart Rate complication gets an upgrade on Series 12 and Ultra 4 models

I really like glancing at my Apple Watch and seeing my recent heart rate. Keeping my resting heart rate low is a good indicator that I’m doing something right with fitness (and managing stress).

For that reason, I often use Apple’s Heart Rate complication on my watch face. 

The small, circular version is just a launcher that displays the Heart Rate app icon. The wide version, though, displays a recent heart rate reading, plus a graph of your heart rate since midnight. 

I use the wide version since it actually displays information. The app launcher version doesn’t have much utility for me.

Based on Apple’s Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 marketing material, however, it looks like the smaller heart rate complication is getting a big upgrade.

Apple shows it displaying an actual heart rate for the first time. That means it can be one of the smaller complication sides, not just a three-wide version. 

The same complication is still just an app launcher on watchOS 27’s release candidate version on Apple Watch Series 11 and Ultra 3.

The reason is probably because the new Health Sensing System reads heart rate every five seconds, a 60x increase over previous Apple Watch versions.

This means the complication can display a live result. The wide version needs space to provide context for when the heart reading was recorded. 

This kind of small change is the sort of thing that adds up and makes for an overall better product that all users can appreciate. 

Apple Watch Series 12 is currently available for pre-order from $399. Apple Watch Ultra 4 is available for pre-order from $799. Both models launch in one week on September 18.

title: iPhone Duo vs. Pixel 11 Pro Fold: 2 Durable Foldables Face Off
snippet: Apple’s and Google’s phones are both rated for dust and water resistance. Here’s how they compare when it comes to other features such as cameras, battery life and displays.
fullText:
Companies often focus on features like thinness and screen size when launching foldable phones. But for many people, one of the biggest concerns is durability. If you’re spending around $2,000 on a phone, you want to know it can withstand whatever life throws at it.

Apple’s iPhone Duo and Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold stand out in the increasingly competitive foldable phone market for one notable reason: They both have IP68 ratings. That means they’re expected to withstand being submerged in water (up to 6 meters for the Duo and 1.5 meters for the Pixel) for up to 30 minutes, and are dust resistant — a rarity in the world of foldables. So in theory, you can take your pricey handset to the beach without worrying about sand getting in and ruining your device.

The two phones also have high price tags. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB, while the Pixel 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899 for the same storage level. Preorders for the iPhone Duo kick off Oct. 16, for an Oct. 23 release. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is available now.

	

			

I’ve had the opportunity to use both phones, and the key difference lies in how each is designed. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold takes on a more traditional book-style design, with a cover screen resembling the measurements of a standard slab phone. Inside, the expansive screen is ideal for watching movies or multitasking.

On the other hand, the Duo’s passport-size design makes for a squatter, more compact cover screen and a short, wide inner display that’s ideal for watching videos in landscape and is well-suited to vertical content in portrait. Like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, it’s designed to adapt more naturally to a wider range of content formats.

Here’s how else the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold compare. 

iPhone Duo vs. Pixel 11 Pro Fold design and displays

The iPhone Duo has a 5.4-inch cover display.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo has a squat, 5.4-inch cover display and a wide, 7.6-inch inside display. Meanwhile, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a taller 6.5-inch cover display and a larger 8-inch main display.

The Duo can be a good fit if you want something compact that essentially expands into an iPad Mini. The Pixel Fold feels very much like a non-folding phone when closed, and opens up to a more expansive, tablet-like display.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 6.5-inch cover screen made with a new glass ceramic that’s more resistant to scratches and cracks, according to Google.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

A key differentiator is the iPhone Duo has a matte, nano-texture inner display that helps to reduce reflections and minimize the crease. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold doesn’t have an anti-reflective display, which makes the phone’s crease more visible. 

Both phones are relatively thin. The iPhone Duo measures 5.2mm thick when open and 11.3mm thick when closed. It weighs 254 grams.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has the iPhone slightly beat, measuring 5mm thick when open and 10.1mm thick when closed. It’s also a little lighter than the iPhone, weighing 239 grams. That’s likely aided by the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s aluminum frame, compared to the titanium one on the iPhone Duo.

The iPhone Duo looks like an iPad Mini. But it isn’t. Is it?Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Both phones let you run up to two apps side by side. 

The iPhone Duo comes with a key concession: It supports only Touch ID, rather than Face ID, for unlocking. By comparison, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold supports Face Unlock.

Both the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold have IP68 ratings for dust and water resistance, but the better design ultimately depends on how you plan to use the phone. If you want a device optimized for consuming a wide range of content, the versatile iPhone Duo could be a better fit. If you prefer a more traditional phone that unfolds into a larger display, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold may be the more natural choice.

The iPhone Duo has two 48-megapixel rear cameras.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo has a 48-megapixel main camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera. Like the similarly passport-sized Galaxy Z Fold 8, there’s no telephoto camera. A 12-megapixel selfie camera sits on the outer display, while an “under-display FaceTime camera” is nestled on the inside.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s shooters don’t quite live up to the camera specs on the non-folding Pro models, but they pull their weight. The foldable has a 48-megapixel wide-angle, 10.5-megapixel ultrawide and 10.8-megapixel telephoto camera on the back. There’s a 10-megapixel selfie camera on the cover and inside displays. Although the foldable Pixel doesn’t have Google’s top-of-the-line camera setup, it performed well in my camera test against another premium foldable, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a triple-rear camera system. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

When taking photos with the rear camera, both the iPhone Duo and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold allow you to preview images using the phone’s cover screen, so you can guide the photographer (or yourself if you’re taking selfies). The phones also both have features designed to draw kids’ eyes to the camera by playing animations on the cover screen, called Kid Cue on the Duo and Made You Look on the Pixel Fold.

We’ll have to see how the iPhone Duo’s cameras perform in the real world, but the Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a leg up with the inclusion of a telephoto camera.

iPhone Duo vs. Pixel 11 Pro Fold processor and battery life

Both devices pack top-end specs, though their storage options differ. The iPhone Duo runs on the new A20 Pro chip, and as usual for its phones, Apple hasn’t stated how much RAM the foldable has — but it does come in 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB options (the latter pushing the price up to a jaw-dropping $3,199 in the US).  The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a Google-designed Tensor G6 chip, 16GB of RAM and options for 256GB, 512GB and 1TB of storage.

Apple doesn’t share specific battery specs, but says the iPhone Duo will give you up to 31 hours of video playback on the inner display, and 44 hours when using the outer screen. When using both screens equally, the company says you’ll be able to go 24 hours before needing to charge.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 4,806-mAh battery, which lasts well over a day with heavy use.

That’s not an iPad, but the iPhone Duo next to the Apple Pencil that you’ll soon be able to use with it.

Both phones support Qi2 wireless charging up to 25 watts, and have built-in magnets to easily attach accessories such as wireless chargers and wallets.

Apple says the iPhone Duo can charge up to 50% in around 20 minutes with a 60-watt adapter or higher. Wirelessly, it can charge up to 50% in around 30 minutes with a 35-watt adapter or higher when paired with a MagSafe charger.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold supports up to 30-watt wired charging, which gets the phone from 0% to 55% in 30 minutes. It takes about an hour and a half to fully charge.

Both the iPhone Duo and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold are designed to handle heavy use across their dual displays. Qi2 compatibility with built-in magnets can make wireless charging a snap. 

Which phone should you pick?

You can prop the iPhone Duo on its side to quickly glance at the time.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold are two foldables designed with slightly different use cases in mind. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a more conventional cover screen paired with a spacious main display. The Duo, meanwhile, has a more compact cover screen and an inner display designed to adapt to different content formats, whether you’re watching a video in landscape or viewing vertical content in portrait.

We have yet to review the iPhone Duo, but based on my limited time with the phone, I can see it appealing to anyone who wants something that feels fresh and smaller-scale. If you’re deep in the Apple ecosystem, you may have already made up your mind that this is the phone for you.

For anyone who wants to preserve the experience of using a slab phone while also tapping into a larger display, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold can be a good fit. Its thin design makes it feel so ordinary that I often mistake it for my iPhone 17 Pro Max when reaching into my bag.

We’ll know more about the Duo’s performance when we have the chance to test and review it. In the meantime, check out the chart below for more specifics about the two phones.

title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Ultra 3: Here’s everything new
snippet: Apple Watch Ultra 4 has the same external look as Ultra 3, but it’s packed with internal upgrades to the chip and health sensors that unlock new and improved features. Here’s everything new in Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Ultra 3. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Ultra 4 has the same external look as Ultra 3, but it’s packed with internal upgrades to the chip and health sensors that unlock new and improved features. Here’s everything new in Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Ultra 3.

Performance: S11 chip and 4GB RAM

Apple often includes a new chip with its latest Watch models, but most chip updates include only minor changes and minimal performance gains. And last year, Apple opted to stick with the same S10 from 2024.

But Apple Watch Ultra 4 has a brand-new S11 chip. S11 unlocks exclusive new software features thanks to its more powerful capabilities.

Apple doesn’t give specific benchmarks to measure the improvements, only saying S11 is its “most powerful wearable chip.”

Apple Watch Ultra 4 also doubles the memory of Ultra 3, with 4GB versus the 2GB of last year’s model.

Health: All-new, more powerful sensors

Apple Watch Ultra 4 has an all-new Health Sensing System that might be the biggest change ever to the Watch’s internal sensors. Apple says the new system “unlocks deeper health and fitness insights.”

Here’s the breakdown of feature improvements, per Apple:

Heart rate tracking: Second-generation electrical heart sensor and always-on optical heart sensor enable high-frequency background heart rate tracking that you can view on new heart rate watch face complication

HRV improvements: “now measured up to 24 times more often and available to view in a new section of the Heart Rate app”

New Recovery HRV: “best for identifying daily signals of stress and recovery”

Step tracking: More accurate, with new Steps complication to track steps in real time from watch face

Battery: Lasts longer and charges faster

One of Apple Watch Ultra’s best features is battery life, and Ultra 4 delivers noteworthy gains in that department. Here’s the comparison:

Apple Watch Ultra 4: up to 50 hours battery life, or 84 hours in Low Power Mode

Apple Watch Ultra 3: up to 42 hours battery life, or 72 hours in Low Power Mode

Apple Watch Ultra 4 can also provide 50% more battery life on a quick 15-minute charge. 15 minutes gets you 18 hours of runtime, versus only 12 on Apple Watch Ultra 3.

Exclusive software features: Readiness app and Audio Intelligence

Readiness is a health feature that’s become common with other wearables, and now Apple has its own version with a Readiness app. Here’s what it does per Apple:

Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduces readiness, a new feature that analyzes a user’s recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score to offer insight into their capacity for the day ahead. Readiness provides a single 0-10 score each day with a clear, actionable recommendation: Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. This helps a user decide how to take on their day, whether they’re headed into a workday or tackling their training plan.

As mentioned above, Ultra 4 also adds new watch face complications for tracking your steps and heart rate.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 will additionally support a suite of Audio Intelligence features, some of which are coming in a software update later this year. Audio Intelligence includes:

Sound Recognition: “[alerts] users who are deaf or hard of hearing of important sounds, even when their iPhone isn’t with them. This feature listens for sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, or a baby crying, and uses on-device intelligence to notify users when they’re detected.”

Live Rewind: “[helps] users recall what was just said in conversation. A double press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so users can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with.”

Siri Recap: [creates] high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment.”

Shazam: “instantly detects the music playing around the user and automatically displays the song title and artist’s name on the Music Recognition widget in the Smart Stack”

Apple Watch Ultra 4 is now available to pre-order at $799. It ships Friday, September 18.

title: Apple shares the data behind Apple Watch Series 12’s biggest health claim
snippet: Apple makes a bold claim when it comes to Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. According to Apple, the new Health Sensing System on both watches “delivers the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” Apple backs up this claim with a new study that shows how Series 12 heart rate sensing compares to other leading wearables, including smart rings and fitness bands. more…
fullText:
Apple makes a bold claim when it comes to Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. According to Apple, the new Health Sensing System on both watches “delivers the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” Apple backs up this claim with a new study that shows how Series 12 heart rate sensing compares to other leading wearables, including smart rings and fitness bands.

Health Sensing System is a major upgrade for Apple Watch

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are a major upgrade due to the Health Sensing System that drives many of the health and fitness features.

“With the release of Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, Apple introduced the Health Sensing System, which includes both updated electrical and optical (photoplethysmography, or PPG) heart sensors and associated signal processing algorithms, as well as several features enabled by the new technology, such as Recovery HRV and the Readiness app,” Apple explains.

How Apple tested Series 12

According to Apple’s nine-page study, testing took place across five sites in the US and Malaysia during July and August 2026. Apple enrolled 1,460 adults, with 1,254 contributing at least one paired measurement to the final analysis.

Participants wore Apple Watch Series 12 on one wrist and a competing wrist-based device on the other. A Polar H10 ECG chest strap served as the reference.

Apple compared Series 12 against the Garmin Forerunner 970, Google Pixel Watch 4, Huawei Watch 5, Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, and WHOOP 5. Participants also wore an Oura Ring 5 on an index finger, following Oura’s guidance.

The tests covered outdoor running, treadmill intervals, cycling, high-intensity interval training, and strength training. Apple also measured background heart rate during everyday activities including resting, desk work, meal preparation, and walking.

These scenarios included challenges such as rapid wrist movement, changing heart rates, and the “cadence lock” that can cause an optical sensor to mistake running rhythm for a pulse.

What Apple found

Apple says Series 12 produced statistically better overall accuracy than every comparison device across both workouts and daily living. Across 159 individual activity and measurement comparisons, Apple Watch achieved statistically better accuracy in 139.

You can read the study and see the results in full here.

title: John Ternus and Greg Joswiak reveal why now is the time for iPhone Duo
snippet: Following this week’s Apple event, new Apple CEO John Ternus and marketing SVP Greg Joswiak sat down for an interview to talk more about the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. In the interview with Tom’s Guide and TechRadar, Ternus and Joswiak discussed why Apple decided that now was the time to enter the foldable market. Ternus also touched on his feelings after his first week as Apple CEO. more…
fullText:
Sc			
	

Following this week’s Apple event, new Apple CEO John Ternus and marketing SVP Greg Joswiak sat down for an interview to talk more about the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

In the interview with Tom’s Guide and TechRadar, Ternus and Joswiak discussed why Apple decided that now was the time to enter the foldable market. Ternus also touched on his feelings after his first week as Apple CEO.

On why Apple felt now was the time to announce iPhone Duo, Ternus explained:

“I think for us, it’s always about when do we feel like we have a product idea that meets our bar for quality and durability, but also for design. What I think is particularly amazing about the Duo is, it’s such a good example of hardware and software coming together to make something really special.

It was like a green field of opportunity for us because there was opportunity to rethink so many different things. And I think you see that in the hardware, and you see that in the software, and the design. It all kind of came together and felt like it was the right product.

Joz, meanwhile, added that what Apple saw other smartphone makers doing in the foldable space “wasn’t very inspiring.”

“If you’ve seen what’s been out there, not only is it just kind of cheap-feeling plastic surfaces, they don’t feel good to touch, they’re kind of wavy, wrinkly,” Ternus added in reference to the displays of competing foldable phones.

Ternus was also asked about the moment he first found out he was going to be CEO of Apple:

It’s amazing, what an extraordinary privilege, right? The reality is I just, I love this place. It’s in my blood. I’ve been here for half my life. I love the people I work with. I love to be able to build the products that we all build together. And so goosebumps, excitement and yeah, just real, like really, really excited about the future.

title: Someone recreated the iPhone Duo’s mesmerizing open animation on the Galaxy Z Fold 8
snippet: It’s been less than a day since Apple announced the iPhone Duo, and someone has already taken the instantly iconic Apple iPhone Duo unfolding animation and applied it to their Galaxy Z Fold 8. Don’t get too excited, because it isn’t exactly available for everyone. more…
fullText:
It’s been less than a day since Apple announced the iPhone Duo, and someone has already taken the instantly iconic Apple iPhone Duo unfolding animation and applied it to their Galaxy Z Fold 8. Don’t get too excited, because it isn’t exactly available for everyone.

If you caught any of Apple’s iPhone event, you’ll undoubtedly be familiar with the iPhone Duo. Much like Google, Apple is entering the space with a passport-sized foldable phone to appeal to a wider number of users over the taller, slimmer design Samsung pioneered for the last few years. Even Samsung has added the shorter, wider form factor to its lineup.

That’s what makes what one user did for their Galaxy Z Fold 8 such a natural next step after Apple’s announcement. Someone recreated Apple’s iPhone Duo unfolding animation for the Galaxy Z Fold 8. They shared their work on Reddit, and it looks extremely close to what the early hands-on and promo videos show on the new folding iPhone.

The animation on the iPhone Duo creates this sort of blue effect, stuck in perceived space. When you open the phone, apps and home screen content stay locked in space while it looks like your phone physically reorients itself around software. It fits right in line with the liquid glass design philosophy, with app icons coming into focus as the phone opens wider.

	

On the Galaxy Z Fold 8, it can be done by assigning hinge extension values to frames of an animation. In effect, opening the Fold 8 plays an animation at the speed the phone unfolds.

That’s where the downside of this fun little trick lies. Since it’s an animation of two screenshots with a blur effect, it can’t be built into the SystemUI. At least, not in the current state Samsung makes it available.

That doesn’t detract from the sheer hype in the comments. It’s clear that even a GoodLock copycat feature would be welcomed with open arms. If one thing was clear, the iPhone Duo shines in UX design, and competition between Android foldables and now Apple’s might mean Samsung adds more refined features that make the overall experience feel cleaner.

title: Thrive Capital led VCs into pro sports ownership; Collaborative Fund just upped that play
snippet: Collaborative Fund just bought into D.C. United and its stadium, with firm founder Craig Shapiro pitching it as a way to showcase for the firm's startups.
fullText:
Collaborative Fund, the 15-year-old, New York-based generalist venture firm that has roughly $1 billion under management and that made early bets on Lyft, Reddit, Sweetgreen, and Olipop, among others, is taking a stake in the soccer club D.C. United and its stadium, Audi Field.

It’s the latest — and smallest — firm to try something that Thrive Capital opened the door to just months ago: turning venture money into pro sports ownership.

To recap, Joshua Kushner’s Thrive launched a new vehicle, Thrive Eternal, explicitly built to hold “iconic franchises and cultural institutions” for decades, funded by many of the same investors already in Thrive’s venture and growth funds. The firm kicked things off by announcing a stake in the San Francisco Giants. Months later, the same vehicle — with former Disney CEO Bob Iger, a Thrive partner, joining as co-owner — bought the Lakers outright for a record $12.5 billion.

That’s new. Historically, money has poured into pro sports two other ways: individual tech fortunes and private equity. For example, Vinod Khosla and his family agreed this summer to buy the Seattle Seahawks for a record $9.6 billion soon after the Khosla family also took a stake in the San Francisco 49ers alongside OpenAI chairman Bret Taylor. That was a personal-wealth play, the kind we’ve seen over and over.

Private equity firms have also been at this for years, including Sixth Street, which holds stakes in the Boston Celtics, the New England Patriots, and MLB’s San Francisco Giants; Ares, which owns a piece of the Miami Dolphins outright and separately financed Chelsea’s stadium plans through a $500 million preferred-equity deal; RedBird, which owns AC Milan outright and holds a minority stake in Fenway Sports Group, the holding company behind Liverpool and the Red Sox; and Arctos, with minority positions scattered across MLB, the NFL, the NBA, and European soccer. (Apollo, the newest entrant, has mostly stuck to sports financing deals so far rather than ownership stakes.)

Thrive and Collaborative are doing neither of those things. At the same time, the two firms’ approaches to sports ownership look very different. Thrive built a stand-alone, permanent-capital vehicle specifically to hold trophy assets. Collaborative is investing out of the same early-stage fund it uses to write seed and Series A checks, and treating the deal less like something to buy and hold and almost more like infrastructure.

In a memo shared with TechCrunch, Collaborative Fund founder and managing partner Craig Shapiro framed the deal as an extension of what the firm already does. “A franchise is the ultimate consumer product,” he wrote, arguing that D.C. United’s status as one of Major League Soccer’s original clubs gives Collaborative access to an institution with a decades-long fan base to build on.

He pointed to the tailwinds around American soccer specifically (a World Cup just behind the sport, the LA Olympics ahead of it, soaring youth participation numbers in the U.S.), as well as D.C.’s ownership of Audi Field in Washington, D.C., plus a talent-development pipeline through Loudoun County, Virginia, and rights to a future Baltimore expansion team.

Indeed, the thesis Shapiro laid out at a TechCrunch StrictlyVC event Thursday night in New York is less about owning a piece of an appreciating asset — the sports team itself — and more about what the team makes possible. Collaborative wants to turn Audi Field into what he describes as a living showcase for its own portfolio.

As a backer of both fitness band maker Whoop and the beverage brand Olipop, for example, Collaborative Fund is imagining a Whoop wearables activation for fans, or Olipop drinks woven into game-day concessions. He’s thinking about the stadium’s foot traffic — tens of thousands of people showing up on a predictable schedule — as a distribution channel at a time when, because AI is making more of daily life feel synthetic, live experiences are becoming more valuable.

Shapiro doesn’t dwell on this, but it surely helped sell Collaborative’s investors that team valuations have been soaring, so the stake could pay off on its own. Soccer valuations in particular have been on a tear. Inter Miami’s franchise value has roughly doubled in the two years since Lionel Messi arrived, MLS’s average club value is up roughly 134% since 2019, and D.C. United’s own valuation has climbed from $35 million in 2008 to $785 million today, factoring in its ownership of Audi Field and the surrounding real estate.

If Shapiro is right that a franchise is also “the ultimate consumer product,” it could be a pretty good place to park money. Time will tell.

The deal is subject to MLS approval.

title: Apple says two iOS 27 features aren’t coming until a ‘future software update’
snippet: This week, Apple announced that iOS 27 will be released to everyone on Monday, September 14. Along with that, the company now says two features included in the iOS 27 betas have been removed and will be released in a “future software update” for iPhone: suggestions in Messages and automatic password changes. more…
fullText:
This week, Apple announced that iOS 27 will be released to everyone on Monday, September 14.

Along with that, the company now says two features included in the iOS 27 betas have been removed and will be released in a “future software update” for iPhone: suggestions in Messages and automatic password changes.

Apple updated its website this week to reflect that it has pulled these features from iOS 27 for now. The change also applies to other platforms, including iPadOS 27 and macOS 27. Reddit users had noticed that the automatic password change feature was removed in iOS 27 beta 5, and Apple has now updated its website to confirm that change.

As a refresher, suggestions in the Messages app use the context of a user’s conversation to add things to Reminders, Notes, or Calendar with just a single tap.

Here’s how Apple describes the Passwords feature:

“Fix passwords with a tap: The Passwords app alerts you to weak or compromised passwords and can update them on your behalf without the hassle.”

The Passwords app attempts to go directly to websites where your password is weak or compromised and update them automatically. At WWDC, Apple explained that the feature uses Apple Intelligence and Safari to “agentically take action on your behalf.”

There are no additional details on when these two features will return to iOS 27. Apple’s website simply says they are coming in a “future software update.”

title: Apple made fun of Android apps on foldables, but iPhone Duo has the same problem [Gallery]
snippet: Apps have always been a problem for foldable displays and, while they’ve gotten a lot better, there’s always room for improvement. Apple was already going to hold an advantage here, as we’ve previously discussed, but a moment during the iPhone Duo’s unveiling sticks out – Apple made fun of how Android foldables sometimes letterbox apps on the inner display, but it turns out that iOS does exactly the same thing. more…
fullText:
Apps have always been a problem for foldable displays and, while they’ve gotten a lot better, there’s always room for improvement. Apple was already going to hold an advantage here, as we’ve previously discussed, but a moment during the iPhone Duo’s unveiling sticks out – Apple made fun of how Android foldables sometimes letterbox apps on the inner display, but it turns out that iOS does exactly the same thing.

In the early moments of the iPhone Duo’s announcement, new Apple CEO John Ternus called out “others” who have already launched foldables, with a background video showing the age-old problem – letterboxed apps.

To quote new Apple CEO John Ternus:

Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together. This results in a square screen that’s poorly suited for the way people use them. Scrolling through vertical content feels compromised, and movies are boxed in by oversized black bars, making a larger screen feel much smaller.

Here’s the clip:

	

This was a pretty major problem in the early days of Android foldables. While Android apps have always been good at scaling, the unique form factors of those early days often found weird middle grounds or, even more frequently, apps just hadn’t been updated to be viewed on anything other than an ordinary smartphone display aspect ratio. At the time, it was a wise move on Google’s part, but the problem has been going away thanks to a push on Google’s part as well as the wider adoption of these form factors. Heck, Android foldables got a tablet layout for Instagram before the iPad did. 

So, while watching today’s event, my reaction to that little dig was that Apple is just finding old problems to make Android look bad, again – not exactly new behavior. 

But then our sister site 9to5Mac dug up Apple’s own documentation of how iOS 27.1 will handle apps on the foldable display and, lo and behold, Apple is doing the same thing.

If an app isn’t updated to support iOS 27, it gets boxed in with black bars on either side, showing a portrait view of the app instead. If it isn’t ready for iOS 27.1, it still can’t take up the display area off to the side where the sidebar is.

This was my actual reaction.

As mentioned, Apple has an app advantage in that iOS developers will likely be much quicker to adopt this new form factor. I’m already jealous of that Slack app Apple briefly showed; Slack, you literally had that on Android half a decade ago, bring it back.

Thoughts?

title: Instagram chief thinks a chronological feed is ‘much worse’ and says the quiet part out loud
snippet: As new legislation in Australia aims to let users opt out of the algorithmic nature of modern social media, Instagram’s Adam Mosseri has said that the experience of a chronological feed is “much worse.” more…
fullText:
As new legislation in Australia aims to let users opt out of the algorithmic nature of modern social media, Instagram’s Adam Mosseri has said that the experience of a chronological feed is “much worse.”

Reported by ABC, Mosseri said that “the average user experience gets much worse” when going back to a chronological feed. The Instagram chief added:

If you go to a chronological feed, it ends up getting overwhelmed with content from companies, brands, and publishers… Creators get drowned out, and then your friends get drowned out even more… You miss a lot more content … and you spend a lot less time on the platform…

That last bit is pretty telling, but there’s certainly a point to be made here.

In a chronological feed versus an algorithmic one, a larger quantity of posts would indeed improve reach and, as such, constantly-online influencers, businesses, and others would absolutely benefit from their ability to post more content. That could drown out content from close friends, assuming the user is actually following all of these other accounts in the first place. 

	

Mosseri says that engagement dropped by as much as 50% when switching back to a chronological feed. While Australia is looking to give users an opt-out from algorithmic feeds, Instagram has already complied with legislation that requires it to give the choice to the user such as in the Netherlands, the report brings out. All users can switch to a chronological feed today, but the app always defaults to the algorithmic feed when it is opened.

title: Apple on wide Android foldables beating iPhone Duo; ‘they got the aspect ratio’
snippet: If it feels like it’s been a quiet week for Android news, it’s not just because Monday was a holiday in the US. As is often the case, pretty much everyone got out of the way of Apple’s latest iPhone announcement, which saw the company launch its first-ever foldable. Joining the party this late is down to lead to some questions towards the company’s leadership, but a new interview with Apple’s fresh-faced CEO helps shine some light on how the brand views its Duo competitors. more…
fullText:
If it feels like it’s been a quiet week for Android news, it’s not just because Monday was a holiday in the US. As is often the case, pretty much everyone got out of the way of Apple’s latest iPhone announcement, which saw the company launch its first-ever foldable. Joining the party this late is down to lead to some questions towards the company’s leadership, but a new interview with Apple’s fresh-faced CEO helps shine some light on how the brand views its Duo competitors.

The folks at Tom’s Guide and TechRadar sat down with Apple CEO John Ternus and SVP of Marketing Greg Joswiak to dish on the iPhone Duo, and the pair had some thoughts for their Android-based competition. Ternus started with a comment on what he sees as “cheap-feeling plastic” surfaces on devices like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold or Galaxy Z Fold 8, praising the Duo’s nanotexture finish as the solution to the typical polymer displays foldables are required to use. Ternus also pointed out that the device was largely kept secret, though that “they” — Samsung and other rivals, presumably — managed to learn about the aspect ratio ahead of time.

Ternus and Joz also commented on the software side of the device, pointing to their relationships with developers as a reason the iPhone Duo will outperform its competitors when the device launches next month. The pair specifically highlighted Slack, Netflix, and Zoom as apps that will be optimized for the foldable come day one, though early adopters should definitely prep themselves for some familiar black borders. Apparently, the month and a half gap between the Duo’s announcement and its launch date is also part of the plan, echoing back to the three-month gap the iPad received in 2010 to give third-parties time to make changes to their apps.

Apple also sees the redesigned iOS experience on the Duo as the smartest way to approach foldable software, calling it “incredibly intuitive” and helping to make the overall experience “continuous. I will say, paired with some truly slick animations when opening the display, Apple’s foldable iPhone could have a leg up on its Android competition in that regard, and I’m fascinated to see how companies like Samsung and Google respond to a company as traditionally conservative in its design doing something as massive as moving the dock. Those answers, I would think, will likely arrive throughout 2027.

	

The entire interview, embedded above, is worth a watch, even if I assume most of the people reading this article likely aren’t interested in switching to the iPhone Duo. Ternus and Joz also tackle the stylus question — in their eyes, Jobs’ famous quote about using a stylus with a smartphone doesn’t apply here — and claim they see the Duo as “a great value.” Plus, it’s a chance to get better acquainted with Apple’s new CEO outside of following orders in renaming Lake Ontario in Apple Maps, just as the Sundar Pichai-led Google did last month.

More on iPhone Duo:

The iPhone Duo is actually a software story

Someone recreated the iPhone Duo’s mesmerizing open animation on the Galaxy Z Fold 8

iPhone Duo hands-on videos reveal Android foldable pain points we know too well

title: iPhone Duo hands-on videos reveal Android foldable pain points we know too well
snippet: Apple has a track record of waiting until the kinks get worked out before it tries its own hand at new devices, but hands-on videos of the iPhone Duo are already starting to show that Apple suffers from some of the same pain points other manufacturers like Samsung do, like the beloved screen crease. more…
fullText:
via Brian Tong			
	

Apple has a track record of waiting until the kinks get worked out before it tries its own hand at new devices, but hands-on videos of the iPhone Duo are already starting to show that Apple suffers from some of the same pain points other manufacturers like Samsung do, like the beloved screen crease.

Samsung has faced some backlash over the years as its continued to develop the Galaxy Z Fold line, as it rightfully should. Flaws exist on these $1,800+ phones, like an ever-present visible crease down the hinge line on the inner display or a less-than-invisible under-display camera.

It turns out Apple hasn’t been entirely successful at perfecting those flaws in its own design. Early hands-on videos are already starting to go live after Apple’s event in Cupertino, and more are very much on the way. Videos like this one from Brian Tong show some interesting details Apple’s keynote left out.

For one, the iPhone Duo’s inner screen is anti-reflective, but it comes off as matte more than anything. It’s a massive contrast from the outer display, which is made from Ceramic Shield 2. Sitting in stark contrast to that matte inner display is the under-display camera, which Apple showed off several times during its keynote. It’s something Samsung dropped from the Galaxy Z Fold design when it launched the latest models, for one reason or another.

	

The iPhone Duo’s under-display camera has no matte finish. That change in finish only serves to highlight a camera that’s supposed to be hidden from view.

Of course, it was never going to be completely hidden, and Apple’s pre-release footage and renders rightfully showed off a camera that was clearly hiding under an area of fewer pixels. Samsung used the same approach in the Galaxy Z Fold 6, but it’s always been just as noticeable. In reality, the camera seems far more noticeable because of the differing reflectivity.

Beyond that, we get a good look at the iPhone Duo’s inner screen crease. It was expected Apple would refine its foldable’s inner display design so a crease would be far less visible than current Android options, but the crease looks just as visible as it does on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra. Apple is using a two-layer flexible glass, which helps prevent a buildup in tension that would cause materials to bind up in the middle.

Still, the crease is a factual aspect of the iPhone Duo. That isn’t to say Apple hasn’t done a good job of hiding it, but it’s an unfortunate aspect of foldable phones for the time being.

The new foldable’s specs also reveal its IP68 water and dust resistant rating is also expected to be temporary, similar to the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold.

If Apple excels anywhere with the iPhone Duo its in how it designed iOS 27 around the new phone. Compared to where Android and One UI are in their respective builds, Apple’s approach feels much more purposeful for a phone that forces you to look at it a different way. It’s only a matter of time before Android manufacturers begin to copy some of these UX design choices. It introduces welcome competition.
