title: Hands-on with Siri Modular, watchOS 27’s new Apple Watch face
snippet: watchOS 27 includes one new watch face: Siri Modular. The new face is available on both Apple Watch Series and Ultra models. However, the version on Ultra has a few more customization options. Check it out. more…
fullText:
watchOS 27 includes one new watch face: Siri Modular. The new face is available on both Apple Watch Series and Ultra models. However, the version on Ultra has a few more customization options. Check it out.

Both versions of Siri Modular use the same layout. There’s a top center line complication, the time (centered), a wide Siri suggestion widget, and a row of three circular complications.

Apple Watch Ultra also supports bezel options, adding one more way to configure the new watch face. 

First, three style options let you adjust the height of the clock. The first option features the tallest clock and three circular complications. The second style is a compact clock with the wide Siri suggestion widget and three circular complications. The third style is a medium clock with a wide complication.

All three modes support displaying the top line complication. None of the modes support displaying the current seconds as part of the clock. 

Both Series and Ultra also include font options for the clock. However, Ultra is only an option on Apple Watch Ultra hardware. Series models only offer Modern, Classic, and Rounded.

Meanwhile, the Ultra includes those bezel options I mentioned. These are like other Ultra-exclusive watch faces.

Lastly, there’s the option to set the watch face color, including lots of new options like Dark Bronze, Radiant Gold, and other new choices.

Siri Modular is part of the new watchOS 27 update, included in today’s release candidate software.

title: iPhone Duo: Here are all the little details you might have missed
snippet: iPhone Duo is the name of Apple’s new foldable model, and it’s perhaps the most fascinating new model since the original iPhone. Here are all the little iPhone Duo details you might have missed. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is the name of Apple’s new foldable model, and it’s perhaps the most fascinating new model since the original iPhone. Here are all the little iPhone Duo details you might have missed.

iPhone Duo tidbits from Apple’s announcement and website

Apple’s first foldable iPhone was unveiled today ahead of becoming available to order next month.

If you’re looking to buy a new iPhone, you might be very interested in the Duo, but are unsure if it’s right for you.

Read more: iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone Duo: Here’s every key difference

The tentpole features of iPhone Duo are pretty clear: it’s a foldable, with two displays, great cameras and battery life, and plenty of unique form factor advantages.

But there were a variety of smaller iPhone Duo details revealed both in today’s announcement and on Apple’s website afterwards.

Camera features

Software exclusives: iPhone Duo has several exclusive camera features available in software, like Smart Take, Kid Cue, and Duo Preview. But most notably, its Main camera lacks the variable aperture feature of iPhone 18 Pro.

Under-display camera: A first in the iPhone, the folding display of iPhone Duo has an under-display camera for a cutout-free inner screen.

Selfie cameras are very different: That under-display camera isn’t nearly as capable as the Center Stage front camera on the outer display, so you’ll want to use the outer camera when possible.

Buttons

iPhone Duo has a Camera Control button, but is missing the Action button that’s been available on other iPhone models for several years now.

Displays

There’s a nano‑texture finish only on the folding iPhone Duo display. You won’t find nano-texture on the outer screen.

Apple Pencil

Apple says iPhone Duo will support Apple Pencil later this year on both the inner and folding displays. However, currently only the USB-C Pencil model is supported, not the Apple Pencil Pro.

Release Date

Unlike iPhone 18 Pro, which goes on sale later this week, iPhone Duo won’t be available to order until October 16. It then ships to all users a week later on October 23.

iOS 27.1

It’s probably not surprising, since iPhone Duo doesn’t ship until late October, but Apple says the new model will run iOS 27.1 when it arrives.

eSIM only

	

You won’t be able to buy an iPhone Duo with physical SIM anywhere in the world. Even in China, where users largely prefer physical SIMs, the iPhone Duo will be eSIM-only.

title: iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone Duo: Here’s every key difference
snippet: Today Apple unveiled three flagship new iPhone models: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max as well as the foldable iPhone Duo. Here’s an overview of the key differences between each model. more…
fullText:
Today Apple unveiled three flagship new iPhone models: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max as well as the foldable iPhone Duo. Here’s an overview of the key differences between each model.

Form factor and dimensions: Foldable vs traditional

It’s the most obvious difference, but should be stated regardless. With iPhone Duo you get a very different form factor: it’s a foldable device. With iPhone 18 Pro, you get a traditional iPhone experience.

If you’ve never used a foldable, it’s hard to explain the difference in how each model might feel in practice. But generally speaking, with iPhone Duo you get essentially an iPhone and iPad in one device. The displays are unique shapes and sizes compared to a traditional iPhone though, which may take some adjustment.

Here is how each model’s dimensions compare:

iPhone Duo might seem more sleek than iPhone 18 Pro Max, but it ultimately weighs slightly more.

Displays: Dual vs single in varying sizes

iPhone Duo has two displays: a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch folding display.

With iPhone 18 Pro, you can choose from the standard 6.3-inch size or 6.9-inch Pro Max model.

So with the Duo, you can enjoy a “small iPhone” experience while also having the option of a larger inner screen than what iPhone 18 Pro Max can offer.

iPhone Duo’s folding display comes with a nano-texture finish, a first in an iPhone.

Cameras: Clear advantage for iPhone 18 Pro

Cameras are one of the most important iPhone features. And in this department, iPhone 18 Pro is the clear winner.

iPhone 18 Pro has the new 48MP Main camera with variable aperture. iPhone Duo lacks the variable aperture feature, so its Main camera lags behind the Pro line.

With iPhone 18 Pro, you also get the Telephoto camera that’s missing from iPhone Duo.

In terms of software features, each model has its own unique exclusives:

iPhone Duo: Smart Take, Kid Cue, Duo Preview

iPhone 18 Pro: Smart focus tracking, Pro controls, Apple Reference Image

iPhone 18 Pro also exclusively supports ProRes video recording up to 4K at 60 fps with external recording, a “studio-quality four-mic array,” Spatial video recording at 1080p at 30 fps, Spatial photos, ProRes RAW, Genlock, and more.

Battery: Excellent battery life on all models

Because iPhone Duo has two displays, its quoted battery life varies depending on which display you’re using. But overall, Apple is promising strong battery life on both the Duo as well as iPhone 18 Pro.

Here are Apple’s quoted numbers:

iPhone Duo outer display: Up to 44 hours

iPhone Duo folding display: Up to 31 hours

iPhone 18 Pro: Up to 36 hours

iPhone 18 Pro Max: Up to 45 hours

Everyone’s use patterns will differ, but if you split the difference between the two iPhone Duo battery estimates, you’re looking at around 38 hours in average video playback.

All the other big and small differences: Face ID, buttons, software, Apple Pencil, more

Authentication differs between iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, with the former using Touch ID and the latter Face ID.

iPhone Duo does not have an Action button, but does offer Camera Control.

iPhone Duo comes with several multitasking advantages in iOS 27, like the ability to use apps in Split View and have unique landscape views. It also has other fun software additions like a partially-folded StandBy mode.

Apple Pencil (USB-C model) will be supported on iPhone Duo later this year, another advantage over iPhone 18 Pro.

A new C2 modem is included in both iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, but curiously not iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Colors for iPhone 18 Pro are Burgundy, Glacier, Black, and Silver. iPhone Duo only offers two colors: Star White and Night Sky.

Finally, design materials differ: iPhone 18 Pro has an aluminum unibody design, while iPhone Duo uses titanium.

Pricing and availability: Big gaps in both

Pricing is another major difference between Apple’s new models. Here are starting prices for 256GB models:

iPhone Duo: $1,999

iPhone 18 Pro: $1,199

iPhone 18 Pro Max: $1,299

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are available for pre-order this Saturday and ship next Friday, September 18. Meanwhile, iPhone Duo won’t be available for pre-order until October 16, and ships October 23.

title: iPhone 18 Pro battery life: how much better is the battery compared to iPhone Duo and iPhone 17 Pro
snippet: Apple has just announced the new flagship iPhone lineup, featuring iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. One of the biggest improvements is battery life. In fact, Apple says this generation represents the biggest jump in battery life iPhone history ever. So let’s break down what’s changed … more…
fullText:
Apple has just announced the new flagship iPhone lineup, featuring iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. One of the biggest improvements is battery life. 

In fact, Apple says this generation represents the biggest jump in battery life iPhone history ever. So let’s break down what’s changed … 

Apple says the boosts to battery life on the new iPhones is achieved through a combination of new physical internal battery designs, improved efficiency due to the new A20 Pro chip, and system software optimizations.

Obviously, real-world battery life will be put to the test when reviewers get their hands on the new iPhones. For now, we can go off the spec sheets which we can demonstrate the relative increases. 

Apple provides battery life stats in terms of hours of streaming video playback to compare with earlier models. 

iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro battery life

For reference, iPhone 17 Pro touts up to 30 hours streaming video playback and iPhone 17 Pro Max gets up to 35 hours streaming video playback. 

With iPhone 18 Pro, the claimed longevity is 33 hours streaming video playback. That’s a 10% improvement compared to iPhone 17 Pro.

For the Max size, battery life goes from 35 hours to a claimed 40 hours streaming video playback on iPhone 18 Pro Max. That’s an increase of about 14%. 

Apple also provided a new battery life metric for the 18 series that attempts to more closely represent real-world usage, than just video playback. This includes a variety of activities like messaging, taking photos, playing games, web browsing, and more, based on what it knows people actually use their iPhones for. 

On that benchmark, iPhone 18 Pro Max will apparently be able to last for 30 hours on a single charge. iPhone 18 Pro achieves 24 hours under the same conditions.

The above figures are based on the iPhone 18 Pro models with eSIM, such as those sold inside the United States. The models sold in many international markets still accommodate a physical SIM tray, which impinges on battery life a little: Apple says the non-eSIM versions get 2 hours less streaming video playback. 

iPhone Duo battery life

Obviously, a lot of attention today is on the shiny new iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone. The Duo actually incorporates two battery cells, one in each side of the device. But it also has to power two displays, including the inner 7.8-inch display that is the biggest ever in an iPhone by a significant margin.

However, its claimed battery life is still respectable. Apple claims users can expect 26 hours streaming video playback when using the large inner display, and up to 37 hours when using the outer display. Assuming heavy usage of the inner display, the Duo’s battery life is roughly equivalent to the iPhone 17 Pro — based on these published numbers.

We’ll know more exactly how the iPhone Duo fares in terms of all-day battery life when people start getting them in their hands. While the iPhone 18 Pro goes up for preorder this weekend, the Duo does not go on sale until October 23, so we’ve still got to wait a little bit for hands-on impressions.

title: watchOS 27 upgrade coming to Apple Watch this month
snippet: watchOS 27 is coming this month, and now we have an official release date. Apple says we can expect the Apple Watch software update on Monday, September 14. The Apple Watch software update brings Siri AI, new ways to launch apps, and more changes to the device. more…
fullText:
watchOS 27 is coming this month, and now we have an official release date. Apple says we can expect the Apple Watch software update on Monday, September 14. The Apple Watch software update brings Siri AI, new ways to launch apps, and more changes to the device.

Siri AI is the biggest addition, giving Apple Watch a dedicated Siri app and a more capable assistant for answering questions. Conversations also sync across supported Apple devices.

As I wrote last week, Siri AI had a rough summer in beta, but watchOS 27 beta 8 brought a major improvement in my testing. Everyday requests finally felt responsive again, while broader knowledge questions made the watch more useful without always requiring the iPhone.

However, watchOS 27 also removes some familiar features. Walkie-Talkie is gone, and double-clicking the Digital Crown no longer provides its previous multitasking shortcut.

Pressing the Digital Crown now opens a dynamic app grid with suggested apps and Siri. The full app launcher remains available, but takes another step to reach.

Other additions include a unified Find My app, expanded Smart Stack suggestions, and improvements to Workout Buddy.

watchOS 27 supports Apple Watch Series 9 and later, Apple Watch Ultra 2 and later, and Apple Watch SE 3.

fullText:
Apple is giving the Apple TV Remote app experience a lot of love in iOS 27. That’s as good a sign as any that a new Apple TV 4K box is on the way. 

It started with iOS 27 beta 1. Apple is restoring the Remote app from its half-app state as a Control Center tile to a full app that can be placed on the Home Screen.

This applies to both iPhone and iPad. Apple Watch has always had a dedicated Remote app. Meanwhile, on the Mac, well, I recently made an app for that. 

Looking ahead, “pdfu” on X has uncovered some really interesting new features coming to the iOS Remote app. These new features aren’t visible yet. Instead, they’re hiding behind feature flags. The code wrangler has managed to show off how they work.

Apple TV Remote is about to get a lot more useful.

iOS 27 RC introduces a refreshed design and two new features, both currently hidden behind feature flags:

1. An app launcher to open apps on your Apple TV.

2. Top Shelf content from the selected app on your Apple TV, with… pic.twitter.com/aOFoToCnrR

— pdfu (@itspdfu) September 9, 2026

It looks like a great addition to iPhone and iPad Remote app. The current version is all about being a virtual directional pad, basically mimicking what the physical remote does through software. This new version goes further by taking advantage of the fact that it’s software.

Apple is also expected to update the actual physical Siri Remote when it releases a new Apple TV 4K — hopefully in the next month or so.

All of this activity around the software remote is a good sign that Apple is giving extra attention to the hardware box. That typically means there’s a new product in the works.

title: It took way too long for someone to make USB-C cables that say what they can actually do [Gallery]
snippet: Life with USB-C is great, except for the one nagging problem that’s been there since the beginning – you never really know what you’re getting. While it’s not quite the “Wild West” anymore, I was thrilled to see that someone finally made a collection of USB-C cables that not only do what they say they’ll do, but literally have their specs printed on the cable itself. more…
fullText:
Life with USB-C is great, except for the one nagging problem that’s been there since the beginning – you never really know what you’re getting. While it’s not quite the “Wild West” anymore, I was thrilled to see that someone finally made a collection of USB-C cables that not only do what they say they’ll do, but literally have their specs printed on the cable itself.

USB-C is probably one of the most underrated things to happen in mobile tech, maybe ever? Even 10 years ago it was still hard to imagine being able to use the same cable type across your phone, tablet, laptop, or anything else, but that’s very much the reality of today. In theory, one could go on a trip with just a single USB-C cable and be able to charge up their laptop, smartphone, tablet, gaming handheld, headphones, and a number of other pieces of tech with just that one cable. There are still dedicated cables for some things, like smartwatches, but the “Universal” part of USB finally feels true.

The problem is just that it’s really hard to buy the right cable.

It’s not hard to find a USB-C cable – they’re literally everywhere. But the one problem with this standard is that it’s so flexible that two different cables can serve wildly different tasks. A basic cable might be able to charge up a phone at around 20W, but not be able to transfer data at all.. Meanwhile, another cable on the higher end might support 12x the power while also being capable of display output and 40GBps of data transfer. Yet, at a glance, they probably look essentially identical. Even if you bought the right cable for a specific application – let’s say charging a laptop at 100W – you might not be able to tell it apart from the dozen others in your bag.

	

I’ve been frustrated by this problem countless times over the years, and equally annoyed that there wasn’t a good solution to finding the “right” cable besides just ordering a new one. So I’m glad to see that someone has finally fixed this – though I’d never have guessed it’d be a YouTube channel’s merch shop.

LTTStore launched “TrueSpec” cables early this year with the promise of not only strictly adhering to USB-C spec on the cables it sells, but also clearly messaging what the cable can do on both the packaging and the cable itself. It took way too long for someone to do this consistently. There have been cables here or there with labels, but it’s been rare and usually with some negative factor, like inconsistent labeling or a small lineup.

“TrueSpec” hits what I’ve wanted. Each cable has a label etched into either end, quickly identifying what power and data transfer speeds the cable is capable of. The cables themselves aren’t anything fancy beyond this label, but the build quality is obvious with some thick rubber sheathing. Admittedly, I do wish the cable was thinner – it’s pretty bulky and heavy, which is a little annoying in a backpack – but the pros outweigh the cons in my book. 

They’re also admittedly not cheap at all. USB C-C cables start at around $22 and A-C at around $17. 

LTT TrueSpec USB C-C cables

LTT TrueSpec USB A-C cables

It’s not like this is some completely unprecedented idea. 

Labels on USB-C cables have been done before, and there are options out there with labels on the cable ends just like this – the organization behind USB-C even has documentation on how to implement this for crying out loud. It’s just so uncommon that “TrueSpec” is easily the most polished and clear effort to actually deliver on this idea. 

LTTStore also sent out some of their other products – this article isn’t sponsored in any way, to be clear – including the infamous LTT Screwdriver and Precision Kit, and I’ve enjoyed using them both. The Screwdriver in, well, screwdriver tasks, and the Precision Kit has been a great add-on to my recent endeavor to clean out my closet of old “spicy pillow” smartphone batteries by removing those batteries from the phone for easier disposal – more on that in a coming 9to5Google Weekender edition.

title: Four ways to achieve shallow depth of field without buying the iPhone 18 Pro
snippet: The variable aperture lens of the shiny new iPhone 18 Pro goes almost one stop wider than the fixed aperture lens in its predecessor: up from f/1.78 in the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48 (a smaller number is wider). In principle, this will allow for slightly shallower depth of field, enabling greater separation between your subject and the background – although it’s a relatively small difference. But there are four ways to achieve shallow depth of field (DOF) with much older iPhones … more…
fullText:
The variable aperture lens of the shiny new iPhone 18 Pro goes almost one stop wider than the fixed aperture lens in its predecessor: up from f/1.78 in the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48 (a smaller number is wider).

In principle, this will allow for slightly shallower depth of field, enabling greater separation between your subject and the background – although it’s a relatively small difference. But there are four ways to achieve shallow depth of field (DOF) with much older iPhones …

Portrait mode

The most obvious method is, of course, to use Portrait mode, which is specifically designed to allow people to be very clearly separated from the background. 

This is a completely artificial effect using computational photography (assisted by LiDAR, on models that support it) to identify the subject and to apply an artificial blur to everything else. Early versions were extremely crude, but it’s become remarkably good in the last few years.

Macro shots

The second approach is Macro mode, which will be automatically enabled when you get extremely close to something. With this engaged, the iPhone selects the wide-angle camera, which can focus at extremely close distances. 

In this mode, only a few centimetres will be in focus, with everything beyond it increasingly blurred. As you might notice from the example below, you should be prepared to spend a lot of time dusting and cleaning before attempting to photograph anything using this mode! You’ll know the mode is active when you see the yellow flower symbol in the bottom right of the display.

Getting close to the subject

You can also achieve a similar result with the standard camera by getting very close to the subject. For example:

Just tap on the object or person you want to be in focus before taking the photo.

Telephoto shots

A final factor affecting DOF is focal length. All else being equal, the longer the focal length, the shallower the depth of field, and so using the telephoto lens on an iPhone can allow us to achieve a somewhat blurred background.

Combining three methods

Combining three methods works best: 

Select the telephoto lens

Get your subject as far away from the background as possible

Get as close as possible to your subject

This is the best approach to take when photographing people, and is especially effective with the iPhone 15 Pro and later due to the longer focal lengths.

Wrap-up

The wider and variable aperture lens is only one of the new camera features of the iPhone 18 Pro, so you may still want to upgrade if photography is a key application of your phone. But if background blur is your goal, there are other ways to achieve the same thing.

title: Hands-on: Honor’s Robot Phone is probably the coolest phone you still can’t buy
snippet: Decked out with a gimbal and shockingly good camera, the Robot Phone is one of the weirdest devices to come out of Honor. Even if you ignore the fact that it’s limited to China, Honor can’t keep up with demand. more…
fullText:
Decked out with a gimbal and shockingly good camera, the Robot Phone is one of the weirdest devices to come out of Honor. Even if you ignore the fact that it’s limited to China, Honor can’t keep up with demand.

When Honor began teasing a device that hid a fully functional gimbal and a 200MP camera tucked away in its camera bar, it truly seemed like an AI-driven fever dream of what future phones might look like.

Having played around with one this past week, I’m not distancing myself from that thought. Still, I can’t deny it’s a ridiculously cool idea, and a now fully functional Android phone the company launched last month.

Honor’s Robot Phone is aimed at creators more than anyone, for obvious reasons. The 200MP camera sits inside the device’s camera bar, which shouldn’t get you any weird looks if you use it in its retracted form. But as soon as you hit a certain dedicated camera app button and move the physical protective cover, that massive camera rises out of the Robot Phone’s rear panel as if it belonged in a horror movie.

	

The additional 50MP ultrawide and 200MP periscope camera do not move.

The camera app leaves controls up to the user, with full pan/tilt controls and a wide range to cover just about anything in view. It can be flipped 180 degrees for selfie capture, or used outward to record or capture the world in front of you.

Beyond that, Honor has packed some really cool film tools and recording formats. There are panning options and automatic spin controls to get neat shots you’d need to be really skilled to get with your regular old phone. The phone, being a product of Honor’s focus on AI, has object and person tracking. It works better than I anticipated during my short time with the phone, and stabilization was shockingly good for what is, again, a gimbal attached to a phone.

Its bag of tricks is huge, and it was a ton of fun to play around with. Honor pushes a little beyond simple camera tools with the AI-assisted mode, which is what some of the earliest teasers for the phone showcased. MagicOS has an AI assistant named “YOYO,” and it charges it with the ability to look around and gather digital information like a pair of smart glasses would.

It has its struggles when asking it questions in English instead of Chinese, but it’s a neat concept if a little unsettling.

Beyond the camera tools and mechanical gimbal, the Robot Phone brings many of the standard feature sets MagicOS 10 builds out for the manufacturer’s other devices. Overall, it’s a fun and interesting concept that deserves a ton of credit in what can often be a monotonous phone landscape.

At RMB 9,999 – nearly $1,500 – Honor’s Robot Phone is priced well, all things considered. That’s the running price for the 12/512GB configuration. The 16GB/1TB model nears $2,000.

But you probably couldn’t buy it if you wanted to. On top of being launched for the Chinese market with no global launch expected, Honor shared that the device reached sales targets almost immediately. It seemingly kept expectations low, and now has to catch up with demand while supplies are difficult to get a hand on for reasonable prices.

Again, I only messed around with the Robot Phone for a short time, but it ended up being one of those hands-on sessions that reminded me phones can be exceptionally fun. I’m not saying every phone should have an extending gimbal and overkill camera setup, but it’s kind of cool that the option exists – even if heavily limited.

title: Where Google Wallet state IDs are available on Android
snippet: States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android. more…
fullText:
States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android.

Update 9/5

How to add your state ID on Android

Open the Google Wallet app on Android 9+

Tap the “plus” button next to “View more” at the bottom

Choose “ID & personal info” and then “Driver’s license or state ID” 

Select your state and follow the instructions

The process involves taking a picture of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of yourself for verification: a “photo from this video will be submitted to your ID issuer.” 

Once approved, the ID will appear below the carousel of payment methods alongside other passes. The order can be rearranged, while you can remotely remove the ID online if your phone is missing: myaccount.google.com > Personal Info > Manage IDs.

	

What Google Wallet state IDs are supported

Arizona (Rolled out October 2023)

Arkansas (Rolled out October 2025)

California (Rolled out August 2024)

Colorado (Rolled out October 2023)

Georgia (Rolled out October 2023)

Iowa (Rolled out June 2025)

Maryland (Rolled out December 2022)

Montana (Rolled out August 2025)

New Mexico (Rolled out December 2024)

North Dakota (Rolled out October 2025)

[New] Ohio (Rolled out September 2026)

Puerto Rico (Rolled out October 2025)

Where state IDs are coming next

Google previously said to expect support in the following places:

West Virginia (Upcoming availability announced April 2025)

Where you can use state IDs

The primary place you can use this digital ID is at TSA checkpoints in some US airports. There are two ways to do so, starting with tapping your phone at the NFC terminal. You then review the information that will be shared with the TSA and authenticate with device unlock. There’s also a QR code method that requires opening the ID in Google Wallet. 

Officially, you still have to carry the physical ID card at all times.

Some apps, like from car rental services, are beginning to accept digital IDs for identity and age verification. On mobile, if an app or website requests your age, it’s as simple as confirming (and authenticating) that you want to share this information with a system-level prompt/sheet. On desktop web, the experience involves scanning a QR code. 

Google wants to make it possible to do that “without any possibility to link back to a user’s personal identity” through what it calls Zero-Knowledge Proof. This technology will be open-sourced for anyone to use. 

Looking ahead, the IDs can be used at DMVs in Arizona, Georgia, Maryland, and New Mexico as part of “improved and streamlined customer experiences.”

	

Google is also working on letting you use digital IDs to “recover Amazon accounts, access online health services with CVS and MyChart by Epic, verify profiles on platforms like Uber and more.”

Using passport as REAL ID

Google in April pointed out how you can “use your ID pass created from a U.S. passport with TSA security for domestic travel at supported airports, even if you do not have a REAL ID driver’s license or state-issued ID.” This comes ahead of the May 7, 2025 deadline. 

To do so, open Google Wallet > Add to Wallet > ID pass. This three-step process involves taking a picture of your passport’s info page, and then scanning the security chip found inside the back cover of your passport. You also have to record a video of your face that Google will review “to make sure you’re a real person, and compare the video to your passport photo to make sure you’re the owner of the passport.”

The NFC and QR code instructions for using this digital passport ID are unchanged from above. You also have to keep the physical version on you when traveling. As a reminder, this won’t work internationally.

title: Here’s how iPhone Duo treats apps not optimized for the foldable display
snippet: Apple has officially announced the iPhone Duo, its first foldable display device. Additionally, the company has detailed how third-party apps will work with the larger display. This includes three modes for apps that target iOS 26, iOS 27.0, and iOS 27.1. more…
fullText:
Apple has officially announced the iPhone Duo, its first foldable display device. Additionally, the company has detailed how third-party apps will work with the larger display. This includes three modes for apps that target iOS 26, iOS 27.0, and iOS 27.1.

iOS 27.1 adds full iPhone Duo app support for the foldable display

Apple details how the new system works in a tech talk video intended for developers. You can watch the video and related content here.

As mentioned, there are three compatibility modes with iOS apps for iPhone Duo.

First, there’s the default compatibility mode that apps will use before being updated for iOS 27.0. It fits the single app view in a safe area around a black background.

For apps updated for iOS 27, the default mode takes advantage of much more of the iPhone Duo display. Here’s how it looks:

There’s still blank space not being used, but it’s a lot better than pre-iOS 27 apps.

Then there’s the full compatibility mode. iPhone Duo arrives in October, and by then, we’ll have iOS 27.1 as well. Apps made for iOS 27.1 will take full advantage of the iPhone Duo display.

title: Honor Magic 9 Pro Max melds a classic ARRI camera with an iPhone-like look, launches this month
snippet: Honor has officially shown off its next flagship, the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, which has a pretty familiar-looking design, a massive camera powered by ARRI, and a release date that’s mere weeks away. more…
fullText:
Honor has officially shown off its next flagship, the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, which has a pretty familiar-looking design, a massive camera powered by ARRI, and a release date that’s mere weeks away.

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is a new entry to the company’s flagship lineup, arriving on top of the Pro that was at the top of the list in prior years – “Pro Max” is a whole trend this year, it seems.

There’s still a ton we don’t know about this new device, but it’s clear that the camera is right at the center of the conversation.

A huge camera lens on the back takes up over half of the phone’s width, with two other cameras flanking it. They all sit on an iPhone-like camera island with an accent color on the bottom half of the device – this is a very obvious case of “inspiration” drawn from Apple’s latest, though Honor argues the arrangement “draws inspiration from the design language of one of ARRI’s most iconic cinema cameras.” 

	

Honor explains:

The design journey of the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max began with a simple question: How can a device inspire the same sense of creative possibility as cinema? For nearly a century, ARRI has helped filmmakers turn imagination into moving images. In 1937, the iconic ARRIFLEX cinema camera revolutionized professional filmmaking with its legendary “three-lens turret”—a design that brought function, precision, and industrial beauty into one form. Today, HONOR joins hands with ARRI to bring that timeless inspiration to the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max through an all-new camera architecture. (Image attached)

There’s clear inspiration in the camera design, but the phone as a whole certainly brings in some iPhone vibes, and it’s a wild change of pace from last year’s Honor Magic 8.

Specs on the cameras and the phone as a whole aren’t official yet, but ARRI is a part of the processing pipeline, just like on Honor’s Robot Phone. 

Hands-on: Honor’s Robot Phone is probably the coolest phone you still can’t buy

The signature color here is “Moss Green” and Honor says it will fully unveil the Magic 9 Pro Max on September 28. That’s only in China, though, with a global release presumably following later on.

title: Apple TV is about to kick off four weeks straight of big premieres
snippet: Apple TV has a strong fall lineup coming up, including four weeks straight of big premieres that kick off next week with critical hit Slow Horses. Here’s what’s coming. more…
fullText:
Apple TV has a strong fall lineup coming up, including four weeks straight of big premieres that kick off next week with critical hit Slow Horses. Here’s what’s coming.

September 16: Slow Horses (season 6)

Slow Horses continues its streak of debuting new seasons every year, and season 6 sounds like a standout winner per reviews.

This British espionage series based on Mick Herron’s novels returns with more dark humor, thrilling plot twists, and the beloved Slough House crew led by Gary Oldman’s Jackson Lamb.

Here’s Apple’s official series summary:

This darkly funny espionage drama follows a team of British intelligence agents who serve in a dumping ground department of MI5 due to their career-ending mistakes. Led by their brilliant but irascible leader, the notorious Jackson Lamb (Academy Award winner Sir Gary Oldman), they navigate the espionage world’s smoke and mirrors to defend England from sinister forces.

You can watch Slow Horses here on Apple TV.

September 23: Brothers

Brothers pairs stars and longtime friends Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson in a new comedy series with a fun premise.

The showrunner, Lee Eisenberg, is best known as writer and producer behind some of the best seasons of sitcom The Office.

Here’s the official series summary:

“Brothers” follows McConaughey and Harrelson, who play fictionalized versions of themselves, and whose lifelong friendship is thrown into chaos when they uncover a decades-old secret: they might actually be brothers. After Woody’s daughter’s wedding falls apart, he loads up the family and heads to Austin for an extended stay at Matthew’s ranch. But what begins as a healing getaway quickly spirals when Matthew’s mother, Ma Mac (played by Holland Taylor), accidentally lets slip a long-buried secret that the two friends might actually be brothers. As Woody turns the ranch upside down in pursuit of the truth, Matthew finds himself juggling an entirely different identity crisis: a potential run for Governor of Texas. The result is a heartfelt, chaotic and wildly funny story about friendship, family, fame and the messy line between myth and reality.

You can add Brothers to your Apple TV Watchlist here.

October 2: The Last First: Winter K2

The Last First: Winter K2 is a documentary exploring the high-risk practice of extreme mountain climbing.

The film has a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score, and many reviews highlight that it offers a unique angle that could surprise viewers. Per Variety: “The Last First is a revealing look at how they risked their lives for an ideal, maybe for an addiction. It’s a movie that shows us the dark side of literally getting high.”

Here is Apple’s official summary:

In “The Last First: Winter K2,” Amir Bar-Lev tells a complex, harrowing and moving story that takes an unflinching look at the industry of extreme mountain climbing and its changing culture. Focusing on a 2021 expedition, this documentary follows Icelander John Snorri Sigurjónsson and the Pakistani father-son team of Ali and Sajid Sadpara, a party of mountaineers who set out to be the first to summit K2 in the winter, when the mountain’s conditions are the cruelest. The men soon find themselves sharing the treacherous ascent with influencer climbers and their film crews, commercial expedition clients, and a Nepalese team no longer content to help Westerners achieve mountaineering glory. “The Last First: Winter K2” takes us to the icy heights and unpredictable weather of K2 and reveals a surprising and layered story — one of strategy and determination, class and caste, money and power — all under life-and-death circumstances.

You can add The Last First: Winter K2 to your Apple TV Watchlist here.

October 7 & 9: Small Prophets and Matchbox The Movie

Small Prophets arrives October 7 as a unique addition to Apple TV’s library. Unlike nearly every other show Apple offers for streaming, it’s not original to the service. Instead, Apple licensed the show after it became a hit in the UK earlier this year. It’s an award-winning comedy that viewers around the globe will soon get to enjoy for the first time.

Matchbox The Movie premieres October 9, a new action-comedy film inspired by the Mattel toys. It’s the kind of movie that feels very theatrical, with big stars and a big budget, but will premiere exclusively on Apple TV.

Here are Apple’s summaries for Small Prophets and Matchbox The Movie:

“Small Prophets” is a comic tale of the eccentric Michael Sleep (Pearce Quigley) who, since his darling Clea disappeared seven years ago, has lived a very ordinary life. He works in a DIY store, visits his dad Brian (Sir Michael Palin) and hopes for Clea to return. One day Brian shares an old recipe involving rainwater, horse manure and more than a little alchemy. With recipe in hand, Michael sets out (albeit with some skepticism) to create homunculi — magical spirits that can predict the future — in the hope they have the answer to his burning question: “will I ever see Clea again?”

“Matchbox The Movie” is an action-packed, globetrotting adventure about a group of friends since childhood who have their lives upended when undercover CIA agent Sean (John Cena), their long-absent former leader, returns to their small town and unwittingly gets them embroiled in a frantic international pursuit to save the world.

Add to your Apple TV Watchlist: Small Prophets and Matchbox The Movie.

title: The Duo is drool-worthy, but the iPhone 18 Pro camera features win for me
snippet: If ever there was a head versus heart moment in terms of Apple tech, it was in yesterday’s unveiling of the new iPhones. I already started the morning by wiping the drool from my desk after watching the iPhone Duo sections of yesterday’s keynote, but the true hero of yesterday’s show for me was the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max, thanks to the new camera features … more…
fullText:
If ever there was a head versus heart moment in terms of Apple tech, it was in yesterday’s unveiling of the new iPhones.

I already started the morning by wiping the drool from my desk after watching the iPhone Duo sections of yesterday’s keynote, but the true hero of yesterday’s show for me was the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max, thanks to the new camera features … 

The variable aperture – with caveat

Given the supply chain needed to introduce a variable aperture lens to the iPhone, it was no surprise that this was well and truly leaked prior to the launch. The only thing that wasn’t completely clear is whether the feature would be included in both iPhone Pro models or just the Pro Max, and the good news is that the former applies.

Apple also confirmed that while the iPhone will vary the aperture automatically in some cases, we can also take full manual control. I said beforehand that we might need to temper our expectations of just how much difference the feature will make.

The main limiting factor of iPhones is not the lens aperture – which is already rather wide – but rather the size of the sensor. Again, all else being equal, the larger the sensor, the shallower DOF you’ll be able to achieve. Compared to DSLRs and mirrorless cameras, iPhones have absolutely tiny sensors, and that isn’t going to change this year. Given the same size sensor and a very slightly wider aperture, physics would suggest that we shouldn’t expect very much.

But I also speculated about whether Apple might have improved the Portrait mode capabilities in this latest model and actually be using a combination of the wider aperture and computational photography in order to deliver a more impressive result than would be obtained from the hardware alone. That remains to be seen, but based on some of the sample photos shown, I do suspect I may have been right about this.

I’ll be experimenting with this and will of course share the results.

Low-light photography and videography

The widest aperture is also close to one stop brighter – up from f/1.78 in the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48. While it may not make much difference to depth of field in itself, it should be a worthwhile improvement for low-light captures, including night shots.

Manual control of shutter speed

In addition to being able to manually control the aperture, we can also select the shutter speed for both still photos and video.

For still photos, that means the ability to take long exposure photos. The promotional video demonstrated using this to achieve motion blur. We don’t yet know the maximum exposure time possible, and whether a combination of the narrowest aperture and computational trickery will allow 30-second exposures, which are commonly used to make flowing water look silky smooth. The same technique can also be used to remove passers-by from a scene.

With conventional cameras, that requires a neutral density filter to cut down the amount of light, but there are third-party iPhone apps that can combine a whole series of photos into a single image to achieve a similar effect. I quite frequently use the Spectre app in this way.

For video, manual control of the shutter speed allows us to use the 180-degree rule. When shooting at 24 frames per second, we want the shutter speed set to 1/48th of a second to achieve the most natural-looking motion blur. This is something we can do in third-party pro camera apps like Blackmagic Cam, but it’s great to have the same capability in the stock Apple one.

White balance control

Another feature found in third-party apps is white balance control, and this too now comes to the stock app.

For still photography, this allows us to adjust the color temperature to our taste, but it’s most important in video footage. Automatic white balance means that the color temperature, and thus the whole look of the scene, can change during a clip. This creates a very visibly amateurish look. Being able to lock white balance for the duration of a clip is a huge improvement.

Cinematic mode for all video footage

Cinematic mode is the video equivalent of Portrait mode, allowing us to apply an artificial shallow depth of field effect. So far, we’ve always had to choose between shooting standard video and Cinematic mode footage – though the latter does actually give us a flat file also. The iPhone 18 Pro lets us decide afterwards to apply Cinematic mode effects to standard video footage.

Additionally, we can now shoot Cinematic video at up to 60 frames per second, allowing it to be used for slow motion footage. 

Smart focus mode for video

Existing iPhones already allow us to set the focus to track a particular person within a scene, but the iPhone 18 Pro introduces a significantly more advanced version of this.

In particular, it appears to use AI to identify a particular individual so that it can continue reliably tracking them even when somebody else passes between us and our subject. Additionally, it will re-lock on them if they leave the frame and re-enter it while shooting.

Histogram

This feature was reported ahead of yesterday’s keynote, so I’ll simply echo what I said then.

Judging exposure visually can be extremely unreliable, especially when viewing the iPhone screen in bright sunlight. Most dedicated cameras support a histogram feature intended to provide an accurate depiction of the exposure.

Battery life

Shooting video can burn through battery life, so an improvement here is welcome. We don’t know the specifics for this use, but since the maximum life of the Pro Max is up from 39 hours to 45 hours, that suggests we should expect to get around 15% more shooting time over last year’s model.

Apple Reference Image

Finally, there is a way to prove the authenticity of a photo should that be required. This is obviously a specialist tool most relevant to roles like photojournalism and law enforcement.

Wrap-up

Sure, some people are going to have eyes only for the iPhone Duo, and that’s perfectly understandable. But if your iPhone is an important part of your camera lineup, then the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are the champions here.

title: Furo’s founders left Silicon Valley — and it’s paying off
snippet: The three 28-year-old founders behind energy startup Furo moved from Silicon Valley and back to Germany, and yet secured $4 million in funding from mostly U.S. backers.
fullText:
U.S. venture capitalists once insisted that international startups move stateside before they would write a check. The three 28-year-old founders behind Furo are convinced that their decision to leave Silicon Valley and move back to their home country of Germany has paid off in both VC dollars and business growth.

The startup, which developed software for industrial battery storage systems, has secured $4 million in funding from mostly U.S. backers. And just a year after its founding, Furo has locked in enterprise clients such as German rail company Deutsche Bahn. 

“We’re currently moving faster in Europe than if we’d have stayed in the U.S.,” Furo co-founder Lena Sophia Voß said.

On paper, Furo is a Delaware C Corp. that raised a funding round led by U.S.-based TQ Ventures with participation from Neo and Sheryl Sandberg’s fund, Sandberg Bernthal Venture Partners. But its journey is also representative of an observation recently shared by VC firm a16z that “there is now an advantage to having one foot in your home country, and one foot in Silicon Valley.”

Furo’s bridge to Silicon Valley was Munich’s Center for Digital Technology and Management (CDTM), which also participated in its round. It was through this program, which is tied to their alma mater TU Munich, that Voß and her co-founders Leonie Wagner and Simon Wittner made it to the Bay Area, where they studied at Stanford and UC Berkeley. 

When they decided to start Furo with the ambition of helping industrial companies reduce their electricity costs, they determined that the problem was more pressing in Europe. Voß said it was especially critical in Germany, where over the last five years the country went from one energy crisis to another.

Furo could have addressed this market from the U.S. — and briefly did so when it joined Neo’s accelerator program under its former name, Lumera Energy. But Voß said being far from Germany made their work more difficult. 

“If you are an early-stage company, very often it’s mostly about your network, and also about being close to your customers,” Voß said.

Amid concerns over immigration restrictions that are also affecting tech employees, the German entrepreneur insisted that in the trio’s case, going home after their respective stints at Apple, Google X, and AI startups was a deliberate move. She said they all had full-time offers from the companies they’d worked at, and all of them could have stayed with visas. 

“So it was a decision to go back to Europe not because we needed to, but because we see that right now, it’s a better time to build an energy startup in Europe instead of the U.S.,” Voß said.

According to Voß, starting Furo out of Munich was “highly beneficial” for its growth, “because a lot of people in our network recommended us to our first customers,” as well as for “operational expertise” and mentorship. “Every time we have a challenge, we know exactly whom to call,” she said, adding that being close to technical universities is also helpful for hiring.

It doesn’t hurt, either that “if you compare the salary of an engineer in the U.S. versus Germany, it is just way cheaper,” Voß said. She recalled that Furo’s U.S. investors wondered whether it would be able to source talent for the amount it had budgeted, which was actually at the top end for salaries in Germany. “So it’s definitely better that you can do more with the money,” she added. 

Salary is just one aspect, though. Voß said the quality of talent is also on par, while workers are more accessible because there is less competition with Big Tech and also thanks to Furo’s CDTM ties. “It’s such a great network in Germany and in Europe that people somehow start to know you.” 

The startup is also maintaining its U.S. network. 

“We’re back in the U.S. three or four times a year for admin stuff, but also to catch up with our investors and maybe see new investors,” Voß said. 

It’s a reminder that, even for startups that are now happy at home, getting the best of both worlds may still mean fundraising from the United States.

Pictured from left to right: Furo co-founders Lena Sophia Voß, Simon Wittner, and Leonie Wagner.

title: Mark Wahlberg is coming to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, and he wants to talk about your work, not his
snippet: Mark Wahlberg joins Bruce K. Lee at Disrupt to discuss investing, entrepreneurship, healthcare, wellness, and building businesses.
fullText:
Let’s just get this out of the way: Mark Wahlberg is as A-list as it gets. He broke out in 1997’s “Boogie Nights,” and in the nearly three decades since, he’s built one of the highest-wattage careers in Hollywood: two Academy Award nominations, a Golden Globe nod for “The Fighter,” multiple Emmy nominations as a producer (HBO’s “Entourage” among them), and a filmography that spans crime dramas, comedies, and action blockbusters. Right now, he’s back on-screen in “By Any Means,” a manhunt thriller set during the 1966 Mississippi civil rights killings.

He’s also signaling where he’s increasingly turning his attention. Wahlberg will sit down with Bruce K. Lee, founder and CEO of Keebeck Wealth Management, on the main stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 to talk about that progression. Grab your ticket here so you don’t miss a moment of this session and Disrupt 2026. Ticket prices increase on September 25.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

From Hollywood to business venture

His acting career is really just part of the picture. Over the past two decades, Wahlberg has built a production company, a restaurant chain, apparel and fitness ventures, a slate of angel investments, and the now-25-year-old Mark Wahlberg Youth Foundation, which supports inner-city kids and teens. He’s used his Hollywood success to launch big projects well outside the movie business — and in a fireside chat at this year’s Disrupt, he’s going to give us a peek into how.

Building an investing mindset

Wahlberg, who’s leaned almost entirely on entrepreneurial instinct about people, culture, products, and markets, is now someone who’s been building institutional-level investing discipline, with Lee as his guide, and with a growing focus on healthcare and wellness startups. It’s a rare, unvarnished look at how someone with Wahlberg’s cultural intelligence has worked his way into some of the most sophisticated rooms in business and finance.

He also discusses where high-profile entertainers and athletes sometimes get it wrong (Wahlberg is candid about having had to unlearn some of his own old instincts); how he’s used the trust built over a massive career to drive access and deal flow; and which technologies he’s most focused on right now and why.

Image Credits:Slava Blazer Photography / Flickr (opens in a new window)

Go inside Wahlberg’s playbook

If you’ve watched Wahlberg build brands, franchises, and businesses over the past decade and wondered, “Who is this guy?,” you won’t want to miss this conversation. Mistakes, mentorship, the mechanics of leveling up in a competitive investing landscape — we’ll cover it all at Disrupt.

Join Wahlberg and Lee on the Disrupt Stage, alongside 250+ of tech’s top leaders across 200+ sessions covering what it takes to build a viable startup and shape the next generation of innovation. Right now, he’s back on-screen in “By Any Means,” a manhunt thriller set during the 1966 Mississippi civil rights killings.

He’s also signaling where he’s increasingly turning his attention. Wahlberg will sit down with Bruce K. title: Hands-on: Orbitkey elevated its time-tested key organizer with a built-in Google Find Hub tracker
snippet: If you happen to walk past the Orbitkey’s setup at IFA in Berlin, you might have seen what the company is known for — key organizers. You’d be forgiven for not thinking these new key organizers had Google Find Hub trackers built in. more…
fullText:
If you happen to walk past the Orbitkey’s setup at IFA in Berlin, you might have seen what the company is known for — key organizers. You’d be forgiven for not thinking these new key organizers had Google Find Hub trackers built in.

Orbitkey isn’t new to Google Find Hub trackers, and certainly not key organizers. But its brand-new Key Organizer Tracker is the culmination of both, blending the visual design of what makes the company’s popular key holders so popular with more utility. I spent some time during IFA with the new key tool, and it’s already part of my EDC going forward.

The Key Organizer Tracker works with both Google Find Hub and Apple Find My networks by keeping a built-in tracker tucked in one of the sides. It looks thick at first glance, but I found that the new tracker/organizer is no thicker than some key-keepers, like the Ridge version I was lugging around. If your key organizer has a belt clip, Orbitkey’s Key Organizer Tracker will take up just as much space.

I’ve been using it for a few days during my IFA trip, and even though I don’t need to pull out my keys while on the go, I’ve toyed around with it enough to appreciate the design. Keys stay tucked and don’t spin, and the post has a semi-locking mechanism that prevents the keeper from loosening unnecessarily. Instead of a piece of spring steel sticking out to keep friction on your keys, Orbitkey uses a patented pressure ring that provides the perfect amount of pushback to keep them from spinning or locking in place.

	

Even the bottom key ring made for accompanying car keys is designed well. It’s fixed at the bottom, where the leather and plastic bend around. It doesn’t slide up into the space where keys sit, which makes pulling it out and grabbing the right key easier.

The tracker itself is no-nonsense, which is perfect. There’s a button for pairing and an LED to indicate status. It has a speaker to play loud chirps through the Google Find Hub app, and it charges via a magnetic pin charger included with the organizer. Orbitkey says the new Key Organizer Tracker lasts for 3-5 months, depending on your use. With how easy it is to charge, even with keys on it, that’s a respectable length of time.

Fit and finish feel great, as well. It has a faux-leather outer layer in tons of color options, and the rest of the keyboard’s build is made of sturdy, quality plastic.

Orbitkey also announced a new standalone tracker to complement the key holder. It’s shaped like a small popsicle stick, so it might not fit in your AirTag-branded accessories. Still, I’ve found it sort of slips into just about any bag. In Orbitkey’s new tech pouches, it fits into a dedicated pocket, so it won’t get lost in the clutter.

It has the same specs as the key tracker, with 3-5 months of battery and the same charging method.

Both the Orbitkey Key Organizer Tracker and the standalone Tracker come in a bunch of colors. Even though my pictures only show the black colorway, the rest of the company’s color options are vibrant. The key organizer comes in Black, Blush, Cobalt, Citrus, and Orange leather-free options. Leather versions come in Black, Tan, and Forest.

The Orbitkey Key Organizer Tracker starts at $69.90, and the Universal Tracker starts at $34.90. Both are on sale now, and the Key Organizer Tracker is currently available for pre-order.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 display corners can bend inward on purpose, Samsung says [Gallery]
snippet: The internet is mad. Shocking statement, I know, but this time it’s about a perceived quality control issue on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 that sees the display corners able to bend or flex inward, but that Samsung says is part of the design. more…
fullText:
The internet is mad. Shocking statement, I know, but this time it’s about a perceived quality control issue on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 that sees the display corners able to bend or flex inward, but that Samsung says is part of the design.

On Reddit, Samsung’s forums, and endless social media posts – as well as a heaping pile of clickbaity headlines – a “flaw” with the Fold 8 is being criticized. Some have noticed that when you apply pressure to the corner of the inner display on Samsung’s new foldable, the corner flexes inward, leaving a small gap between the display and the bezel until the pressure is released. It seems to be more pronounced on some devices rather than others – on my personal Fold 8, it’s barely noticeable.

Reactions have varied, with one thread calling on Samsung to recall the device due to this.

Via @TheGalox_
Via Samsung forums

Samsung says, though, that this is normal behavior.

	

In a statement to Business Post as well as a reply apparently through its forums, Samsung explains that the corners of the display flex to protect the display in the case that something is trapped within the folded display, as well as to “reduce the impact of interference or pressure between internal components of the display.” The statement explains:

If something like sand adheres to the top surface of the internal display, the screen could get scratched when the Fold is folded. We designed it so the display indents slightly to provide a cushioning effect and prevent damage. Since this feature was prepared to ensure consumers do not experience inconvenience, we have not provided a separate official explanation.

One of the main concerns here was in regards to water resistance, with many assuming that this gap would let water get into the internals of the device. This was tested directly by one user, who applied pressure to the display corners while the Fold 8 was entirely submerged in water, with the foldable coming out unscathed. 

What do you think?

fullText:
As the debut of Googlebook quietly approaches, a week full of new laptop launches at IFA continues to make me wonder why literally anyone should be even a tiny bit interested in Google’s new platform.

This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every weekend, and catch our weekday roundups too!

Googlebook made its debut earlier this year as the company’s Android-based desktop platform that will replace ChromeOS and, frankly, I’ve spent the last couple of months just sitting here stewing over the complete lack of information on what this platform is supposed to do and why anyone should care. Truly, I cannot remember the last time I was this skeptical about a Google product – is this how other people felt about Stadia?

At this point, not much has changed.

	

We’ve seen leaks of some of the first Googlebook laptops from Asus and Lenovo, while Acer was spotted teasing its Googlebook at IFA in Berlin. Some early apps have shown up too, including “Magic Pointer” which is the one new feature Google has actually shown off from this platform, a “Desktop Camera” app, and “Look up” which is in fact not a reference to that DiCaprio movie but instead an AI-powered experience that lets you interact with text to find relevant information such as definitions, flight tracking, and more. That one works on some Android phones, too. 

Yet, I still cannot fathom where Googlebooks fit into the larger market. ChromeOS had a clear selling point – stable and usable software on low-cost hardware, with later generations adding in some clever AI features and using more capable hardware. But where Googlebook might have been interesting from a cost perspective, a focus on “premium” hardware combined with RAMageddon and a sea of MacBook Neo competitors… I just don’t get it folks. 

The new IdeaPad Vibe from Lenovo and the Dell 14S were both announced this week as direct answers to Apple’s hit budget-conscious laptop, and Google is literally going in the opposite direction.

Damien laid out some potential ideas back in June, such as a focus on AI-aided vibe coding, but it’s still hard to imagine Google’s pitch at this point. Windows laptops are getting more affordable in the wake of the MacBook Neo, and is anyone looking to spend money on tech they don’t need to right now? Maybe I’m just having trouble seeing the potential or the positives here, but I can’t remember the last time I was so sour on a potential new Google launch. 

What do you think?

title: The iPhone Duo Isn’t the Pocket iPad… or Is It?
snippet: Commentary: I can’t figure out if the Duo would replace my iPad, or if it’s just a portable alternative.
fullText:
I’m having deja vu after Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event, which introduced the company’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo. It’s on two levels: Back in 2020, Microsoft introduced its take on a folding phone, also called the Duo. I remember talking about it with Panos Panay, at that time Microsoft’s chief product officer, and realizing that a hinged, dual-screen phone was in some ways the phone of my dreams, but not in all the ways I wanted.

But that’s not all. I’m writing these thoughts about the iPhone Duo on a Magic Keyboard-equipped iPad Air that sometimes — but not always — replaces my MacBook. I’m having similar feelings about the iPhone Duo and the iPad.

Could the Duo be the iPad-to-go of my dreams? Could it easily evolve to meet my needs? Or would I still find myself wishing to go back to the iPad sometimes?

	

			

Not quite an iPad

Apple has a knack for expanding and blending its product lines while approaching, but never reaching, a place where one actually replaces the other. A case in point: The iPad’s decade-plus evolution to a device that can feel uncannily Mac-like at times, yet still not be a Mac.

I’m getting the same vibes from the iPhone Duo. The device is “inspired by the versatility of iPad,” according to Apple, but it’s not actually an iPad. 

Unfolded on a table, it looks like an iPad.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

And yet, iPad Mini-like

I felt excitement about the iPhone Duo as I watched the news literally unfold. I haven’t cared about many folding phones because they either didn’t seem like true tablets or they looked pocket-unfriendly. The iPhone Duo’s size seems right, and its aspect ratios and design remind me of an iPad Mini. 

But also, it supports the Apple Pencil! And it can run some split-screen apps in ways that look like an iPad. Could iPad apps, of which I have tons already, run on this too? Would this be a way to have the best of both worlds in my pocket for a breathtaking $1,999-and-up price?

I’m curious how well the Duo handles the Pencil. The iPad Mini supports the Pencil Pro, but the Duo doesn’t.Josh Goldman/CNET

What it still seems to lack

The Duo doesn’t run iPadOS. Its iOS variant has what looks like a different layout, with side-oriented menus and docks, repositioned notification indicators, different layout orientations for apps, and a focus on continuity between single and dual-screen views of the same apps when folded and unfolded. 

The Pencil support is for the USB-C Pencil, not any of the Pencil 2 or Pencil Pros, which have advanced pressure sensitivity, hovering input features and gyro-enabled brushes. And I’d need to carry that Pencil around in my pocket or some sort of future Pencil-enabled case, since Apple didn’t announce a tinier Pencil that could connect with the Duo.

And as I type up this story on an iPad keyboard, I wonder how well the Duo supports keyboard accessories or windowed layouts that could give me the workspace that iPads can. Possibly? I’m sure I could pair a keyboard, for instance. But would it feel good? Or would I even want it?

You can get a lot of other Apple devices for the Duo’s $2,000 price tag. Or, at least, two.Patrick Holland/CNET

A price difference

I also wonder whether the Duo would replace an iPad Mini, which it clearly looks set up to do. The iPad Mini is far less expensive, starting at just $599. There’s another OLED-screened model expected this fall, maybe at the same time as the iPhone Duo, which arrives Oct. 23. You could buy an iPad Mini and an iPhone 18 Pro for less than the cost of an iPhone Duo.

But not that much less. You’d be spending at least $1,798 compared to the Duo’s $1,999 base price.

Alternatively, a basic iPad and an entry iPhone 17E would collectively cost $1,148.

So the Duo doesn’t make sense, right? Unless it can be both? Would it be both? Or would I suddenly have two iPad-like devices, one for my pocket, one for my home?

Could the Duo’s design influence future iPads?Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

A sign of things to come from Apple?

I’m a little annoyed that the Duo isn’t entirely an iPad, but why do I feel less upset than I do about the iPad not fully being a Mac? It might be because the iPad itself has always been a bridge device, something that’s a bit iPhone, a bit Mac. 

I have a feeling that the Duo’s destiny isn’t set in stone, that this phone will transform into new forms and accessory uses. It might even become a dockable computer. After all, didn’t new CEO John Ternus reframe the iPhone as an intelligent hub? Am I hallucinating? Dreaming stupid dreams? Perhaps. Sometimes a decade can pass while you’re waiting for Apple to do something it never does.

Microsoft’s Surface Duo disappeared from the market after just a few short years, around the same time that Microsoft’s broader Windows Phone ambitions – merging the worlds of phone and desktop designs and functionality – turned to dust. 

In 2026, the iPhone Duo will not be a full iPad. But maybe this new melting identity of the iPhone is a sign that all product categories are starting to flex. Even the iPad. I just wonder if the Duo’s going to feel like it’s truly the best of both worlds, or if I’d still prefer going back to an iPad after all.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Scott Stein
						

						

							Editor at Large						
					

											

								

											I started with CNET reviewing laptops in 2009. Now I explore wearable tech, VR/AR, tablets, gaming and future/emerging trends in our changing world. Other obsessions include magic, immersive theater, puzzles, board games, cooking, improv and the New York Jets. My background includes an MFA in theater which I apply to thinking about immersive experiences of the future.

title: Apple hid a classic Mac easter egg in the iOS 27 Settings app
snippet: Many have complained that Apple design has been sapped of some of its trademark whimsy in recent years. Well, here’s the latest example of how the tides seem to be changing. Buried in the Settings app on iOS 27, Apple has hidden an easter egg that hails back from classic Mac OS; Clarus the Dogcow. Here’s how to trigger it … more…
fullText:
Many have complained that Apple design has been sapped of some of its trademark whimsy in recent years. Well, here’s the latest example of how the tides seem to be changing. 

Buried in the Settings app on iOS 27, Apple has hidden an easter egg that hails back from classic Mac OS; Clarus the Dogcow. Here’s how to trigger it …

iOS 27 includes a new feature that lets user customize the intensity of the Liquid Glass transparency effects, with a slider ranging from Clear to fully Tinted. You can find that setting on your iPhone by going to Settings -> Appearance -> Liquid Glass. 

In this pane, Apple includes some faux website user interface so you can preview how the Liquid Glass appearance changes as you adjust the slider. There’s a little scrollable region including some text and photography from Apple Park. 

Here’s where the easter egg comes in: scroll all the way to the bottom and keep pulling up with your finger and it will reveal a photo of a Clarus the Dogcow figurine next to the Apple Park pond. Rainbow text reading ‘Moof!’, the noise a dogcow makes, also appears in the example search text field. 

And if you type ‘Moof!’ to Siri in Spotlight, it will even reply “Nice dogcow.”.

For those unfamiliar with the history, Clarus the Dogcow relates back to an icon created by Susan Kare for the original Mac, as a glyph for the Cairo font (the classic Mac’s icon font, similar to Windows’ Dingbats). It has essentially no utility; it’s just a bit of fun.

You can also find the same easter egg on MacOS Golden Gate in the Appearance menu of the System Settings app.

Still rolling out (beta)

These are Messages features that Google announced or have been spotted in the wild by beta users.

Customizable attachments grid

Google is testing two designs, with the one on the right taking up more of your screen.

	

Learn more

Instead of a top toolbar, long-pressing on a message or image opens a floating menu as the background blurs. Another press lets you copy just a part of the chat. Previously, you had to copy the entire message.

iOS 27 adds replies & photo reactions to Android-iPhone RCS

When iOS 27 launches this fall, Android-iPhone conversations over RCS will gain support for inline replies that include quotes, as well as photo reactions with the actual emoji instead of just the text description. This feature is currently in beta.

More

Read receipts redesign II

In recent weeks, Google Messages has mostly reverted to the two-circle read receipts underneath the message design after trying a single circle within the bubble.

Google is now testing a variant that uses the old icons but moves the timestamp and encryption lock. You now view that information by swiping left, with direct replies accessed by a right swipe.

Learn more

Messages for web removing QR code pairing

Going forward, Messages for web users will have to use Google Account sign-in. As of late April, the QR code method is still available.

Learn more

Read receipts redesign I

Read receipts are now placed in a circle at the bottom-right corner of message bubbles and images. You swipe left to see timestamps and the encryption lock, while you can swipe right to reply. This first started appearing in August of 2024, but is now seeing wide beta and stable availability.

[Rolling out] Google Keep in Google Messages

The new Google Keep integration lets you quickly create and share notes inside chats. If you don’t see a contextual suggestion to “Create list,” open the ‘plus’ menu for a new “Keep Notes” tile.

This will slide up a sheet that shows your list of notes and the “Create a note” button. Upon selecting or starting a note, you’ll see a send button in the bottom-right corner. Afterward, there’s a live preview in the conversation thread.

As of early September, Google Messages is still rolling out the Keep integration.

Chat theme

Google Messages now lets you extensively customize conversations with a “Chat theme.” Replacing “Change colors” from 2024, you access this new option from the three-dot overflow menu. Be on the lookout for a red badge when this is rolled out for your phone. Themes will only appear on your device.

The Colors carousel themes message bubbles. There are nine options, with Dynamic Color being the first option and responding to the background of your chat.

	

The Wallpapers option lets you change the background of the conversation. In addition to uploading your own image, Google provides the following collections: Animals, Architecture, Black & White, Cityscapes, Landscapes, Macro, Space, Sunsets, and Textures.

title: Samsung is shutting down ‘Quick Measure’ and ‘AR Doodle’ apps for Galaxy phones
snippet: Samsung is shutting down two long-available augmented reality (AR) apps on Galaxy phones, with “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” both going away later this year. more…
fullText:
Samsung is shutting down two long-available augmented reality (AR) apps on Galaxy phones, with “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” both going away later this year.

Confirmed in Galaxy Store listings for both the “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” apps, Samsung will be shutting down these AR experiences on December 31, 2026. Samsung explains that both will be “returning with improved services in the future.”

“Quick Measure” is an AR app that lets you get measurements of real-world distance from your phone, while “AR Doodle” lets you “draw” on real-world locations through the camera app.

The shutdown will block new downloads of both apps, while also pulling the plug on any future updates. The app won’t just stop working immediately, but any OS updates will break the apps in time. Notably, Samsung seems to have hidden both app listings on the latest One UI versions, making them inivisible in the Galaxy Store.

	

Samsung says:

Please be advised that service for the Quick measure app is scheduled to be terminated on 31 December 2026.

After this date, new downloads and update support for the existing app will be discontinued. You may continue to use the app if it is already downloaded, but please be aware that some features may not function properly.

Additionally, compatibility support for the Quick measure app will no longer be provided for future OS updates.

We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause and thank all our customers for their loyal use of the Quick measure app. We are committed to returning with improved services in the future.

It’s unclear when these replacement apps might arrive, but it’s certainly a shame to see these going away.

title: Google Messages slowly rolling out fix for bug that randomly sends old texts to other people
snippet: A bug in Google Messages is causing the app to randomly send old text messages to other random people and, while it’s still happening, a fix is slowly on the way. more…
fullText:
A bug in Google Messages is causing the app to randomly send old text messages to other random people and, while it’s still happening, a fix is slowly on the way.

The issue at play here sees Google Messages reviving old messages that were sent to a contact and sending those alongside another new message to a different contact. You can see the problem, right? A message meant for your significant other could theoretically be sent to your parents, for example. It’s been reported by many users in recent weeks, with the problem even visible in real time; some have tested sending themselves messages only to see old messages randomly inserted into the same thread.

Highlighted by Droid-Life, there are still reports of this behavior popping up right now, with some reports popping up just in the past day.

It’s not happening for everyone, but it’s obviously a major issue for those affected. Sending old messages to random people could, at the very least, result in confusion, but could go as far as revealing private information. 

	

In a statement, Google confirmed that it is aware of the issue and has a fix, but it’s not rolling out quickly. Google said:

We’re currently rolling out a fix that will reach everyone over the coming weeks. Please ensure you stay up to date with the most recent version of Google Messages.

That was on September 2, and reports continue to pop up now, the better part of a week later. Updates continue to land on Google Play, so go check for a patch if you’re affected. Let us know in the comments below if you’re running into this bug.
