title: Ninja Takes on Caraway With Cheaper, ‘More Durable’ Ceramic Cookware
snippet: Ninja’s NeverQuit Cookware is available for purchase now.
fullText:
One thing about Ninja: the company will keep its fan base happy with new release after new release. On the heels of launching its first-ever water filter, the HydraSense, Ninja’s first-ever ceramic-coated cookware,  Ninja NeverQuit, is here and it’s poised to challenge some of the leaders in the category.

The new line of cookware is dishwasher-safe and oven-safe up to 550 degrees Fahrenheit. The pieces stack for easy storage, and the lid handles can be pushed down to save even more space. Ninja says the ceramic cookware is twice as durable as competitor Caraway, but the company didn’t share what testing, if any, supported that claim. We also haven’t gotten our hands on the pans yet to independently test its durability or do a side-by-side comparison with Caraway or other ceramic cookware.

	

			

	

			

									

						A Guide to Nontoxic Cookware					

							

		

One thing is certain, Ninja’s new cookware is more affordable than Caraway. The NeverQuit three-piece frying pan set is $250, while Caraway’s three frying pans with lids set sells for $395.

Ceramic-coated cookware is often favored because it’s nonstick, easy to clean and can be made without chemicals typically used in non-stick cookware, such as PTFE (Teflon). Ninja says the NeverQuit coating is “designed without lead, cadmium, PFAS, PFOA, PTFE or hard anodization.”

The new line is available in a three-, six- or 12-piece set. The 12-piece set includes 8-inch and 10.25-inch frying pans, a 4-quart pan with lid, a steamer basket, a spatula, a pasta ladle, a 6-quart stock pot with lid, a 6-quart metal strainer basket and a spoon rest.

Ninja also teased an upcoming stainless-steel cookware line named “Ninja Eversear,” but hasn’t announced a launch date just yet.

title: ‘P-Valley’ Season 3 Sets Release Date on Starz. Catch a New Trailer, Details Here
snippet: The long, long wait will soon be over, even if Diamond has rotted in that car trunk by now.
fullText:
Uncle Clifford will be turning the lights back on at The Pynk, because P-Valley season 3 is due to arrive on Starz in December. Created by Katori Hall, the popular drama has been absent from TV screens since season 2 ended its run in summer 2022, leaving fans to wonder about the fate of the Chucalissa strip club and its colorful characters, like Nicco Annan’s Uncle Clifford, Mercedes (Brandee Evans), Keyshawn (Shannon Thornton) and Lil’ Murda (J. Alphonse Nicholson). The first two episodes of the new season will debut on Friday, Dec. 4.

A finale cliffhanger at the end of the last season saw Tyler Lepley’s Diamond stuck in a car trunk as part of a gang’s revenge plan. Since then, fans have joked about whether he’s still alive due to the show’s lengthy hiatus. It’s unclear whether Lepley and co-star Miracle Watts, who played Big Bone, are returning in season 3. Meanwhile, Keyshawn’s failed attempt to escape her abuser led to a sad turn of events where she wound up in jail. The series will pick up where it left off and take viewers through to the conclusion of this story in this final season. 

First look photos for P-Valley, season 3, show Mercedes, Keyshawn, Lil’ Murda and cowboy-costumed Kiwi, Roulette and Big L. Starz

Hall, who is the showrunner and creator, penned a heartfelt letter to fans, acknowledging the time it took to bring P-Valley from its roots as a stage play to its curtain call on Starz. 

“Adapting my play into three seasons of television over the past decade has been the ride of a lifetime, filled with massive highs and lows that echo the ever-changing TV landscape,” Hall wrote. “The rarest honor a showrunner can have in today’s industry is to end a series on her own terms. This is why I chose to say goodbye with grace, grit and glitter, lowering the curtain on P-Valley at season 3 with a farewell y’all truly deserve.”

Season 3 also features Gail Bean, Harriett D. Foy, Psalms Salazar, Morocco Omari, Dominic DeVore, Jordan M. Cox, Thomas Q. Jones and Loretta Devine among the cast. The first two seasons of P-Valley are available to binge-watch on Starz.

fullText:
KeySmart might make one of the best-designed Android Find Hub trackers in the shape of a credit card, and it’s down to $38 right now.

The KeySmart SmartCard is one of the best form factors in a tracker. title: Google details ADB Wi-Fi 2.0 for more reliable wireless Android debugging
snippet: Available as a part of Android 17, Google is making wireless debugging a whole lot more reliable with ADB Wi-Fi 2.0. more…
fullText:
Available as a part of Android 17, Google is making wireless debugging a whole lot more reliable with ADB Wi-Fi 2.0. 

Wireless debugging has been around in Android for quite some time now, but it’s not always been the most reliable offering. Between more complex pairing and general hiccups in usability, wired has still been the primary choice for many. 

Google is aiming to fix that with ADB Wi-Fi 2.0. In a post, Google details what has changed with the new process, explaining three core updates:

A new server stack (adb): Previously, wireless device connections would sever when network configurations changed or devices were turned off. This meant that connections would drop for common occurrences. With our new mDNS stack, we’ve replaced both Bonjour and legacy mDNS so that your wireless devices more reliably stay connected as you go about your day.

Smarter network handling (adbd): Previously, the workstation’s mDNS client would sporadically drop services. Now, the daemon automatically turns off ADB Wi-Fi when it detects an untrusted network and re-enables itself once running on a user-allowed network.

Improved discoverability in Android Studio: Previously, Wi-Fi pairing was difficult to find. Now, you simply enable wireless debugging on your phone and it will show in Android Studio’s Device Manager.

Google says that these changes have made auto-connect around 32% more reliable, while connections are 66% faster for roughly 90% of connections tested. 

	

For Android Studio, wireless debugging can be used via the “pair over Wi-Fi” button, with a QR code connecting your device to your computer for an ADB connection.

title: The race to build great iPhone Duo apps is about to begin
snippet: When iPhone Duo arrives next month, many third-party apps might not work as well as Apple’s built-in apps. There’s a reason for that, at least initially, though the situation should improve over time. more…
fullText:
When iPhone Duo arrives next month, many third-party apps might not work as well as Apple’s built-in apps. There’s a reason for that, at least initially, though the situation should improve over time.

Three levels of iPhone Duo app support

We shared a look yesterday at how third-party software will work with iPhone Duo. There are three compatibility levels. Apps built for iOS 26 and earlier run in a mode that doesn’t take advantage of the larger display at all. If Apple released the iPhone Duo today, this is how all third-party apps would look.

iOS 27 comes out on Monday, though, and Apple is now accepting app submissions built for the new operating system. iPhone apps built for iOS 27 look much more at home on iPhone Duo. There’s still unused screen space, but it’s not nearly as rough as the other compatibility mode.

Then there’s full iPhone Duo app compatibility. This mode will see apps take full advantage of the iPhone Duo display, including moving controls previously in toolbars previously at the top over to the side.

Standard apps get a head start

If an app uses standard system controls without any custom work around toolbars and navigation bars, this mode will be what you can expect when iPhone Duo ships.

However, it’s very common for apps to use custom solutions for toolbars and navbars. Just take a look at apps that you frequently use. If they don’t look like Apple’s stock apps, there’s a good chance that they’re doing custom work in their app that won’t automatically translate.

For that reason, these kinds of apps will require a lot more work than just building against the iOS 27.1 SDK. The “automatic” compatibility really only works for apps that are strictly standard and already follow Apple’s layout suggestions without deviating at all. 

The race begins (soon, but not yet) with new developer tools

The good news is that Apple will provide developers with tools to prepare their apps for the iPhone Duo before it reaches customers next month. The bad news is that this work can’t start yet.

Apple will need to release a new version of Xcode and the first iOS 27.1 developer beta before developers can test their apps. This will provide a virtual iPhone Duo through Xcode’s simulator, which will help with initial support. However, most developers won’t have access to a real iPhone Duo until launch day. 

And for apps that do a lot of custom layout work, iPhone Duo software optimization will likely be a longer road. And that’s before any considerations for all the special modes that the iPhone Duo supports. 

A valuable new audience for developers

But while the iPhone Duo will be niche to start, it’s also an iPhone and not a virtual reality headset or a specialized version of an otherwise specialized product.

iPhone Duo’s $2000 starting price also means that app developers can expect Duo users to be more likely to spend on the App Store. Prioritizing software updates for Duo customers might just be good business.

Still, iPhone Duo optimizations for major social media apps, banking apps, and any number of games? That will be a big area to watch over the next several months. Just don’t expect everything to be perfectly prepared on day one.

Given how new and ambitious iPhone Duo is in terms of iOS layout and features, we should expect it to be a rare gem to celebrate when a third-party app ships a great iPhone Duo app — at least for the first several months. 

iPhone Duo will start arriving to customers on October 23. Pre-orders begin October 16.

title: The iPhone Duo is Apple at its absolute best (and a little bit at its worst)
snippet: Wow. After Samsung had a seven-year head start on Apple in the foldables market, the company really had to live up to its ethos of waiting until it could do a far better job than everyone else, and boy did it deliver with the iPhone Duo! It was abundantly clear that Apple had thought through every detail of what a foldable iPhone needed to be, and has taken advantage of every benefit the form factor has to offer … more…
fullText:
Wow. After Samsung had a seven-year head start on Apple in the foldables market, the company really had to live up to its ethos of waiting until it could do a far better job than everyone else, and boy did it deliver with the iPhone Duo!

It was abundantly clear that Apple had thought through every detail of what a foldable iPhone needed to be, and has taken advantage of every benefit the form factor has to offer …

It starts with the basics. Prior reports talked about Apple waiting until it could make the crease virtually invisible and ensure the hinge design would be robust enough to survive endless cycles of folding and unfolding, and while the latter remains to be seen, we can already see the work that went into that hinge design.

There’s the under-screen front-facing camera that’s visible when you need it and almost invisible when you don’t.

Apple also thought about all of the different ways in which the device could be held or positioned, and how the software could best take advantage of that.

I’m not sure who first said it, but I think it’s absolutely true that great design is something no-one else thought of, yet looks blindingly obvious in hindsight. The OG iPhone was a great example of this. Other smartphones had physical keyboards and required* a stylus to use them, while the iPhone is used with your finger and a keyboard only appears when it’s required. It was obvious afterwards that of course smartphones should work this way.

*Yes, the Duo supports the Apple Pencil, but it doesn’t require one.

For me, there were plenty of examples of this in the Duo presentation. Why should we need to first isolate a subject in a photo and then copy it into another app when we could simply drag it there directly from the original photo? That’s completely obvious after the fact.

Replacing a camera self-timer with the device simply waiting until everyone stops moving and then taking the photo automatically. Obvious!

	

Then there were the UI features that have no reason to exist but simply look beautiful, like that blurring effect as you fold the phone.

I could go on at some length, but the bottom line is that I had extremely high expectations for this device yet was still blown away by just how good it appears to be. I’m British; the only time we ever use the word “wow” is sarcastically – but I still had to open this piece with it, without a trace of sarcasm.

This device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo. 

And that brings me to that “little bit the worst of Apple” remark in the headline. The company has the ability to create product videos that make us feel we can reach out through the screen and touch the device. Apple can create strong desire for a product we have absolutely no business buying. I’m not the target market for the iPhone Duo, but I do, absolutely, unquestionably want one. How about you?

fullText:
OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics. This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem. In normal circumstances, this would have been celebrated as a historic achievement.

Instead, many mathematicians have watched OpenAI’s relentless advance with growing unease. To them, the company appears less like an enthusiastic newcomer than an impossibly well-resourced interloper, charging into problems they have dedicated their lives to studying with little apparent regard for long-standing norms or the consequences for those left in its wake. At the heart of that unease is a sense that OpenAI is doing mathematics for different reasons. Mathematicians want to advance the field. OpenAI wants to win.

Mathematics is not normally this dramatic, so how did things get this bad? 

This week, The Verge spoke with more than a dozen mathematicians, including Tristan Buckmaster and Andreas Thom, who are at the center of recent controversies surrounding OpenAI’s work in the field. Even those skeptical of the most serious allegations described a field shaken by the tech giant’s conduct and fearful of what it might do next in its determination to trounce its rivals.

Buckmaster has accused OpenAI of failing to adequately explain whether work he did through its tool Codex could have contributed to its recent successes. In a statement to The Verge, OpenAI spokesperson Laurance Fauconnet strenuously denied that material from his prompts had played a role: “We can say categorically that it is impossible for Dr. Buckmaster’s Codex prompts over the last two months to have influenced the system in any way, including training.”

Buckmaster remains unconvinced. “Given their behavior up until this point, one should take such statements with great skepticism,” he said.

Mathematics is not normally this dramatic, so how did things get this bad? A rumor was all it took for tensions to boil over.

OpenAI says it heard some researchers were making progress on Millennium Prize problems and decided to see whether one of its advanced, unreleased models could make headway too. It turns out it could. OpenAI says it took roughly 10,000 agents, tens of millions of dollars of compute, and just 88 hours to find a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.

The company had also discovered who it was racing against: Buckmaster, an NYU professor, and Levent Alpöge, a researcher at one of its fiercest rivals, Anthropic. Among several lines of research, the pair were pursuing Navier-Stokes, though had not yet completed a proof. Some details of what happened next are fiercely contested, but the two sides broadly agree on the basic sequence of events. One thing is particularly clear: Alpöge’s involvement was a problem for OpenAI, despite his saying it was a “personal collaboration” independent of his work with Anthropic.

Even those skeptical of the most serious allegations described a field shaken by the tech giant’s conduct and fearful of what it might do next in its determination to trounce its rivals.

Buckmaster said he contacted OpenAI after learning the company had become aware of their progress and was racing toward a solution of its own. He said discussions with OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck grew contentious and, in his view, threatening, but the company offered a path forward for him — one that excluded Alpöge. Buckmaster said he was offered practically “unlimited compute” to finish his own work, and the opportunity to be the sole author of OpenAI’s paper announcing the breakthrough, which would of course credit its tools.

“All I had to do was throw Levent under the bus,” Buckmaster told The Verge in a phone interview. He said he flatly rejected Bubeck’s offer, which he viewed as a “bribe,” and also began questioning whether OpenAI may have benefited from his use of Codex, one of the company’s AI tools he had been using to tackle the problem. OpenAI has denied that anyone — or any agent — accessed his specific user data, and until its more recent comments acknowledged it could not rule out the possibility data derived from his use of the products was used to improve the model.

Buckmaster ultimately decided to go public with both his work and his account of OpenAI’s conduct. His office, he said, had been transformed into something of a “war room,” with colleagues helping scrutinize his mathematics, coordinate outreach, and even get in touch with lawyers.

Bubeck has rejected Buckmaster’s characterization of the conversations on social media and in an interview with The New York Times. He acknowledged offering OpenAI’s resources to help Buckmaster complete his own proof or to have him take over the writing of the company’s. Strikingly, Bubeck said OpenAI had made similar arrangements with other mathematicians, though did not identify them.

But his account nevertheless makes clear that Alpöge’s affiliation with Anthropic was a sticking point. “From our perspective, how can we have an internal OpenAI project with an Anthropic employee?” he told the Times.

If the goal is to compete in mathematics, there are few bigger trophies than solving a Millennium Prize problem. The seven problems, set out by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, are widely considered among the most formidable challenges in the field. Each carries a $1 million bounty for whoever solves it. Many had already endured decades of intense scrutiny by the time the prizes were established. In the quarter-century since, only one — the Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres — has fallen.

For an AI company looking to prove that its models are the best at mathematics, then, they are irresistible targets. To Buckmaster and many other mathematicians The Verge spoke to, that helps explain why OpenAI moved so ferociously when it heard others were closing in — particularly once a rival AI company appeared to be involved.

For Buckmaster, the episode reinforced something he already believed strongly from a previous spell collaborating with Google DeepMind: “All these tech people are obsessed” with solving big famous problems and are “obsessed with scooping,” he said. “Its all about competition.”

In that world, Tristan Buckmaster said there is an intense fixation on prestige, fame, being first, and being seen to be first. “That’s the only currency,” he said.

He said what often gets “lost” when companies race to solve famous problems are the mathematicians themselves — not just the people whose accumulated work makes these breakthroughs possible, but the reasons they do mathematics to begin with. Yes, some may pursue prestige, but most are simply not trophy hunters. Andras Juhasz, a professor of mathematics at the University of Oxford, described mathematics as an elegant discipline that is part science, part art, with many different motivations driving those working there. “Often there is no immediate practical application,” he said. “They do it because it’s beautiful. They enjoy it. It’s the sense of discovery. It’s natural.”

Unlike classroom-level mathematical exercises, frontier mathematics rarely has a prescribed route to an answer. Researchers can attack problems from any number of angles, some radically different, which makes the ideas that lead to a solution — and who developed them — especially important, perhaps more so than solving a problem itself. Mathematicians care deeply about this lineage because it is how the field expands, with new techniques and methods often proving more consequential than the problem they were designed to solve.

To Buckmaster, his exchanges with Bubeck typify the chasm that separates the worlds of research mathematics and Big Tech, and highlight the differences between what is considered valuable in research. Reading from notes he took while chatting with Bubeck, he said the OpenAI researcher was visibly taken aback when he rejected the company’s offer to take credit. “I could see Sébastien’s face. He was shocked when I said I don’t care about the Millennium Prize,” he recalled.

Buckmaster said he had encountered a similar mentality among tech researchers before. In that world, he said there is an intense fixation on prestige, fame, being first, and being seen to be first. “That’s the only currency,” he said.

Buckmaster isn’t the only mathematician to come away from an encounter with OpenAI concerned about the company’s motivations. Andreas Thom, a professor at the Technical University of Dresden in Germany, found himself at the center of a controversy last month after OpenAI announced an impressive mathematical result that built heavily on work by him and fellow researcher Gábor Kun. The company quietly amended its announcement to acknowledge the pair’s contribution without announcing or publicly disclosing the change.

Thom described the ordeal as “not a very pleasant experience,” but told The Verge he had largely put it behind him until Buckmaster went public. His allegations prompted Thom to revisit an unresolved question about OpenAI’s breakthrough: whether conversations he and his colleagues had with ChatGPT about the research could have been used to help improve the models that ultimately cracked the problem he’d spent years working on.

Only OpenAI has the information needed to answer that question, Thom said. “To be honest, I suspect that they don’t even know.” The people training the models and using them to produce mathematical results are “a different kind of people,” he said. To him, that’s hardly an excuse for the uncertainty. “Because it effectively means that they don’t really care, right?”

“The prospect of competing with powerful AI companies, whose resources far exceed those available to academic research groups, could make them even more reluctant to pursue ambitious questions.”

The tension echoes fights already playing out elsewhere. Writers, musicians, artists, and media companies have all challenged AI companies over systems built from vast stores of human-created work, often without permission, recognition, or compensation. While mathematics may seem a world apart, the underlying question is the same: What do companies owe to the people whose accumulated work they ingested to build their systems?

In Thom’s case, the question remains unresolved. OpenAI did not respond to The Verge’s question on whether data from conversations Thom and his colleagues had with ChatGPT could have contributed to the company’s solution that built on his work.

More broadly, Thom said he resents what he sees as a failure to recognize the “the communal effort that this entire community has put into all the research results” underpinning AI’s recent mathematical advances. Companies, he said, “are just now using [it] as if it was kind of nothing.”

“I think there is a certain attitude that I don’t like in that,” he said.

It’s not that mathematicians are strangers to competition — researchers care deeply about priority and bitter disputes over who came first litter mathematical history — but while competition does not preclude cooperation, these are no ordinary competitors. Scooping in mathematics has historically been relatively difficult for obvious reasons: Very few people have the specialized expertise to swoop in on a discovery at speed. AI companies operate on a different scale. Researchers worry they could turn scooping into something of an industrial process mathematicians would have little chance of fighting back against, rapidly spinning up thousands upon thousands of agents and enormous amounts of compute whenever word spreads that a breakthrough is close.

To Buckmaster, OpenAI could have easily collaborated with researchers rather than race them to results. Indeed, the company seemed perfectly willing to work with him. The problem was Alpöge, or, more specifically, his ties to Anthropic.

“They were in such a rush to publish, to beat Anthropic,” he said. They barely took note of the researchers caught in the middle.

For all the rush, OpenAI won’t know whether it has won the Millennium Prize for solving Navier-Stokes for years. The Clay Mathematics Institute requires a period of two years to have passed since a result was published, during which it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.” For now, Navier-Stokes occupies a peculiar limbo: The Institute has removed it from its list of unsolved problems, though hasn’t yet declared it solved. “The process is deliberately unhurried,” the Institute said in a statement.

OpenAI, meanwhile, has already moved on. In a statement to The Verge, OpenAI’s Fauconnet said that “since the completion of Navier-Stokes we have made substantial progress on another Millennium Prize problem,” adding that the company is “working through how to share these results thoughtfully.”

Which problem remains unclear. Unconfirmed speculation on social media suggests this could be the Hodge conjecture, which concerns, very roughly speaking, how complex geometric shapes can be understood in terms of simpler building blocks. Rumors are also circulating that Anthropic is closing in on a Millennium Prize problem of its own.

As the two giants of AI race to collect yet more mathematical trophies, they are discovering that astonishing results alone are not enough to earn the trust of the community they are transforming.

Mathematicians are beginning to push back. Many The Verge spoke to, even the most enthusiastic proponents of AI in the field, worried the companies were having a chilling effect on research, pushing mathematicians to be more secretive about unfinished work for fear someone may swoop in and beat them to it. Several said colleagues who had previously compiled lists of important unsolved problems were reconsidering the practice, concerned that what was intended as a useful resource for the field could instead become a list of targets for AI companies.

Resistance is becoming increasingly public. In June, mathematicians published the Leiden Declaration, a set of principles for the responsible use of AI in mathematics that has been endorsed by the International Mathematical Union and signed by nearly 3,900 people, an increase of nearly 500 people since I last covered it in mid-August. It urges policymakers, governments, the media, and other groups to not buy into “the hype” created by companies who “overstate the capabilities of their products.” As the Millennium Prize controversy raged, OpenAI withdrew its sponsorship of an undergraduate mathematics hackathon at Caltech following fierce opposition decrying the intrusion of corporate interests and worries the event would create a deluge of low-quality “slop mathematics.”

“They don’t care anything about us as a community. It’s all about this petty drama between two trillion-dollar companies that are acting like children.”

Shing-Tung Yau, a professor of mathematics at China’s Tsinghua University, an emeritus professor at Harvard, and a recipient of the prestigious Fields Medal, told The Verge he worries about the potential effect on young researchers. “Working on hard problems already carries considerable risk for Ph.D. students and junior faculty,” he said. “The prospect of competing with powerful AI companies, whose resources far exceed those available to academic research groups, could make them even more reluctant to pursue ambitious questions.”

Yau declined to weigh in on allegations that researchers’ work may have been used by OpenAI, but said he is in favor of an independent review to establish what happened. More broadly, he worries that a lack of transparency and rush to announce first could obscure the intellectual lineage behind a breakthrough. Mathematical credit, he said, should reflect intellectual contributions, not who had budget for the most compute or made the loudest announcement.

Yau pointed to another problem, too. OpenAI and other AI companies occupy a peculiar position as both the providers of important research tools and, in a way, researchers. It “raises a serious conflict-of-interest concern,” he said, particularly as they could benefit from privileged access to customers’ unfinished and unpublished work.

“That concern deserves a substantive response,” he said. “It should not simply be dismissed as ordinary competition.”

A lot of this growing sense of unease comes down to trust. Mathematicians do not have to accept the most explosive allegations against OpenAI to worry about a company that both provides their research tools and, simultaneously, competes with them.

“Yeah, quite honestly, I don’t think that some data security announcement or whatever will really solve it,” Thom said. “I don’t really trust them.” Buckmaster felt similarly: “Why should we trust anything they said?”

Buckmaster said the reaction from colleagues to his going public had been overwhelmingly positive. But there was an undercurrent of something else too: fear. He told The Verge he initially intended to thank those who supported him when he went public with his experiences. He elected not to after many expressed discomfort at the idea of having their names publicly attached. “The reality is that mathematicians are actually scared of them,” Buckmaster said, referring to the AI companies.

And fear is hardly a solid foundation on which to build a productive and healthy research community. Buckmaster isn’t convinced it matters much to those companies involved. “They don’t care anything about us as a community,” he said. “It’s all about this petty drama between two trillion-dollar companies that are acting like children.”

To them, the company appears less like an enthusiastic newcomer than an impossibly well-resourced interloper, charging into problems they have dedicated their lives to studying with little apparent regard for long-standing norms or the consequences for those left in its wake. title: Google Pixel Tablet has been discontinued, out of stock everywhere
snippet: The Pixel Tablet is done, as Google has officially pulled the plug on the slate by entirely deleting the listing on its store. more…
fullText:
The Pixel Tablet is done, as Google has officially pulled the plug on the slate by entirely deleting the listing on its store.

Google launched the Pixel Tablet in 2023 as a hybrid of a typical Android tablet and a Nest Hub smart display. It was met with mixed reactions, but still serves as the only tablet in Google’s lineup. 

And now it’s done.

While updates are set to continue through 2028, Google has quietly removed the Pixel Tablet from its Store. A direct link to the listing now redirects to the homepage, while there’s also no mention of the Pixel Tablet anywhere on the Google Store besides a few accessories that remain. The change was spotted by Jetstream earlier today. 

	

Sales of the Pixel Tablet closed up in late August (thanks Noah!), but the listing was still working roughly a week ago – we checked it when Nest prices went up, and the Tablet was still listed as out of stock at the time (August 31). It’s the same old pattern, a device goes out of stock before being removed from the store. Generally speaking, removing the device from its store is Google’s way of marking a device as discontinued – another recent example would be Nest Mini and Nest Audio, which were removed and confirmed as discontinued not long after going out of stock. 

Google never did ship a Pixel Tablet sequel, with rumors of some big upgrades being canceled over profitability concerns. Had a sequel continued on, it allegedly would have arrived in 2025, with a third-gen release in 2027 that was also shelved.

	

While third-party retailers often have stock left over when Google ends its own sales of a product, Pixel Tablet is out of stock everywhere we’ve looked. Amazon doesn’t even have any third-party sellers with stock left.

RIP.

title: Motorola teases wide Razr Fold as its ‘next move’ in response to iPhone Duo debut
snippet: Apple’s iPhone Duo announcement has triggered a couple of companies, and it’s apparently warranted at least one teaser for even more foldables. This one seems to be a wide version of the Motorola Razr Fold. more…
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone Duo announcement has triggered a couple of companies, and it’s apparently warranted at least one teaser for even more foldables. This one seems to be a wide version of the Motorola Razr Fold.

After years of watching manufacturers improve on the concept of a foldable phone, Apple has a genuine answer – the iPhone Duo. In a lot of respects, it looks like the original Pixel Fold. But software seems to be a heavy selling point, with plenty of tricks and touches that sell the idea of an iOS-powered foldable.

The fallout has been interesting. Samsung’s team took to Twitter/X to acknowledge Apple’s release, with a slew of posts that almost seem clingy. They didn’t have anything solid to offer, though. But Motorola did.

The mobile company responsible for the Razr of years past and the Razr foldables current posted a snarky little video on Instagram in response to the iPhone Duo’s existence. A series of shots shows Razr phones spanning back a few generations snapping shut. The iconic pink Motorola Razr flip phone starts it off. The last recognizable phone in the video is a Motorola Razr Fold, which launched earlier this year.

	

Right after that, the video ends with a blacked-out foldable that resembles the iPhone Duo’s short and stout nature. It’s not Apple’s new release, but it’s possible it could be a wide Razr Fold from Motorola. In the post, Motorola calls it its “next move,” which seems telling enough.

If our eyes can be trusted, there are a couple of details to pick out for what could be a wide Motorola Razr Fold. The camera bar spans the entire width of the phone’s rear panel. A button can also be seen on the top left of the inner display view. The iPhone Duo has two volume rockers on the right side.

It’s just a silhouette, and those little details could prove to be completely off. But Motorola isn’t ready to say what the device is, or when it will launch. It simply wants users to know it exists since the hype for short and wide foldables seems to be growing, thanks to Samsung and now Apple.

title: Samsung reacts to Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo; ‘reheating our leftovers’
snippet: Samsung is apparently of two minds when it comes to reacting to Apple’s first foldable device, with some interesting reactions to the iPhone Duo’s unveiling, calling the device “a Sims sequel” and “reheating our leftovers.” more…
fullText:
Samsung is apparently of two minds when it comes to reacting to Apple’s first foldable device, with some interesting reactions to the iPhone Duo’s unveiling, calling the device “a Sims sequel” and “reheating our leftovers.”

Apple’s first foldable is official, with the iPhone Duo sharing a form factor similar to that of Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8. Samsung’s device has been very well received since its debut in July, though one could argue that the new shape was somewhat of a reaction to Apple’s imminent arrival on the scene. Chicken or egg, your choice, but Samsung’s public reaction has been quite something to watch.

The foldable pioneer was welcoming to Apple ahead of the launch, but the Twitter/X feed tells another story. Samsung called the iPhone Duo a “Sim sequel” and “So far, so same,” referring to how much of what the iPhone Duo can do has been seen on existing Android foldables, including Galaxy Z Fold 8. 

Samsung further poked fun at Apple only having one foldable form factor and, for whatever reason, took issue with the idea of using the Duo as a clock, but also called the iPhone Duo a case of “reheating our leftovers.” 

	

Let us know when you're done reheating our leftovers 😉

— Samsung Mobile US (@SamsungMobileUS) September 9, 2026

	

Bold statement given the complete 180-degree turn the Fold 8’s design is compared to Samsung’s long history of book-style foldables. Surely a coincidence, but I digress. 

Samsung even pulled Duolingo into the conversation to poke fun at Apple’s branding – Duolingo itself had already done – with Duolingo replying to call Samsung an “ugly stranger” in reference to a viral meme.

Apple’s iPhone Duo launches in October for $1,999.

title: Boox Picco is exceptionally tiny for an e-reader, but it parts ways with Android and third-party apps
snippet: Boox offered some wandering the halls of Messe Berlin at IFA 2026 the opportunity to check out its most exciting upcoming release – a tiny e-reader called the “Picco” that you could probably pocket and take anywhere. more…
fullText:
Boox offered some wandering the halls of Messe Berlin at IFA 2026 the opportunity to check out its most exciting upcoming release – a tiny e-reader called the “Picco” that you could probably pocket and take anywhere.

Boox laid out a product trajectory over the last few years that builds on Android to offer an e-reader experience open to third-party apps. That includes Google Play Books, Kindle, and so much more.

The Boox Picco, which is slated for a November release, won’t offer that experience.

Instead, this e-reader experience hinges on a “take anywhere” design coming in at somewhere just under 4 inches. At that size, it’s the ultimate travel e-reader if you’re ok with a rather small viewing area.

	

It’s garnered a lot of hype for an e-reader, and it deserves a lot of it. It’s small, thin, and has some of Boox’s best features, like an adjustable front light for reading at any time of the day. It even has a set of custom buttons and page rockers built specifically for an easy experience.

Related: The Boox Go 10.3 Gen II is as massive as it is minimal, and I love that for it

But the Boox Picco won’t run Android, and that feels like a big loss. Android e-readers, like much of the company’s backlog, allow users to install third-party apps beyond what the OS offers. In essence, it opens the doors to your existing libraries you’ve built over time from apps like Kindle or Google Play Books. Without those apps, you’re left with the Boox store and epub files.

The Picco will come with a companion app that lets users transfer files to the reader, and even though what we got hands-on time with was an early unit, it seemed like a solid system. But this leaves you limited on options, and you’ll have to find epub versions of your favorite stories and publications.

You might also be disappointed if you were expecting MagSafe compatibility or Qi2.2 support to get it to stick to the back of your phone.

I can’t let that entirely detract from the absolutely adorable e-reader. The early unit we played around with felt great in hand, and even with a tiny screen, I can see plenty of uses for such a small device. It’s essentially the size of a mini field journal, and carrying it on you in your bag or even pocket all day is a no-brainer if you know you’ll get some downtime to catch up on a book or two.

The lack of Android probably also facilitates a more compelling price. Boox says the device will be listed for somewhere around $100, though no details are final. If the Boox Picco hits that price tag and the experience is as easy as it seems it will be, the Picco might deserve every bit of praise it’s getting before it’s even released.

Boox plans to launch the Picco sometime in November.

title: Google Photos trash bin now deletes media after 30 days, down from 60 days
snippet: Google Photos has updated its trash bin timeline, cutting the time from 60 days to 30 days as of September 2026. more…
fullText:
Google Photos has updated its trash bin timeline, cutting the time from 60 days to 30 days as of September 2026.

The trash bin in Google Photos gives users a chance to recover deleted photos and videos for a limited period of time. That period was 60 days for the longest time, effectively giving users about two months to recover anything that might have been deleted by accident or simply needed to be recovered. 

Google has now cut that to 30 days.

The change is rolling out now, as noticed in an app pop-up by the folks over at Android Authority earlier this week. It’s also live on a Google support page where the company explains:

	

Photos and videos that you delete will stay in your trash for 30 days before they are permanently deleted. Photos and videos that were permanently deleted can’t be restored.

That previously read as 60 days, with the change apparently being effective as of September 4, 2026, according to archived versions of that page. Just a day prior, it still read as 60 days.

title: Matt Mullenweg returns as Automattic CEO two days after getting booted
snippet: Two days after being placed on a paid leave of absence, Matt Mullenweg says he has been reinstated as CEO of Automattic, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch. WordPress Executive Director Mary Hubbard confirmed Mullenweg's return to the CEO role in a Friday post on X, which the official WordPress account shared and Mullenweg reposted. I'm relieved and pleased to see Matt Mullenweg return as CEO of Automattic, the largest financial contributor to the WordPress project. Having WordPress's Co-founder and Project Lead at the helm gives me confidence that their support will remain strong. Matt has my support. - Mary Hubbard (@4thhubba … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Jay Peters

 

is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Two days after being placed on a paid leave of absence, Matt Mullenweg says he has been reinstated as CEO of Automattic, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch. WordPress Executive Director Mary Hubbard confirmed Mullenweg’s return to the CEO role in a Friday post on X, which the official WordPress account shared and Mullenweg reposted.

As 404 Media reported on Wednesday, Mullenweg had told staff in Slack that morning that CFO Mark Davies “conspired” with the board of directors, who voted to “put me on a paid leave of absence.” (Mullenweg said he voted against that.) He also told staff that the board had voted for Davies to become interim CEO. Davies, in a separate message, said that Mullenweg would still be a board member, according to 404 Media. An Automattic spokesperson told The Verge that Mullenweg was “currently on leave” from the company and confirmed Davies’ interim appointment.

In the message viewed by TechCrunch, however, Mullenweg wrote that the board is “back in agreement” and that he’s “in control of Automattic.” He added that “A lot happened in the past 48 hours that we need to sort out, and I hope much of it was a misunderstanding, because I have huge respect and regard for those involved.” TechCrunch reports that Davies’ Slack account has been deactivated and that Mullenweg had removed “all” admins from Automattic’s Slack.

404 Media also reported on Mullenweg’s posts about his apparent return, saying he made the posts “late Thursday evening.”

Automattic, which owns companies like Wordpress.com, Tumblr, and Beeper, didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment from The Verge. At 12:20PM ET on Friday, Mullenweg posted on X that “If you don’t have a coup attempt every few years, you’re not hiring strong enough leaders,” adding in a separate post that “I think this was my fifth.” Mullenweg also published a blog post on Friday titled “Major Life Announcement” about making an offer to buy a houseboat.

Updates, September 11th: Added 404 Media’s report and a post from WordPress’ executive director.

title: Matt Mullenweg tells (trolls?) Automattic staff, saying he’s back in control after CEO ouster
snippet: In a Slack message seen by TechCrunch, Matt Mullenweg told Automattic employees he’s back in control of the company, days after its board put him on leave. Automattic has not yet confirmed the apparent reversal.
fullText:
Matt Mullenweg has posted a message to Automattic’s Slack, claiming he is back in control as CEO of the WordPress.com parent company, according to a screenshot of the message seen by TechCrunch, which was confirmed by multiple employee sources. The post arrives only days after Automattic’s board voted to oust Mullenweg as CEO for unknown reasons. 

Automattic has been asked to confirm if Mullenweg’s statement is true, but has not yet responded to repeated requests for comment.  Mullenweg responded to our inquiry, saying a blog post is forthcoming. When it dropped, it was about him buying a houseboat.

Friday afternoon, Mary Hubbard, the Executive Director of WordPress.org, wrote on X that she was “relieved and pleased to see Matt Mullenweg return as CEO of Automattic.”

This story is still developing.

Founder advice: If you don't have a coup attempt every few years, you're not hiring strong enough leaders.

— Matt Mullenweg (@photomatt) September 11, 2026

On Wednesday, the WordPress founder and a key advocate for the open source community told his team via Slack that Automattic’s board members had “conspired” behind his back by voting to put him on a paid leave of absence. The company’s chief financial officer, Mark Davies, was made interim CEO in the process, Mullenweg said.

At the time, a spokesperson from Automattic confirmed to TechCrunch that Mullenweg was on leave and Davies was interim CEO.

Early Friday morning, Mullenweg shared the following new message on Automattic’s Slack: 

“(Don’t call it a comeback…) Howdy everybody! Happy to announce the board is back in agreement, and I’m in control of Automattic. A lot happened in the past 48 hours that we need to sort out, and I hope much of it was a misunderstanding, because I have huge respect and regard for those involved.” 

He also posted a link to the YouTube video for LL Cool J’s “Mama Said Knock You Out.”

As of the time of writing, no one at Automattic had heard a confirmation from the board. Mark Davies’ Slack account was also deactivated, sources said.

However, TechCrunch heard yesterday that Mullenweg had removed all Slack admins from the Automattic Slack and made an odd post about being a “pirate” in which he cursed. (Mullenweg famously does not curse). 

Given this situation, it’s hard to know if he’s now trolling or if legitimate changes have been made. 

We asked Mullenweg if he was trolling on Slack, and he replied, “I’m not a troll I’m a pirate, obviously.” 

After his surprise removal as CEO this week, Mullenweg’s public and private social media posts suggested he wasn’t done fighting the decision. On Reddit, he told those speculating what this meant for the open source community that they didn’t know what they were talking about after initially replying, “Hey y’all. I’m here, just fine,” to a Reddit post linking to the 404 Media article that first broke the news.

On X, Mullenweg also posted that “Things are different than they appear,” and said he was in need of sysadmins and security researchers to help him move some of his stuff hosted at Automattic elsewhere, even though he supported Davies as CEO.

In both places, he suggested that Silver Lake, the PE firm that’s the majority owner of the hosting company WP Engine, which is currently embroiled in a lawsuit with Mullenweg and Automattic, was involved in this plan to “destroy” his life.

On Friday morning, Mullenweg posted on X, “Boards are never boring,” followed by a laughing/crying emoji.

 

This story was updated after its initial publication with additional comments and links to social media posts. 

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

		Sarah has worked as a reporter for TechCrunch since August 2011. She joined the company after having previously spent over three years at ReadWriteWeb. Prior to her work as a reporter, Sarah worked in I.T. across a number of industries, including banking, retail and software.

You can contact or verify outreach from Sarah by emailing sarahp@techcrunch.com or via encrypted message at sarahperez.01 on Signal.

title: Motorola’s wide Razr Fold wants to have ‘3D glass’ and a creaseless display
snippet: The puzzle pieces for the Motorola wide Razr Fold are slowly coming together. A recent World Power Consortium listing for the device, along with leaked internal mockups from Motorola’s design team, more or less cements a Wide Razr Fold in the works to take on the Galaxy Fold 8 and iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
The puzzle pieces for the Motorola wide Razr Fold are slowly coming together. A recent World Power Consortium listing for the device, along with leaked internal mockups from Motorola’s design team, more or less cements a Wide Razr Fold in the works to take on the Galaxy Fold 8 and iPhone Duo.

Earlier this month, we obtained internal concept images of what’s very likely the Motorola Razr Fold Wide, though it probably won’t go by that name. They were never published because we didn’t feel there was sufficient supporting evidence at the time. There was no teaser from Motorola at the time, though the images we obtained contained watermarks from Lenovo/Motorola. Those are key to why we’re now posting these.

Motorola’s concept sketches show off a surprising amount of detail. For instance, portions of the mockup are backed by descriptions like “bezel-less” and “3D glass,” referring to the cover display. The latter descriptor sits next to a drawing of a Razr, not the Fold. It still may refer to a new push for a different cover display panel. It’s possible “3D glass” refers to curved screen edges similar to what we often see on the Motorola Edge series.

It also looks like Motorola wants to get closer to Apple’s design philosophy with a bezel-less front display, even with sharp left corners and rounded right edges. Without a bezel, the cover display would have to have the same look as the iPhone Duo. The other option is something like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which uses bezels to soften the harsh corners on the left of the screen.

	

Another page in the document suggests Motorola wants to get as close as possible to a creaseless display with the wide Razr Fold, as seen plainly written across one of the images. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo get extremely close to this, but not quite. Maybe Motorola has the ability to reduce the inner display’s crease to nothing, maybe it’s just marketing talk. Either way, the existing Razr Fold has a more noticeable crease than most, so there’s plenty of room for improvement.

What makes these leaked images worth noting is that the same watermark is used in WPC listings for Motorola Razr devices. It showed up on the existing Razr Fold’s listing back in April, and what brought this to our attention was a new listing posted this week that’s also for the existing Razr Fold, but a Verizon variant of the device. As of now, that doesn’t exist, but the model number is identical outside of a “V” designation that points to a Verizon variant. This updated model also jumps up to the Qi 2.2.1 standard version, though still without magnets inside.

It’s hard to make any definite assessments around the Razr Fold on Verizon based on this listing alone, but the watermark tells us that the leaked materials are almost certainly a real indicator of what Motorola wants to deliver on its wider Razr Fold release.

title: Pebblebee’s latest Android Find Hub trackers have bright neon colors, available today
snippet: Pebblebee is launching its latest batch of Android Find Hub trackers, with new “Hotline Pink” and “Techno Lime” colorways that are available today. more…
fullText:
Pebblebee is launching its latest batch of Android Find Hub trackers, with new “Hotline Pink” and “Techno Lime” colorways that are available today.

In its lineup of Clip 5 color batches, Pebblebee’s latest theme is “Neon Pulse.” This includes very bright and vibrant “Hotline Pink” and “Techno Lime” colors that look great in person.

Pebblebee started these occasional color drops last year with the first batch including Emerald Storm and Amethyst Purple, the second Hot Coral and Subzero, and the Summer drop with “Creamsicle Crush” and “Tidal Cyan.”

The new colors follow up on that Summer drop with similarly-bright offerings, with the green being especially bright in person. 

	

Functionally, these remain the same as a standard Pebblebee Clip 5, offering integration with both Android Find Hub and Apple Find My, a rechargable battery via USB-C, as well as a built-in light and 130dB siren. It also integrates with Pebblebee Alert, which offers some safety features.

These new colorways are available today on Amazon and through Pebblebee’s website for $35.

title: Xiaomi 18 Fold goes on sale with full specs and a Galaxy Z Fold 8 comparison [Gallery]
snippet: Following an appearance at IFA 2026 last week, Xiaomi has posted the full details of its new wide Fold, while it’s also been directly compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8. more…
fullText:
Following an appearance at IFA 2026 last week, Xiaomi has posted the full details of its new wide Fold, while it’s also been directly compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

Pre-orders for the Xiaomi 18 Fold are now open in China and, with that, a full breakdown of the foldable’s specs. This includes a 5.38-inch outer display, 7.58-inch inner display, as well as the Xiaomi XRing O3 chipset that was previously announced. But, going further down the list, there are some other powerful specs on offer.

A 6,000 mAh battery (with 67W wired charging/50W wireless) powers the show, way bigger than the 4,800 mAh battery in Samsung’s device. That’s despite a clear difference in size. As The Verge shows in a hands-on, Samsung’s wide foldable is both taller and narrower than Xiaomi’s when folded. The same article calls out that Xiaomi’s device has almost the exact aspect ratio as an IMAX display. 

Images via The Verge

Xiaomi’s listing further details the dimensions at 117.8 x 83.6 x 10.68mm when the foldable is closed, opening up to 163.8mm wide and 5.02mm thick when unfolded. Storage and memory options range from 12GB + 256GB up to 16GB + 1TB. 

	

The triple camera array around back includes a 200MP main sensor, 50MP 3.5x telephoto, and a 50MP ultrawide too. 

Colors include “Warm Gold,” “White,” “Black,” and “Nishino Red” (translated).

There’s also a light pink “Ceramic” model.

The Xiaomi 18 Fold is available for purchase now in China starting at ¥10,999. Directly converted, that’s just shy of $1,640 USD. It’s still unclear if or when this foldable might make its way to global markets, but it’s certainly an intriguing release.

title: Jell-O and Beer May Hold the Keys to Brewing Houses on Mars
snippet: The yeast used won’t brew beer, but it can help brew a building.
fullText:
Establishing life on another planet is a multifaceted process with many problems. Housing is one major challenge, but a new study suggests researchers have found a way to build living quarters on Mars using materials already present on the planet, along with a couple of other clever ingredients. 

The study, published on Sept. 10 in the journal Chem Circularity, reports that researchers found a way to turn the sand on Mars into what is functionally low-grade concrete using little more than gelatin, yeast, and the natural Martian environment. Combine the three ingredients, and the dry, cold, low-pressure environment of Mars freeze-dries the mixture, turning it into a porous, foam-like material strong enough to build houses on the red planet. 

“My inspiration came from freeze-dried fruits that become harder,” senior author Jishen Qiu of The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology said in a statement. “So, I asked myself if we can take advantage of that and make some materials.”

According to Qiu, the concrete produced by this method measures 10 to 12 megapascals (a metric unit of pressure), putting it on par with low-grade concrete here on Earth. This concrete is strong enough to build a one- or two-story house on Earth, and since Earth has three times the gravity of Mars, it’s more than strong enough to build structures on Mars too. 

Radiation protection is a bit more tricky, but Qiu told CNET in an email that it could involve a double wall packed with roughly 2mm of Martian soil. More study is needed.

The gelatin is run-of-the-mill porcine gelatin, which means it’s made from pigs, and it’s quite literally the same stuff that Jell-O uses to make its jiggly dessert. For the yeast, Qiu created a specially engineered version covered in the same proteins mussels use to attach themselves to rocks. These two ingredients, along with pounded-up Martian rocks and water, create the material. 

Mars’ frigid cold, low-pressure environment effectively freeze-dries the material, causing water to sublimate, which means it turns directly from a solid to a vapor, leaving the Martian concrete behind. Because this process is so fast, items must be 3D-printed in real time to work properly.

“Based on our experiment, a normal constructional printer can work in such a harsh environment,” Qiu told CNET. “The mixer may be sealed to control the air pressure before the material [is] extruded out. Casting or printing into standard blocks would be feasible.”

The team tested it by 3D printing two small beehive-shaped structures about the size of a wine cork in a simulated Martian environment, but the team believes the process can scale up. Once the structures have reached the end of their usefulness, people on Mars can break them down, mix them in a bioreactor, and brew a new building with the same materials, as long as there’s still yeast alive to reproduce. 

An elegant solution to a long-standing problem

Houses on Mars made with this method would resemble beehives, but be made of what is essentially concrete. Nin Liu

Delivering humans to Mars is already a tall order. Elon Musk tried to get it done by 2025 and missed the mark by at least a decade. However, getting people there is only half the battle. Once there, they need a place to live that can withstand the Martian environment, which includes temperature swings of nearly 100 degrees Celsius and virtually no radiation protection from the sun due to the thin Mars atmosphere. 

There are many ideas about the subject, ranging from inflatable domiciles to the idea of letting self-propagating fungi grow whole buildings. Some enterprising scientists from the Indian Space Research Organisation even made space bricks from Martian soil, guar gum, urea, nickel chloride and a bacterium called Sporosarcina pasteurii, which converts urea and calcium into calcite. This lets the soil harden into something resembling concrete.

NASA held a habitat challenge from 2015 to 2019 that tasked companies and researchers to 3D-print homes using unique methods and materials. The winners took home over $2 million in prizes. In short, no stone has been left unturned, and people are using all sorts of exotic materials to try to find the best solution for habitats on Mars, including Qiu.

The team’s approach relies directly on constructing the buildings in the Martian environment as part of its build process, while most other approaches build in Earth’s atmosphere and then subject the structures to Mars’ atmosphere to see if they survive. Qiu says that taking advantage of Mars’ existing environment makes the whole process “mechanically more efficient.”

This method may also help build structures for NASA’s planned moon base. Qiu says that it’s entirely possible to brew houses there, provided that there’s enough water on the moon, or at least enough recycled water to mix the materials together.

“I always ask myself: Is there any physical law or fundamental mechanism that prevents us from doing this?” Qiu said. “I can’t see any at this point in time. We are confident in scaling it up. It would surprise me if materials for future Martian engineering will not be as diverse as those used in Earth engineering, and biology will certainly contribute.”

title: Android rolling out passkey transfers between password managers
snippet: Google announced today that Android now offers a system-level way to transfer passwords and passkeys between credential managers. more…
fullText:
Google announced today that Android now offers a system-level way to transfer passwords and passkeys between credential managers.

In the past, transferring credentials between password managers involved “downloading them into an unencrypted text file, which left them unprotected on your device.” Meanwhile, passkeys did not originally offer a transfer method, thus requiring you to manually “recreate them across multiple sites and apps.”

Android wants to solve these issues by offering an operating system-backed transfer method:

Start the move: Open your new password manager app and choose the option to import or copy your passwords and passkeys from another provider. The password manager will then hand the task over to Android.

Let Android securely coordinate the data transfer: Android will automatically detect existing password managers on your device and show you which you can import from.

Review and authorize: Once you tap “Continue,” Android will bring you to your existing password manager to select, review, and authorize the transfer. Then your data will be quickly and securely transferred between the apps in just a few seconds.

The screenshots above show the import flow for Google Password Manager.

	

At launch, the transfer experience is supported by Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Other partners can participate by supporting the Credential Manager’s Credentials Transfer API.

title: Annoyingly, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the best advert for an iPhone Fold yet
snippet: Samsung has beaten Apple to the punch, but I’m annoyed that while it’s, in fact, a fantastic device, it’ll only help bolster the sales of the long-rumored iPhone Fold. more…
fullText:
Samsung has beaten Apple to the punch, but I’m annoyed that while it’s, in fact, a fantastic device, it’ll only help bolster the sales of the long-rumored iPhone Fold.

It is a really ironic position for Samsung to find itself in. They have spent years flexing their engineering muscle, burning through iterations, and pushing folding display technology to its absolute limit to lead this space. Although I would argue that some others are doing the “traditional” foldable better now.

Yet despite all the leading, innovating, and market domination, Samsung’s latest flagship wide-body foldable might just end up courting buyers right into Apple’s hands with its iPhone Fold.

The cynic in me sort of feels that, like the Galaxy S25 Edge, getting ahead of Apple was a calculated play to try and court those who are intrigued by the form factor, but maybe not ready to commit to the very compromised 1:1 aspect-ratio’d Z Folds. It’s hard to argue that most folding phones are narrow devices that feel like holding a thick TV remote when closed.

	

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is refreshing compared to Samsung’s previous folding phones because it’s leaning into the entertainment strengths that are supposedly why folding phones are so popular. As with any tech product, there are always going to be compromises, especially when it’s a 2-in-1 experience. Foldables are mature, but the wide body feels like it’s ready to be fully explored. In my mind, a wide-body folding phone is the optimal design. The final form is the tri-fold, which, coincidentally, Samsung has managed to ship to those with deep enough pockets.

Back to the Fold 8: for the most part, many reviews have pointed out how refreshing the Z Fold 8 is despite the fact that Oppo and Google did it first. Samsung has just done it better than anyone thus far. In fact, the Z Fold 8 is easily one of my favorite smartphones of the last few years. As soon as I picked it up, it made sense. I carry it as a secondary phone with a backup SIM. It is my Balatro-playing, web-scrolling, book-reading, movie-watching phone. It’s a small tablet, but also a small phone; there’s literally nothing to hate in my mind.

It probably doesn’t help that Samsung grapples with a fundamentally different challenge than Apple. Samsung is forced to lead the space, combat a wave of aggressive Chinese competitors, and constantly prove why it deserves to be the king of Android hardware. It has to innovate in public, iterate openly, and deal with the early design missteps that come with pioneering new categories.

When everyday people see the Z Fold 8 in public or read reviews praising its new wide-body format, they don’t necessarily think about switching to Android. Instead, they think, “If a folding phone can finally look and feel this good, I can’t wait to see what Apple does with an iPhone Fold.” Samsung is doing all the heavy lifting of educating the public and legitimizing the form factor, only for Apple to potentially reap the rewards.

Cards on the table, I do not like iOS, but I’m under no illusions that Apple will have optimized every single aspect of the experience to maximize the experience on the inner and outer screen. Android’s foldable software has improved significantly over the years, but app optimization across varying aspect ratios on Android remains a hit-or-miss affair depending on whether developers care to update their apps. I’m having a great time, but some things could be better. Apple doesn’t have that problem—when Apple drops a new form factor, developers fall in line almost immediately.

We might have differing opinions on our mobile OS of choice, but 9to5Mac’s own Fernando Silva had some very positive things to say about the wider Galaxy Z Fold 8. While we’ve had folding devices for almost a decade, it’s interesting to see the critiques from an Apple-centric position. I implore you to go check it out.

In hindsight, the iPad Mini was the very first step ahead of a potential iPhone Fold. It’s a compact tablet running iPadOS with multi-window capabilities tailored for small-format tablet displays. The second step was the ultra-thin design language introduced with the iPhone Air. Apple’s undoubted prowess in the tablet space has likely held back some internal ambitions to ship a folding phone. They didn’t want to cannibalize their own iPad Mini sales until the market was mature enough to justify merging those two product lines. The tech market is mature now, so for Apple, it’s clearly time to enter the space.

When an iPhone user looks at a Galaxy Z Fold 8, they see an incredible piece of engineering, but they also see One UI, a different app ecosystem, and a departure from their comfort zone. Instead of acting as a gateway to convert those users to Samsung, the Z Fold 8 serves as a proof of concept.

It proves to the “average user” – a phrase I’m not all that fond of – that folding phones are no longer delicate, awkward experiments with annoying aspect ratios. It reassures them that the hardware is ready, leaving them content to simply wait for Apple to drop its own version. Samsung has built a fantastic device that, annoyingly, has accidentally become the ultimate marketing campaign for Apple’s next big thing.

snippet: As it gears up for launch later this month, Oppo has teased the Find X10 Pro Max with its new addition to the lineup and a triple 200MP camera setup that sounds a bit insane. more…
fullText:
As it gears up for launch later this month, Oppo has teased the Find X10 Pro Max with its new addition to the lineup and a triple 200MP camera setup that sounds a bit insane.

In a post on Weibo, Oppo teases that the Find X10 Pro Max will be the “most powerful” device in its class in regards to imaging this year, and it certainly sounds like it.

As rumored, the post confirms that the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max will come with not one, not two, but three 200MP cameras around back. The main sensor has “DeepPix technology” along with improvements to dynamic range and stabilization, all while managing f/1.5 aperture for increased light capture. The 200MP ultrawide shooter features a 124-degree field-of-view and f/2.2 aperture. The telephoto camera, finally, pairs its 200MP sensor with even better stabilization compared to the main sensor, f/2.1 aperture, and has macro capabilities. The only thing not mentioned is the optical zoom. 

All three cameras can capture in 8K, the post mentions. 

	

It sounds wild, and we’ll find out more soon as the Find X10 series is now confirmed to be launching in September, and more teasers are also set to drop in the coming days, too, the post teases.

title: Sony WH-1000XM4C launch for $299 alongside two more affordable headphones
snippet: As rumored, Sony is reviving its WH-1000XM4 headphones with a new WH-1000XM4C reboot, bringing some new colors to a much more affordable entry to the market compared to the company’s flagship. more…
fullText:
As rumored, Sony is reviving its WH-1000XM4 headphones with a new WH-1000XM4C reboot, bringing some new colors to a much more affordable entry to the market compared to the company’s flagship.

Sony’s flagship headphones are very good, but they’re also pricey. The current WH-1000XM6 retails for $460, though you can often save when buying on deals. But, now, Sony has a more affordable entry in this lineup with the new WH-1000XM4C.

This is a reboot of Sony’s 2020 flagship, which was equipped with USB-C and all of the sound and ANC you’d expect from a high-end pair of over-ear headphones. 

What’s new? Not a whole lot. Sony says to expect the same overall ANC and audio performance, but with the “latest sound tuning.” The hardware is mostly identical, though with new colors including Lavender, Black, and Platinum Silver.

	

They’re available for $299, well below Sony’s current flagship and in line with competitors such as Nothing Headphone (1). It’s borderline impossible to get a brand new pair of WH-1000XM4 nowadays, and even on the used market, you’re still spending around $250 or so in some cases. You might be able to find WH-1000XM5 for less – Amazon has frequent sales – but it’s likely these will see discounts in time too.

Beyond this, Sony is also introducing WH-CH730N and WH-CH530N as even more affordable over-ear headphones. At $179 and $69, they won’t deliver quite the same sound or ANC, but the value is there for certain. 

All three pairs support Fast Pair on Android. WH-1000XM4C will be later this month, with current shipping estimates on pre-orders landing around September 30, while the other two are launching this month.

snippet: The absolute last chance to apply to host an official Side Event during TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is tonight, September 11, at 11:59 p.m. PT.
fullText:

No more extensions. No more chances.

Don’t just bring people together. Create value.

Turn connections into opportunities

Put your team directly in front of founders, investors, customers, partners, and other decision-makers who can unlock your next deal, partnership, investment, hire, or collaboration.

Build relationships that go deeper

Create the kind of conversations that are harder to have on a crowded conference floor — and deepen relationships with the people most relevant to your business.

Put your brand at the center

Own the conversation around a topic your audience cares about and give your brand a meaningful role in the Disrupt ecosystem.

Bring your existing network together while creating opportunities for members to meet new people, exchange ideas, and make valuable connections of their own.

fullText:
Jacob Kastrenakes

 

is The Verge’s executive editor. He has covered tech, policy, and online creators for over a decade.

You only get one chance at a first impression, and getting to introduce Apple’s first folding phone is certainly a strong way to start things off as Apple’s CEO. On The Vergecast today, we’re talking all about Apple’s launch event: how John Ternus did in his first appearance as CEO, what we make of the new iPhones, and whether Apple is stepping into dangerous territory with its new AI features on the Apple Watch.

First up, Allison Johnson joins me to discuss the new iPhones, which she had a chance to test in Cupertino. Both of us have some questions about the new variable aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro — and whether the real upgrade simply lies in the wider aperture, not the ability to stop it down. Then we dig into the iPhone Duo and how Apple decided to pick and choose the best parts of Android foldables.

After that, Victoria Song joins me to discuss the new Apple Watches, which she also had a chance to test out. We dive into the new sensor array and whether it allows for legitimately new metrics or just more vibesy health data. And then we both break down a little while figuring out what it means that Apple added the ability for both new Apple Watches to have an always-on microphone that summarizes all of your conversations.

This is an Apple-packed episode, so from there we jump to a special segment with Nilay Patel and David Imel, who speak with AI researcher CJ Trowbridge about the state of running local LLMs on the Mac. Finally, it’s the long awaited return of the Thunder Round, as we race through stories so that Allison can make it to the airport. We’re chatting OpenAI math drama, digital ocarinas, and more.

title: Snap adds social event planning feature with Snapchat Plans
snippet: Snap is launching a new mobile app feature called Snapchat Plans. While it may sound like a new subscription service, Plans is actually a set of features that encourages hanging out in person. more…
fullText:
Snap is launching a new mobile app feature called Snapchat Plans. While it may sound like a new subscription service, Plans is actually a set of features that encourages hanging out in person.

Snap wants Snapchat users to meet up and hang out

“IRL meet-ups often start from a simple spark of conversation: A message turns into an idea, an idea turns into a plan, and time spent together becomes a memory,” Snap says.

“That’s why today we are introducing Snapchat Plans, a new suite of features that gives Snapchatters a new way to create, share, and manage their real-world plans with friends, all in one place.”

Snap highlights three current features, and one more coming soon, around Snapchat Plans: 

Send and receive invitations from mutual friends 

Track key details like time, date, and attendees 

Keep plans in one easy-to-find place

And soon, Snapchatters will be able to create events directly within a chat

The company explains how creating Snapchat Plans works in the app:

Snapchatters can add a title, choose a date and time, invite up to 200 friends, and personalize their event with dynamic Bitmoji-powered cover art that automatically updates as the plan comes together. Invitations are then delivered directly within a one-on-one chat with each invited friend, where guests can quickly RSVP with Going, Maybe, or Can’t Go without interrupting the conversation.

Here’s how it looks:

Importantly, Snap says that Snapchat Plans are both private and invite-only, so everything stays between friends. You can learn much more from Snap’s announcement post here.

Earlier this summer, Snap added a new Now Playing map feature to Snapchat.

Not a Snapchat user? Apple has its digital event planning service called Invites.
